issues.title: codex exec "<prompt>" hangs indefinitely when stdin is a non-TTY pipe with no writer

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: windows-os
labels.description: Issues related to Codex on Windows systems

labels.name: exec
labels.description: Issues related to the `codex exec` subcommand

issues.body:
Summary
When codex exec is invoked with a prompt as an argument from a non-interactive child shell (e.g. a CI runner, an editor's task runner, or another agent that spawns child processes), it hangs forever waiting for stdin EOF — even though the prompt was passed via the positional argument and stdin is never used.

This is a deterministic deadlock, not a flake. Reproducible on Windows 11 with codex-cli 0.128.0 and prior versions.

Repro

# Inside a non-interactive child shell (here: a parent process spawning powershell.exe with piped stdio):
& codex exec "Reply OK only."
# Hangs. Process has 0% CPU. No `docker.exe` MCP child spawned. No rollout
# file written under ~/.codex/sessions. Stays hung until manually killed.
The same call with stdin redirected from NUL completes in ~11 s with normal output:


cmd /c "codex exec `"Reply OK only.`" < NUL"
# OK
# tokens used: 19,542
Diagnosis
Stack inspection (no MCP child, 0 CPU, no rollout output, only stderr line Reading additional input from stdin...) plus --help text confirm that exec reads stdin when it is detected as a non-TTY pipe and appends the contents as a <stdin> block after the prompt argument:

If stdin is piped and a prompt is also provided, stdin is appended as a <stdin> block

In a non-TTY child shell with inherited but unwritten stdio, read() on stdin blocks indefinitely because the writer side is open but no bytes ever arrive and no EOF is delivered.

Why this matters
Standard for tools that spawn codex exec programmatically (Claude Code, GitHub Actions runners, nohup, Start-Process without -RedirectStandardInput NUL, agent orchestrators).
The codex app-server path (used by the Claude Code Codex plugin) is unaffected because the plugin actively writes JSONL and closes stdin.
Indistinguishable from a real hang/network problem from the caller's perspective — no logs, no rollout, no exit code, just silence.
Common mitigations (timeouts, retries) make the symptom worse: the next retry hangs the same way.
Proposed fix (one of)
When a prompt argument is present and stdin is a non-TTY pipe, only read stdin if data is actually available within a short timeout (e.g. poll for readability for 200 ms; if nothing, treat as empty and proceed).
Add an explicit --no-stdin flag (or invert the default to require - for stdin reads), so non-interactive callers can opt out cleanly.
Document the failure mode and the workaround prominently in codex exec --help, and emit a stderr warning after, say, 5 s of waiting so the deadlock is at least detectable.
Option 1 is the friendliest default and matches what most callers expect when they pass a prompt argument. Option 2 is the smallest behavior change.

Workaround (current)
POSIX shells: codex exec "<prompt>" < /dev/null
Windows cmd: codex exec "<prompt>" < NUL
Windows PowerShell child: cmd /c "codex exec "<prompt>" < NUL" (PowerShell has no clean pipe-to-NUL syntax)
Or wrap once: a codex-safe.cmd shim that forwards args and redirects from NUL.
Environment
Windows 11 26200 (Home)
codex-cli 0.128.0 (npm install path: C:\Users\<u>\AppData\Roaming\npm\codex.cmd → node_modules\@openai\codex-win32-x64\vendor\x86_64-pc-windows-msvc\codex\codex.exe)
Reproduces from PowerShell child invoked by Claude Code's Bash tool (PowerShell runs & codex exec "<prompt>" with inherited piped stdio)
Also reproduces from Start-Process powershell -ArgumentList ... without -RedirectStandardInput NUL

issues.body:
## Summary

Existing ChatGPT conversations intermittently fail to load in the Windows desktop app (Windows package `OpenAI.Codex 26.1013.4894.0`). The user has experienced this twice. During the failure the same conversations remain accessible in the mobile app over LTE. On the latest occurrence, sending a prompt from mobile was followed by recovery of conversation loading on desktop.

This mobile-to-desktop recovery pattern is observed, not a proven causal mechanism. Mobile changes both client and network, so the evidence does not isolate client state, request-specific backend handling, or routing differences.

## Latest occurrence

2026-10-21, around **11:12 KST / 02:12 UTC**. A separate earlier 09:xx local network problem is explicitly out of scope.

There were **13 logged failed requests between 02:04:44 and 02:17:08 UTC** with `status=500` and a specific response body:

```json
{"detail":"Can't load conversation [redacted]"}
```

These are request failures, not 13 separate outages:
- Conversation A: 7 failures across initialization and both conversation-read routes.
- Conversation B: 4 failures across initialization, conversation retrieval and paginated message retrieval.
- Conversation C: named in 2 failures while retrieving `/pins`.

Routes included:
- `POST /conversation/init`
- `GET /conversations/{conversation_id}`
- `GET /conversation/{conversation_id}`
- `GET /conversations/{conversation_id}/messages`
- `GET /pins`

## Timeline and log evidence

All timestamps below are UTC on 2026-10-21. IDs and local paths are redacted.

```text
02:00:13.251 chatgpt_conversation_refetch_completed conversationId=[A]
             currentNodeApplied=true statusAfter=idle
02:04:44.748 sa_server_request_failed method=post
             routePattern=/conversation/init status=500
             errorMessage={"detail":"Can't load conversation [A]"}
02:12:36.860 sa_server_request_failed method=post
             routePattern=/conversation/init status=500
             errorMessage={"detail":"Can't load conversation [A]"}
02:23:39.673 chatgpt_conversation_refetch_completed conversationId=[A]
             currentNodeApplied=false statusBefore=error statusAfter=error
02:28:24.409 chatgpt_conversation_refetch_completed conversationId=[A]
             currentNodeApplied=false statusAfter=error
02:28:29.111 chatgpt_conversation_refetch_completed conversationId=[A]
             currentNodeApplied=false statusAfter=error
```

The lines above are abbreviated extracts, not verbatim complete log lines. The completed refetches retained an error state. We cannot establish from these fields alone whether this is a UI recovery defect or retained conversation execution state.

## Observed reproduction / recovery sequence

1. Open an existing conversation on Windows desktop.
2. Conversation loading fails.
3. Open the same conversation in the mobile app over LTE: it works.
4. Submit a prompt from mobile.
5. Desktop conversation loading subsequently recovers.

The user reports two occurrences of the desktop/mobile discrepancy. The latest prompt/recovery sequence was reported by the user; its exact send/recovery timestamps were not captured independently.

## Local checks

- Installed Windows package: `OpenAI.Codex 26.1013.4894.0`.
- Read-only `PRAGMA quick_check` passed for `state_5.sqlite`, `thread_history_1.sqlite` and `logs_2.sqlite`. These checks do not verify cloud conversation storage.
- No contemporaneous ChatGPT/Codex application crash or hang event was found in Windows event logs.
- Subsequent read-only `read_thread` calls returned one recent turn for all three affected conversations. This does not prove complete historical integrity or that the UI had recovered at the time of those reads.
- Relevant raw desktop logs were preserved locally with SHA-256 hashes.

## Requested investigation

Please correlate conversation initialization, paginated reads and pins failures, and inspect desktop recovery after a refetch succeeds. In particular:
- Can a new mobile message change shared conversation state or emit an update that unblocks the desktop?
- Does desktop initialization/pagination use a different path from mobile?
- Why does the logged error state persist after completed refetches?

OpenAI Help Center's AI-assisted support mentioned an active incident affecting Conversations and Codex in ChatGPT Desktop, but did not establish that this recurrence shares that incident's cause. It could not provide a case number or human handoff and suggested in-app feedback or this issue tracker.

Private conversation identifiers, titles, email, credentials, message content and local paths are intentionally omitted from this public issue. Conversation identifiers and fuller extracted evidence can be supplied through an appropriate private OpenAI support channel if needed.

issues.body:
### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

0.162.0-alpha.17.2

### What subscription do you have?

Pro Max $500

### What platform is your computer?

arm

### What issue are you seeing?

## Environment

- Bundled Codex CLI: 0.162.0-alpha.17.2
- macOS / Apple Silicon
- Native Sign in with ChatGPT
- Model: gpt-6.1-sol
- Reasoning effort: high
- Reproduced with both WebSocket and HTTPS/SSE

Configuration:
model_context_window = 1000000
model_auto_compact_token_limit = 900000

Runtime effective window: 828400
Runtime auto-compaction threshold: 784800

## Problem

Historical reasoning already represented in server input usage is estimated again by the client, inflating the counter used for auto-compaction.

In a long session, the UI showed 459164 tokens used, approximately 55%, while compaction started:

459164 server-reported tokens
+324498 estimated historical reasoning tokens
+4737 estimated pending tool-result tokens
=788399 client compaction count

This crossed the effective threshold of 784800. The arithmetic was reconstructed exactly from the recorded history. Compaction took approximately 199 seconds.

## Minimal reproduction

1. Start an ephemeral app-server thread with gpt-6.1-sol and effort=high.
2. Ask it to find the smallest positive integer x satisfying:
   x mod 7=2, x mod 11=3, x mod 13=5.
   Request only the answer, without tools.
3. Wait for completion, then send another user message requesting only OK.
4. Compare server usage / thread/tokenUsage/updated with the core post-sampling token counter.

Observed results:

| Transport | Server total | Client compaction count | Extra estimate |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| HTTPS/SSE | 20815 | 21059 | 244 |
| WebSocket | 20830 | 21098 | 268 |

In the SSE capture, both responses returned reasoning.context="all_turns".

The second response's per-item attribution reported 81 input tokens for the earlier reasoning item, confirming it was already counted by the server. Its encrypted length was 2168 bytes, but the client added another 244-token estimate.

## Signal observations

Successful native codex doctor WebSocket handshakes reported:
reasoning header: false

The inspected code adds historical reasoning estimates when server_reasoning_included=false. It relies on x-reasoning-included, while the effective response.reasoning.context="all_turns" is not used to correct that flag.

## Expected behavior

Use server-reported usage plus genuinely new local items, without estimating already-counted historical reasoning again.

Please investigate whether the per-response effective reasoning context or usage attribution should determine this accounting contract, instead of relying exclusively on a handshake/response header.

## Limits

The original session's raw headers and per-item attribution were not captured. The entire historical estimate cannot be equated one-for-one with actual duplicate server tokens.

The minimal reproduction directly demonstrates double-accounting. No answer-quality benchmark or installed-patch comparison was performed.

Related reports: #39767 and #49026.

No credentials, private prompts, local paths, account/session identifiers, or raw business logs are included.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. Start an ephemeral app-server thread with gpt-6.1-sol and effort=high.
2. Ask it to find the smallest positive integer x satisfying:
   x mod 7=2, x mod 11=3, x mod 13=5.
   Request only the answer, without tools.
3. Wait for completion, then send another user message requesting only OK.
4. Compare server usage / thread/tokenUsage/updated with the core post-sampling token counter.

Observed results:

| Transport | Server total | Client compaction count | Extra estimate |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| HTTPS/SSE | 20815 | 21059 | 244 |
| WebSocket | 20830 | 21098 | 268 |

In the SSE capture, both responses returned reasoning.context="all_turns".

The second response's per-item attribution reported 81 input tokens for the earlier reasoning item, confirming it was already counted by the server. Its encrypted length was 2168 bytes, but the client added another 244-token estimate.

## Signal observations

Successful native codex doctor WebSocket handshakes reported:
reasoning header: false

The inspected code adds historical reasoning estimates when server_reasoning_included=false. It relies on x-reasoning-included, while the effective response.reasoning.context="all_turns" is not used to correct that flag.

### What is the expected behavior?

Use server-reported usage plus genuinely new local items, without estimating already-counted historical reasoning again.

Please investigate whether the per-response effective reasoning context or usage attribution should determine this accounting contract, instead of relying exclusively on a handshake/response header.

issues.body:
### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

Windows package: `OpenAI.Codex_26.818.5229.0_x64__2p2nqsd0c76g0`

Bundled child-session runtime: `0.149.0-alpha.4.1`

Workspace dependencies shown by the app: `26.819.11345`

### What subscription do you have?

ChatGPT Pro

### What platform is your computer?

Microsoft Windows 11 Pro `10.0.26200`, x64

### What issue are you seeing?

A parent task running through Codex Desktop Voice/realtime coordination had effective Full Access:

```text
approval_policy = never
sandbox_policy = danger-full-access
permission_profile = disabled
```

All visible configuration layers (User config, project config, and Admin config) also showed **Never ask for approval** and **Full access**. The global config contained:

```toml
approval_policy = "never"
sandbox_mode = "danger-full-access"
```

The parent then used the official `create_thread` tool to create a project task with:

```json
{
  "target": {
    "type": "project",
    "environment": { "type": "worktree" }
  }
}
```

The call did not contain a permission override. The current `create_thread` tool schema does not expose one.

Nevertheless, the worktree child started its first turn with:

```text
approval_policy = on-request
approvals_reviewer = user
sandbox_policy = managed / restricted workspace
network = restricted
permission_profile = managed
```

The child immediately displayed manual approval dialogs for routine operations such as `git fetch` and a read-only WSL command. Its task-level UI showed **Approve for me**, even though the parent and every default configuration layer were Full Access. The user did not select that mode.

The persisted task records confirmed the divergence:

```text
parent: approval_mode=never, sandbox_policy.type=disabled
child:  approval_mode=on-request, sandbox_policy.type=managed
```

This appears intermittent rather than a deterministic default. In a sample of the 20 most recent delegated child tasks stored locally, 18 started with `never/disabled` and 2 started with `on-request/managed`.

Changing the child back to Full Access while its first turn was running updated pending app state, but the active turn retained its original managed permission snapshot until a later turn.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. On Codex Desktop for Windows, set User, project, and Admin defaults to **Never ask for approval** + **Full access**.
2. Start a parent task and verify its effective turn context is:
   `never / danger-full-access / disabled`.
3. From that parent, call the official `create_thread` tool for a saved Git project with:
   `environment: { type: "worktree" }`.
4. Let the child begin its automatically started first turn.
5. Inspect the child's task permission selector, first `turn_context`, and persisted task row.
6. Intermittently observe that the child starts as:
   `on-request / user / managed`.
7. Ask the child to run `git fetch` or another operation outside its restricted writable roots.
8. Observe a manual approval dialog.

### What is the expected behavior?

A child created with `create_thread` should inherit the effective Full Access mode from the host/defaults or the Full Access parent:

```text
approval_policy = never
sandbox_policy = danger-full-access
permission_profile = disabled
```

If permission inheritance isn't intended, `create_thread` should expose an explicit permission profile or create the child paused so the user can choose before its first turn starts.

Permission changes made while a turn is active should either apply to subsequent tool calls or clearly state that they only apply to the next turn.

### Additional information

This is related to, but distinct from:

- #25590 — permission drift when resuming an existing thread. This report occurs at **new worktree-child creation**.
- #25810 — broader new-thread/handoff behavior where the reported host-level state was `guardian-approvals`. Here the parent, host selection, and all config layers were verified Full Access at creation time.
- #33282 — `create_thread` failing to inherit **Auto Approval**. This report reproduces the same creation boundary with **Full Access / never / danger-full-access**.

Official configuration references:

- https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/config-file/config-basic
- https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/config-file/config-advanced

Thread IDs, repository names, account details, and local paths are omitted. I can provide focused redacted task records and rollout excerpts if needed.

issues.title: [Windows] Recent task history returns empty items: rollout uses original thread ID but projection rows use another UUID

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: windows-os
labels.description: Issues related to Codex on Windows systems

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

labels.name: session
labels.description: Issues involving session (thread) management, resuming, forking, naming, archiving

issues.body:
### What version of the Codex App are you using?

Windows installed package: `OpenAI.Codex 26.901.6511.0` (queried via Get-AppxPackage, not the About dialog). The affected rollout's session_meta reports `cli_version: 0.153.4`.

### What subscription do you have?

Not verified during this investigation.

### What platform is your computer?

Windows 11 Pro, 10.0.22631, x64.

### What issue are you seeing?

Recent conversation messages repeatedly disappear from the desktop history of a long-running local task. The messages still exist in the raw rollout AND in the history database, but recent history rows are keyed under a different thread ID from the one used to open/read the task.

The desktop `read_thread` tool returns completed turn metadata with `items: []`, including for a completed turn whose final assistant message is present in both storage layers. The missing message tells the user the task is blocked and asks them to free memory before continuing, so the missing history hides an actionable next step. This is an observed workload message, not evidence that memory pressure caused the history bug.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

The triggering transition is not yet reproducible on demand. This is a read-only diagnostic reproduction on an affected existing task, observed September 7, 2026:

1. Open the affected long-running local task. The user reports a missing recent section of its conversation, and reports this has happened before.
2. Call the desktop `read_thread` tool with its original ID, `turnLimit: 8`, `includeOutputs: true`, and `maxOutputCharsPerItem: 10000`.
3. Observe completed recent turns with timestamps and durations but empty `items` arrays. A later repeat also returns empty items for newer turns.
4. Locate the missing final message in the raw rollout at `2026-09-07T09:01:56.287Z`, followed by a normal `task_complete` event at ordinal `38877`.
5. Compare the thread ID used in `state_5.sqlite`, the rollout metadata, and `thread_history_1.sqlite`. The IDs disagree as detailed below.

No database or original rollout was modified in this investigation. No restart, forced crash, or recovery command was attempted. Earlier recovery/history of this task has not been reconstructed, so this report does not claim that a particular native operation created the split.

### What is the expected behavior?

Reading/opening a task should recover its persisted messages under a consistent thread identity. If storage contains conflicting identities, surface a recoverable history error instead of silently presenting empty turn bodies. A supported reconciliation/rebuild path would help.

### Additional information

Identifiers below are abbreviated as A (the original visible task ID) and B (a different UUID appearing as a suffix in its current rollout filename). Local usernames, project paths, and unrelated conversation contents are omitted.

Observed storage mapping:

```text
state_5.sqlite / threads:
  id = A
  rollout_path = sessions/2026/09/07/rollout-<timestamp>-A_B.jsonl
  No threads row exists for B.

Current rollout first record:
  type = session_meta
  ordinal = 30942
  payload.id = A
  payload.forked_from_id = null
  payload.cli_version = 0.153.4

thread_history_1.sqlite / thread_history_projection_state:
  A: next_rollout_byte_offset = 420401846
     next_rollout_ordinal = 30949
  B: next_rollout_byte_offset = 108246479
     next_rollout_ordinal = 38950

Older physical rollout named ...-A.jsonl:
  size = 420401846 bytes (exactly A's saved projection offset)

Recent missing completed turn, starting at ordinal 38856:
  thread_turns: exists under B, not A
  thread_items under B:
    2 agentMessage, 2 commandExecution, 1 reasoning
  The final agentMessage text is intact under B.

read_thread(A) for this same completed turn:
  status = completed
  items = []
```

At the inspected snapshot, A's latest projected agentMessage was at ordinal `30936`, while B's was at `38943`. The task can continue running even while history reads return empty bodies.

This suggests an identity mismatch between task/rollout resolution and projected item lookup. That is a diagnostic hypothesis, not a confirmed code-level root cause. In particular, this evidence does not establish whether the filename suffix is being interpreted as an identity, or whether an earlier recovery operation introduced inconsistent state.

Related: #42387 describes a cursor left at an older rollout's EOF after file rotation. This report adds a distinct observation: newer turns and item bodies are successfully materialized under B while the visible task and session_meta still identify A. #42197 and #42241 describe explicit ordinal mismatch errors; no matching projection/ordinal-error lines were found in the inspected September 7 desktop text logs here.

Full rollout/database files are not attached because they contain private project content. The issue is supported by read-only SQL results and a recovered message, rather than an assumption that the original data was deleted.

The user explicitly authorized the site and set its browsing permission to Always allow in the Browser settings. The setting is visibly saved. Read-only inspection confirms three facts:

2. Global browser config: the target origin is in `origins.allowed` and is absent from `origins.denied`.
3. The active conversation's browser permission record still includes the same origin in `origins.denied`.

Attempting to read the already-open tab through the supported browser tool fails before page content is returned:

> Reason: A saved user permission setting blocks this action.

The error identifies the target origin and prohibits alternative access routes. No workaround was attempted and no permission files were edited. The agent cannot verify who or what originally produced the saved denial.

## Current-state reproduction

1. In the active conversation, an existing target-site tab is open.
2. Browser settings show Always allow for the target origin; both global rule stores confirm allow.
3. Ask the agent to read the existing tab through the supported browser tool.

The initial sequence that created the denial is unknown, so this is a reproduction from the existing blocked state rather than a clean-install reproduction.

Please provide a supported UI or documented tool action to revoke this conversation's saved denial and request permission again. If the global Always allow setting intentionally does not affect existing conversation denials, please expose the stricter rule and its recovery control in the UI.

issues.title: [macOS Desktop] @ browser discovery self-probes trigger untrusted-process-ancestry warnings

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

issues.body:
### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

26.1013.40934 (build 20770), production channel; desktop app installed as ChatGPT.app, bundle identifier com.openai.codex.

### What subscription do you have?

Omitted for privacy; this report concerns local browser discovery and native process validation.

### What platform is your computer?

macOS 27.0.1, Apple Silicon / arm64. Chrome 155.0.8059.85.

### What issue are you seeing?

Opening the @ browser/app picker repeatedly produces native-pipe trust-rejection warnings even when browser discovery is functioning. A focused diagnostic identified the desktop main process itself as the discovery client.

Sanitized message (timestamps and all local identifiers omitted):
```text
[browser-use-native-pipe-server] browser-use native pipe rejected socket peer reason=untrusted-process-ancestry
```

Read-only inspection of the installed app indicates that the Chrome-tab mention discovery scans same-user sockets in a shared native-browser discovery directory, connects to candidates, and only then checks getInfo to determine whether a candidate is a Chrome extension. That directory also contains in-process IAB / MCP Apps endpoints.

The native authorizer checks whether the connecting process descends from the server process before checking signing identity. A process is not its own descendant, so the app probing its own endpoint produces the same ancestry-rejection reason. This appears to be an interaction between endpoint discovery and the ancestry rule, rather than evidence that the browser connector signature is damaged.

Scope: this report establishes the self-probe warning path. It does not establish that all intermittent missing-browser or disconnected-browser symptoms have this cause. Normal browser inventory succeeded during and after this investigation.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. Start the macOS desktop app with the Chrome integration available and a normal local chat with built-in browser backends initialized.
2. Type @ in the chat input to open the app/browser picker; no message needs to be sent.
3. Observe the desktop native-pipe logs. Close and reopen the picker to repeat the scan.
4. Compare the discovery client process with the desktop main process. In the observed run, a temporary same-user, owner-only diagnostic listener recorded the peer PID through macOS LOCAL_PEERPID during two picker scans. In both cases it mapped to the desktop main process; the matching rejection messages appeared in the same scan windows. The observer recorded only process attribution, did not collect page content, and was removed afterward.

Isolated control using the original, unmodified browser-use-peer-authorization.node and the app-bundled signed Node runtime:
```js
const authorizer = require(process.env.AUTH_ADDON);
// In an independent test server connection handler:
const result = authorizer.authorizeSocketPeer(socket._handle.fd, false);
```

| Connecting process | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Same signed Node process connecting to its own test listener | authorized: false; untrusted-process-ancestry |
| Signed Node child connecting to the parent test listener | authorized: true; signingIdentifier: node |
| System/Homebrew Node child (control) | authorized: false; missing-code-signing-identity |

The test listeners were separate from the application endpoints and were cleaned up. The existing validator was not changed or bypassed.

### What is the expected behavior?

Opening the @ picker should discover supported browser providers without probing the app’s own protected endpoints as if they were external Chrome providers and emitting misleading trust-rejection warnings.

Please distinguish expected discovery filtering from actual failed browser connections. If in-process self-connections are intentional, handle that narrow case deliberately while preserving signing checks, descendant-process restrictions for other clients, browser permissions, and chat isolation. Suggested regression cases: same-process discovery, trusted child client, unrelated same-user client, and unrelated native-browser endpoint.

### Additional information

Related: #54720 reports a separate shared-server topology with the same rejection reason. This report is specifically about desktop-main-process self-probes during @ picker discovery; a common root cause with shared-server or remote failures has not been established.

The desktop app and bundled Chrome native host both passed signature verification outside the agent sandbox. Signature checking inside the restricted sandbox initially gave misleading failures, so those results were not treated as proof of corruption. The app updater reported no available production update at investigation time.

No app code, native authorizer, browser manifest, or trust policy was modified. No browser security controls were disabled. Unrelated local installation anomalies are intentionally excluded.

Privacy: no account/subscription details, usernames, home paths, hostnames, process IDs, socket names, chat/session IDs, browsing history, website titles/URLs, full logs, or diagnostic attachments are included. Only the generic error text, product versions, reproduction procedure, and summarized control results are published.

issues.title: Retained images exceed Responses WebSocket size limit: five retries before HTTP fallback; 16 MiB ± 1 byte reproduction

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

labels.name: connectivity
labels.description: Issues involving networking or endpoint connectivity problems (disconnections)

issues.body:
### What version of the Codex App are you using?

Desktop bundle: `26.1013.40934`, build `20770` (read from the installed app's Info.plist).
Installed bundled CLI reports `0.163.0-alpha.10.2`. The already-running process was not restarted or binary-matched during diagnosis, so this does not establish its exact build.

### What subscription do you have?

ChatGPT Pro, using ChatGPT sign-in.

### What platform is your computer?

macOS 26.6.2, Apple Silicon (arm64).

### What issue are you seeing?

An existing image-heavy conversation repeatedly displayed:

```text
Reconnecting 5/5
stream disconnected before completion: websocket closed by server before response.completed
```

Each WebSocket handshake succeeded, but the client retried the full request five times before falling back to HTTP. HTTP then succeeded and the conversation resumed.

This is related to #55317 and #38846. This report adds an independent, minimal **JSON-whitespace boundary control at 16 MiB ± 1 byte**, and focuses on byte-aware preflight/fallback and loss of Close-code diagnostics. It does not reproduce or claim the heartbeat timeout discussed in #55317.

#### Original incident evidence

On 2026-10-21 (UTC+08:00):

- 10:07:29: WebSocket connected successfully.
- 10:07:43–10:08:02: retries 1/5 through 5/5, each with the error above.
- Reconnection logs contain `non-incremental request reason="connection_closed"`.
- 10:08:08: `falling back to HTTP`.
- The subsequent HTTP request log records `pre_compression_bytes=19094865 post_compression_bytes=11130448` using zstd.
- 10:08:15: HTTP 200; assistant output and tool execution subsequently resumed.

The HTTP body's uncompressed size is **19,094,865 bytes (18.21 MiB)**. This is a measured HTTP fallback body, not a captured byte-for-byte copy of the failed WebSocket message.

A read-only reconstruction using the last `compacted.replacement_history` plus subsequent `response_item` records, up to the turn's start, found:

- 152 history items.
- **9 retained inline user images: 18,189,822 data-URL bytes (17.35 MiB)**.
- Serialized reconstructed history: 18,972,342 bytes, before additional runtime instructions/tool schemas and any runtime filtering.
- The most recent recorded compaction had retained historical images; the images alone exceeded the boundary measured below.

The historical failure's Close code was not preserved. Therefore, attributing that original incident to size rejection is a strongly supported inference, **not a claim that its actual Close frame was captured as 1009**.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

#### Controlled transport test (completed)

Using a separate Python standard-library WebSocket probe, connect to the same authenticated Responses endpoint, `wss://chatgpt.com/backend-api/codex/responses`, through the existing local HTTP CONNECT proxy.

Serialize this synthetic warmup event as compact UTF-8 JSON:

```json
{"type":"response.create","model":"gpt-6-astra","instructions":"Diagnostic warmup.","input":[],"tools":[],"store":false,"generate":false}
```

For each target size, append ASCII spaces **after the closing JSON brace**, so the message remains valid JSON with identical semantic content:

```python
payload = json.dumps(event, separators=(",", ":")).encode("utf-8")
payload += b" " * (target_bytes - len(payload))
assert len(payload) == target_bytes
```

Use a fresh WebSocket connection per case. Send one logical Text message in 64 KiB continuation fragments, with FIN only on the last fragment. Mask client frames and respond to server Ping frames. Do not negotiate permessage-deflate. Read the raw server Close frame as well as response events.

| Exact logical message bytes | Upgrade | Result | Total elapsed |
| ---: | --- | --- | ---: |
| 1,024 | HTTP 101 | `response.completed` | 3.32 s |
| **16,777,215 (16 MiB − 1)** | HTTP 101 | **`response.completed`** | 6.68 s |
| **16,777,217 (16 MiB + 1)** | HTTP 101 | **Received Close 1009, empty reason**; no response events | 7.11 s |

All three cases used the same endpoint, account, model, proxy and selected upstream node. Only the trailing whitespace byte count changed. No original images, prompts or conversation history were transmitted by the probes. `generate=false` produced no model output.

This brackets a size-sensitive rejection within two bytes around 16 MiB on this route. It does not establish the exact inclusive configured limit, which backend/edge component enforces it, or limits for other endpoints. Fragmentation does not bypass the logical-message limit.

#### Network context

Clash uses mixed port 7897. The desktop and backend processes inherited HTTP/HTTPS proxy variables plus a SOCKS5 ALL_PROXY value. Matching local socket ports against the Clash connection table confirmed active backend connections to chatgpt.com using HTTP CONNECT. The synthetic probes explicitly used that same HTTP CONNECT proxy without changing network configuration.

Below-boundary success and above-boundary Close 1009 on the same route give a more specific explanation than a general proxy outage. They do not prove that every reconnect error has this cause.

### What is the expected behavior?

- Consider a serialized-byte budget separately from token/context limits, including retained inline image data.
- When the request is known to exceed the supported WebSocket budget, select a supported transport or recovery path before repeatedly uploading it.
- Preserve Close code/reason and classify a received 1009 as non-transient for an unchanged payload; avoid retrying the same oversized request five times.
- Provide an actionable error and a supported way to recover an affected conversation without losing useful context.

HTTP fallback already recovered this incident. The issue is the avoidable retry loop and misleading generic network diagnosis.

### Additional information

The public source's `Message::Close(_)` branch returns a generic error without including the code/reason:
https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/4ebc485ca321243727539187169425fcf972f2c4/codex-rs/codex-api/src/endpoint/responses_websocket.rs#L945

The probe uses the documented warmup behavior:
https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/websocket-mode

No original screenshots, private prompts, raw rollouts, account/thread/turn identifiers, credentials, personal filesystem paths or proxy server addresses are included in this report. Original history and application/network settings were not modified.

prs.title: Preserve code cell response metadata in rollout traces
prs.body:
Preserve code cell response metadata in rollout traces

## Why

Reducing code cell lifecycle events discarded their response payload references and lost the initial response status when the runtime status changed.

## What changed

Store the initial response status and separate raw payload IDs for the initial response and final result on `CodeCell`. Carry payload references through queued lifecycle events so they survive replay when the source item arrives later.

## Testing

Extend lifecycle tests to verify distinct initial and final payload IDs and the preserved initial status for yielded cells that complete and failed cells whose lifecycle events precede their source item.

prs.title: Share prepared MCP tool definitions across sessions
prs.body:
Share prepared MCP tool definitions across sessions

## Why

Sessions using the same MCP catalog can repeat schema normalization and retain duplicate tool specifications.

## What changed

Split immutable MCP tool metadata and normalized specifications from per-handler caches, and reuse matching definitions within each `McpManager`. Require matching tool metadata, agent-plugin mode, and schema budget before reuse.

Keep shared definitions behind weak references and prune expired entries on cache misses so completed sessions do not keep their schemas alive. Build definitions outside the shared index lock.

prs.title: Avoid redundant clones when sending app-server notifications
prs.body:
Avoid redundant clones when sending app-server notifications

## Why

Targeted notification delivery and broadcast routing clone the message for every recipient, then discard the original.

## What changed

Use `std::iter::repeat_n` to move the original message to the last recipient, avoiding one clone per nonempty recipient list while preserving delivery behavior.

## Testing

Expand notification tests to cover empty, single, and multiple recipient lists, checking payloads, target order, and shared timestamps. Add broadcast coverage for zero, one, and two eligible recipients, verifying that uninitialized clients, clients without the required experimental API support, and clients that opted out are skipped.

## Why

Disabled or failed protected shell snapshots prevent commands from running when credential masking is enabled.

## Testing

Verify the warning, successful execution with restored credentials, continued filesystem sandbox and network policy enforcement, and masking recovery after snapshot storage is repaired.

prs.title: Resolve MCP backend identity from runtime events in rollout traces
prs.body:
Resolve MCP backend identity from runtime events in rollout traces

## Why

MCP callable namespaces and tool names can differ from their backend identities or match built-in tool names. Classifying calls by name can misidentify MCP calls and incorrectly parse namespaced `write_stdin` calls as terminal operations.

## What changed

Resolve `ToolCallKind::Mcp` from the runtime invocation's server and tool as soon as the runtime starts, before MCP correlation assignment. Preserve the caller-facing summary and raw invocation, and skip built-in runtime handling for MCP calls.

Only create dispatch-based `write_stdin` terminal operations for calls without a namespace.

## Testing

Add replay regression coverage for prefixed and unprefixed MCP aliases, names that match built-in tools, and `write_stdin` arguments with and without a session ID. Verify backend classification, preserved callable identity and dispatch lifecycle, and the absence of terminal operations and sessions.

type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

issues.body:
This EPIC tracks a series of investigations as to whether there is value in AST aware file read, search, or codebase mapping.

AST aware tools can be used to 1) more precisely read method bounds with a single tool call, reducing turns from misaligned reads, and reducing noise in tokens, 2) navigate to usages and definitions of syntax elements via syntax aware search (AST grep), and 3) compress high level context about the codebase, such as the location of specific classes and their members by collapsing code down to just top level classes and types and their children's signatures.

```
 1. tilth (Rust)
  tilth is built specifically to generate a structural outline of a codebase. It uses Tree-sitter under the hood but ships as a single binary. It gives you an
  immediate map of the repository's symbols.
   * Installation: cargo install tilth (or download the binary from their releases)
   * Usage:
       * tilth map . (Prints a tree-like overview of the whole codebase structure)
       * tilth read <file> (Prints the structural outline of a specific file)


  2. glyph (Go)
  glyph is another single-binary tool designed to generate clean, multi-file symbol maps. It's excellent if you want to quickly see the skeleton of a
  directory of source code.
   * Installation: go install github.com/benmyles/glyph@latest
   * Usage: glyph cli './**/*.go' (Prints a tree of functions, structs, and methods)


  3. ast-grep (sg) (Rust)
  While primarily known as a structural search-and-replace tool, ast-grep is the industry standard for distributing Tree-sitter as a fast, single binary. You
  can use it to extract landmarks via the command line.
   * Installation: brew install ast-grep or cargo install ast-grep
   * Usage: You can write quick one-liners to extract specific symbols (like all function declarations) and format the output.


  4. The Classic: Universal Ctags (C)
  If you truly want zero modern dependencies, u-ctags is the classic UNIX approach. It uses a hybrid regex/parser approach rather than full AST generation, so
  it's incredibly fast and supports over 100 languages out of the box.
   * Installation: brew install universal-ctags
   * Usage: ctags -R --output-format=json .
   * Note: It outputs a flat list of symbols (or JSON) rather than a visual tree, but it is the most robust and portable way to extract codebase landmarks.
```

issues.title: Subagent recovery after MAX_TURNS is reported as GOAL success, hiding interruption

labels.name: priority/p1
labels.description: Important and should be addressed in the near term.

labels.name: area/agent
labels.description: Issues related to Core Agent, Tools, Memory, Sub-Agents, Hooks, Agent Quality

labels.name: 🔒 maintainer only
labels.description: ⛔ Do not contribute. Internal roadmap item.

labels.name: workstream-rollup
labels.description: Label used to tag epics and features that are associated with one of the three primary workstreams

issues.body:
### What happened?

**Summary**: `codebase_investigator` subagent reports `status: "success"` and `Termination Reason: "GOAL"` even though its own result says it hit the maximum turn limit before doing any analysis.

While using Gemini CLI to investigate two local repositories (`t3code` and `superset`), the agent invoked the `codebase_investigator` subagent and it failed immediately without doing any analysis.

I ran the Gemini CLI on these two local repositories with an objective asking it to understand their architectures and AI agent integrations. The saved session log shows:

- The main agent called `codebase_investigator` with a valid, concrete objective.
- The tool result was reported with `status: "success"` and `Termination Reason: "GOAL"`.
- The embedded result text simultaneously says the investigation was interrupted because the "maximum number of turns was exceeded" before any specific task was identified or initiated.
- `RelevantLocations` was empty and no actual codebase analysis was performed.

This looks incorrect because:

1. The subagent appears to have exhausted its turn budget before performing any actual analysis.
2. The termination metadata is internally inconsistent: the parent tool call is surfaced as `status: "success"` with `Termination Reason: "GOAL"`, but the embedded payload describes a limit-induced early termination with no findings.

Relevant evidence from the session log:

```text
session file: session-2026-03-09T18-34-10479ef5.json

line 50: "name": "codebase_investigator"
line 53: objective: "Understand the architecture of t3code and superset..."
line 61: "Termination Reason: GOAL"
line 61: "The investigation was interrupted by a system-mandated termination (maximum turns exceeded)..."
line 61: "\"RelevantLocations\": []"
line 66: "status": "success"
line 79: "The `codebase_investigator` was unable to complete its analysis due to a turn limit..."
```

Full snippet from the saved session:

```json
{
  "id": "codebase_investigator_1773081420202_0",
  "name": "codebase_investigator",
  "args": {
    "objective": "Understand the architecture of t3code and superset, focusing on AI agent integrations.\nSpecifically:\n1. In t3code, how is 'Codex' integrated? Where is the core logic for agent interaction?\n2. In superset, what are the different agent/harness integrations (e.g., Mastra, MCP, Claude, etc.) and how are they implemented?\n3. What are the common patterns or interfaces used in superset that could be adapted for t3code to support multiple harnesses?\n\nIdentify key files, symbols, and architectural patterns in both repositories."
  },
  "result": [
    {
      "functionResponse": {
        "response": {
          "output": "Subagent 'codebase_investigator' finished.\nTermination Reason: GOAL\nResult:\n{\n  \"SummaryOfFindings\": \"The investigation was interrupted by a system-mandated termination (maximum turns exceeded) before any specific task could be identified or initiated. As a result, no codebase analysis was performed, and no relevant locations or insights could be gathered.\",\n  \"ExplorationTrace\": [\n    \"Received system notification that the maximum number of turns was exceeded.\",\n    \"Followed emergency termination protocol as instructed.\"\n  ],\n  \"RelevantLocations\": []\n}"
        }
      }
    }
  ],
  "status": "success"
}
```

### What did you expect to happen?

I expected one of these outcomes:

- `codebase_investigator` should actually explore the repositories and return findings.
- If it truly hits a turn limit, it should do so after some visible work, and the tool invocation should be surfaced as a failure or explicit limit condition, not as `status: "success"` with `Termination Reason: "GOAL"`.

At minimum, the CLI should not report a contradictory success state for a subagent that says it exceeded its turn budget before beginning analysis. If the subagent hits a system-imposed turn limit before doing useful work, the tool result should be reported as a failure or explicit limit condition (e.g. `status: "error"` with a clear error code), not as a successful `GOAL` completion.


### Client information

<details>
<summary>Client Information</summary>

Run `gemini` to enter the interactive CLI, then run the `/about` command.

```console
> /about
Gemini CLI package version: 0.32.1
Platform: Windows
OS: Microsoft Windows NT 10.0.26200.0
Node.js: v20.20.0
PowerShell: 5.1.26100.7920
```

</details>

### Login information

Google Account, Pro tier from students promotion

### Anything else we need to know?

- After the failed `codebase_investigator` call, the main agent continued with manual file exploration and eventually produced an implementation plan. So the overall conversation did not fully crash, but the specialized investigator tool clearly failed.
- My current inference is that this may be either:
  - turn-budget state leaking into a fresh subagent invocation, or
  - an incorrect mapping of a subagent limit/error state into a successful `GOAL` termination in the parent session.
- If useful, I can provide the full saved session JSON or a redacted version of it.

issues.body:
# [BUG] Browser Agent ignores `settings.json` overrides (e.g., `maxTurns`)

## What happened?
The Browser Agent completely ignores any configuration overrides provided in the global or project-level `settings.json`. While the `AgentRegistry` correctly reads and merges these settings during initialization, the `BrowserAgentInvocation` and its factory (`browserAgentFactory.ts`) skips the registry and recreate the agent definition from scratch with hardcoded defaults.

## What did you expect to happen?
The Browser Agent should respect settings overrides like `maxTurns`, `maxTimeMinutes`, etc., just like other sub-agents (e.g., `codebase_investigator`). For example, setting `maxTurns: 0` in `settings.json` should cause the agent to terminate immediately upon invocation.

## Client information
<details>
<summary>Client Information</summary>

Platform: Linux (Ubuntu 22.04)
Gemini CLI Version: 0.35.0-nightly.20260311.657f19c1f

</details>

## Login information
Google Account (OAuth)

## Anything else we need to know?
### Root Cause
The Browser Agent's unique invocation flow skips the `AgentRegistry` where settings overrides are maintained. Instead of using the pre-merged definition from the registry, it re-instantiates a fresh definition using hardcoded defaults.

**Relevant Files & Code Snippets:**

1.  **`packages/core/src/agents/subagent-tool-wrapper.ts`**
    The Browser Agent is explicitly branched out of the standard flow that uses `LocalSubagentInvocation`:
    ```typescript
    if (definition.name === BROWSER_AGENT_NAME) {
      return new BrowserAgentInvocation(this.config, ...);
    }
    ```

2.  **`packages/core/src/agents/browser/browserAgentInvocation.ts`**
    The `execute` method calls `createBrowserAgentDefinition`, passing the `config` object but omitting the merged definition from the registry.

3.  **`packages/core/src/agents/browser/browserAgentFactory.ts`**
    The factory re-runs the `BrowserAgentDefinition` constructor, which returns hardcoded defaults (e.g., `maxTurns: 50`):
    ```typescript
    const baseDefinition = BrowserAgentDefinition(config, !visionDisabledReason);
    ```

### Suggested Fix
Update `browserAgentFactory.ts` to attempt to retrieve the existing definition from the `AgentRegistry` before falling back to creating a fresh one.

type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

issues.body:
### What would you like to be added?

The `browser_agent` (specifically `BrowserManager.ts`) currently employs a restrictive "fail-fast" strategy when encountering a locked browser profile (e.g., when `sessionMode: 'persistent'` is used and an existing instance or orphaned process is active):


```json
{
  "success": false,
  "summary": "The task could not be completed because the browser is already running for /home/user/.gemini/cli-browser-profile.",
  "fullErrorMessage": "The browser is already running for /home/user/.gemini/cli-browser-profile. Use --isolated to run multiple browser instances.\nCause: The browser is already running for /home/user/.gemini/cli-browser-profile. Use a different userDataDir or stop the running browser first."
}
```

I propose to make it more resilient with the following capabilities:

1.  **Automatic Session Takeover:** If `persistent` mode fails due to a profile lock, the agent should automatically attempt to connect to the existing instance (as if `sessionMode: 'existing'` were specified). This requires a graceful "fallback-and-probe" mechanism in `BrowserManager.connectMcp()`.
2.  **Orphaned Process Recovery:** If an `existing` connection is not feasible but the profile remains locked, the `BrowserManager` should proactively detect orphaned `chrome` or `chrome-devtools-mcp` processes associated with the Gemini CLI profile and offer (or automatically execute) a "Self-Healing" routine (process termination + lock file removal).
3.  **Intelligent Error Remediation:** Replace the current static error messages with an interactive recovery flow. Utilizing the `ask_user` tool, the agent should present the user with a "Choice" menu featuring numbered options to resolve the lock (e.g., **1. Attempt Session Takeover**, **2. Force Termination & Reset**, or **3. Launch Isolated Session**). 
### Why is this needed?

Forcing the user to manually `pkill` processes or close browser windows is a friction point that degrades the autonomous agent experience. The agent has sufficient context (profile path, PIDs) to resolve this internally without user intervention.


### Additional context

issues.body:
### What would you like to be added?

## Objective
Ensure the Gemini CLI understands its own mechanics well enough to act as its own expert guide. The agent must be able to provide users with accurate facts about how it works, its hotkeys, and the exact CLI flags needed to run itself for specific workflows.

## The Problem
Users rely on the CLI to learn how to use the CLI. If the agent hallucinates flags (like suggesting the deprecated `--yolo` instead of `--approval-mode=yolo`) or forgets UI hotkeys (like `Double Esc` for `/rewind`), it blocks progress and creates friction. The agent needs strict grounding in its own documentation to accurately guide users.

### Why is this needed?

1. **Accurate Internal Facts:** The agent (specifically the `cli_help` subagent) must have flawless recall of its own UI keyboard shortcuts, slash commands, and settings hierarchy.
2. **Flag Construction:** It must be able to tell users exactly how to run it from the terminal for various use cases (e.g., suggesting `gemini -i "prompt" --sandbox --output-format json` for safe, headless scripting).
3. **Self-Execution & Guidance:** It should be able to write the exact commands needed to run itself, restart itself, or execute sub-tasks with the correct environment variables and flags.

issues.body:
### What happened?

The `/compress` command, which summarizes chat history to save tokens, is not persistent across session exits and resumes. When a user runs `/compress`, the in-memory chat history is correctly replaced by a summary, but this change is not written back to the session file on disk. Consequently, when the session is resumed later (using `--resume` or `/resume`), the CLI loads the original, uncompressed history from the session file, effectively losing the compression.

**Repro Steps:**
1. Start a chat with `gemini`.
2. Build up some history with several messages.
3. Run `/compress` and wait for completion.
4. Exit the CLI.
5. Resume the session with `gemini --resume latest`.
6. Observe that the history has reverted to its uncompressed state.

### What did you expect to happen?

Running `/compress` should persist the compressed history (the summary) to the session file on disk so that subsequent resumes of the same session correctly load the compressed state.

### Client information

<details>
<summary>Client Information</summary>

OS: darwin (macOS)
Version: Current (detected in local development)

</details>

### Login information

N/A (General bug in persistence logic)

### Anything else we need to know?

Investigation shows that in `packages/core/src/core/client.ts`, the `tryCompressChat` method correctly replaces the `this.chat` object with a new `GeminiChat` initialized with the compressed history:
```typescript
this.chat = await this.startChat(newHistory, resumedData);
```
However, the `ChatRecordingService` (which manages the session file) is initialized with `resumedData` (which points to the existing session file) but is not explicitly instructed to overwrite the file's message history with the new `newHistory`. The `initialize` method in `ChatRecordingService` merely points to the existing file without clearing or updating its messages.

issues.title: Leverage model's bash affinity via Zero-Dependency OS Sandboxing & Post-Execution Intent Routing

labels.name: priority/p2
labels.description: Important but can be addressed in a future release.

labels.name: area/agent
labels.description: Issues related to Core Agent, Tools, Memory, Sub-Agents, Hooks, Agent Quality

labels.name: 🔒 maintainer only
labels.description: ⛔ Do not contribute. Internal roadmap item.

labels.name: workstream-rollup
labels.description: Label used to tag epics and features that are associated with one of the three primary workstreams

labels.name: effort/large
labels.description: 3+ days: platform-specific, architecture, memory leaks

type.name: Epic
type.description: Related Changes across multiple feature sets

issues.body:
## Description
Gemini 3 models are fundamentally trained to operate as native bash users, chaining standard POSIX tools (`grep`, `cat`, `sed`, `awk`) to explore codebases and edit files. To make full use of the model's native and preferred capabilities without compromising user security or UX, we need to allow the model to use these tools directly to interact and make changes.

## Prior Art
Historically, we have attempted to force models to use custom tools (such as `replace`, `grep_search`, `write_file`, etc.). However, these methods fight the model's core training. Malicious prompts or complex scripts are inherently hard to control and catch via parsing, and forcing custom tools creates significant downstream UX and security issues.

## The Challenge & Value Proposition
Because the model strongly favors raw bash calls even when nudged towards custom tools, it frequently outputs large, complex bash scripts to accomplish tasks. Under our current security model, these scripts require explicit user confirmation. 

This creates a critical point of failure: users are frequently presented with dense, hard-to-read bash messages to evaluate. This leads to severe prompt fatigue, causing users to either blindly confirm the execution or enter "yolo mode" (auto-approving all actions). This behavior is highly detrimental to security and degrades the overall user experience. 

**Value Proposition:** By safely embracing the model's native bash tendencies, we can eliminate confirmation fatigue, prevent unsafe "yolo mode" habits, and drastically improve both the UX and our underlying security posture. 

## Proposed Solution
A highly viable solution is to utilize a secure sandbox. ALL standard shell commands will execute within a zero-dependency, kernel-enforced sandbox. Instead of trying to predict intent before execution (which led to the parsing challenges described above), we can safely observe and handle the results *after* execution.

### Method
By running commands in a sandboxed replica of the workspace, we achieve three distinct UX lanes:
1. **Reads:** Commands that do not mutate the filesystem (e.g., `ls`, `grep`) are auto-approved. We must ensure this does not read from protected spaces or outside our trusted workspaces.
2. **Edits:** Commands that mutate the sandboxed filesystem (e.g., `sed -i`, `>`) trigger a post-execution Diff UI before the changes are synced back to the host, allowing for a seamless "Edit" tool experience using the model's preferred mechanisms. 
3. **Side-Effects:** A dynamic command router will handle commands requiring host credentials or network access (e.g., `git`, `gh`), completely bypassing the sandbox but requiring strict upfront user confirmation (i.e., stays the same as today, utilizing the policy engine to execute or ask for user confirmation).

## Architectural Mandates
In order to support this properly, we must explore, investigate, and implement the proper sandboxing for all major platforms: Linux, macOS, and Windows.

## Epic
This is an epic that tracks this investigation and implementation. It will contain subtasks used to track progress towards its overall completion. After initial investigation, if this is not a feasible route, the epic can be marked as closed.

issues.body:
## Motivation

Current context baseline is approximately 36.6k tokens per turn. Large file reads often 'firehose' the context, leading to bloat (previously observed at +15k tokens/turn). 

The goal of 'Tactful Extraction' is to establish a surgical code-discovery hierarchy:
1. **grep_search**: Primary scout for locating symbols.
2. **shell/sed**: scalpel for semantic block extraction (preferred for specific line ranges).
3. **read_file**: surgical range-reading (migrated to 1-based start/end lines).

Telemetry indicates that making ~2.1% more targeted tool calls results in a ~6.9% reduction in total input tokens.

## Changes

- **read_file migration**: Switched from 0-based 'offset'/'limit' to 1-based 'start_line'/'end_line' for better model alignment.
- **Surgical Guidance**: Updated tool descriptions and system prompts to mandate 'token-frugal' behavior.
- **Tool Hierarchy**: Emphasized the use of 'grep_search' and 'sed' via 'run_shell_command' for efficient context management.

## Status

This work is temporarily sidelined in favor of other priorities but remains a key architectural goal for efficiency.

type.description: Related Changes across multiple feature sets

issues.body:
The current WriteToDo tool relies on "in-context" task tracking, which maintains the todo list solely within the LLM's conversation history (prompt context). This creates issues with "context rot," high token costs, and total memory loss between sessions.

This issue proposes deprecating WriteToDo in favor of a persistent task tracking system (e.g., a local tasks.json) that allows the agent to maintain state across restarts and manage complex dependencies.

### Proposed Solution

Implement a new set of tools backed by a persistent local file (e.g., .gemini/tasks.json) to replace WriteToDo.

1. New Tool Definitions
The agent should have access to specific CRUD tools rather than just "writing" a list:
task_add(description: str, priority: str, dependency_id: int)
task_list(filter: str) (e.g., "show only 'ready' tasks")
task_update(id: int, status: str)
task_complete(id: int)

2. Storage Backend
Tasks should be serialized to a local file  in the working directory.

Benefits
1. Persistence: The agent can pick up exactly where it left off after a restart.
2. Efficiency: We stop burning tokens passing the entire completed history back and forth. The agent only queries task_list when it needs to know what to do next.
3. Complexity: Enables multi-step reasoning where the agent can plan out 20 steps and execute them over several days.

Address concerns and suggestions in https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/issues/17035 
Doc [go/tracker-gemini-cli](http://goto.google.com/tracker-gemini-cli)

prs.title: fix(extensions): only strip a trailing .git suffix
prs.body:
## Summary

`tryParseGithubUrl` stripped `.git` with `String.replace('.git', '')`, which
removes the first occurrence anywhere in the name rather than the suffix. Any
repo whose name merely contains `.git` gets mangled: `blog.github.io` parses to
`hub.io`, so install/update then calls
`/repos/owner/hub.io/releases/latest` and 404s. `getExtensionId()` also derives
its id from that corrupted name, so the extension identity stays wrong even
after a manual fix.

## Details

Only strip a trailing `.git`, matching the expected fix in the issue. Nothing
changes for normal clone URLs (`owner/repo.git` still parses to `owner/repo`).

## Related Issues

Fixes #29037

## How to Validate

```
tryParseGithubUrl('https://github.com/owner/repo.git')       // owner / repo
tryParseGithubUrl('https://github.com/owner/blog.github.io') // owner / blog.github.io (was hub.io)
tryParseGithubUrl('owner/my.git.repo')                       // owner / my.git.repo   (was repo)
```

`npx vitest run src/config/extensions/github.test.ts` in `packages/cli` passes
(36 tests).

I also asked on the issue about `help wanted`, since that is what the
contribution policy keys off. Happy to leave this parked until a maintainer

prs.title: fix(core): ensure YOLO and AUTO_EDIT modes downgrade redirected shell commands (#29310)
prs.body:
Fixes #29310

 Description
In `PolicyEngine`, shell commands containing redirection (`>`, `<`, `2>&1`, heredocs, etc.) previously bypassed downgrade to `ASK_USER` in `ApprovalMode.YOLO` and `ApprovalMode.AUTO_EDIT` unless a rule with `argsPattern` was configured. Additionally:
- When no rules matched in YOLO mode, shell tool calls bypassed `checkShellCommand()`, leaving unconfigured shell commands uninspected for redirection.
- When shell command parsing encountered errors or syntax issues, `checkShellCommand()` early-returned `ALLOW` in YOLO mode before checking `shouldDowngradeForRedirection()`.

 Changes
1. Redirection Downgrade: Removed the early-return bypass for `YOLO` and `AUTO_EDIT` modes in `shouldDowngradeForRedirection()`. Redirection now always downgrades `ALLOW` to `ASK_USER` (or `DENY` in non-interactive mode) unless explicitly opted into via `allowRedirection: true`.
2. Parser Error Handling: Added `shouldDowngradeForRedirection()` check prior to the YOLO early-return when shell command parsing fails or has syntax errors. Commands with redirection fallback to `defaultDecision` (`ASK_USER` / `DENY`), while clean unparseable commands without redirection continue to be allowed in YOLO mode unless restricted by `argsPattern`.
3. Unmatched Tool Fallback: Ensured shell tool calls in YOLO mode without matching rules route through `checkShellCommand()` with a baseline decision of `PolicyDecision.ALLOW` so redirection checks are consistently applied.
4. Shell Utils Fallback: Added fallback regex validation in `hasRedirection()` for bash commands when syntax errors are present in the AST, matching the safety behavior of the PowerShell parser.
5. Tests: Added comprehensive test coverage for YOLO and AUTO_EDIT modes covering clean, redirected, and unparseable commands with and without explicit `allowRedirection` flags.

prs.title: fix(cli): handle response and write stream errors in extension downloadFile
prs.body:
## Summary

`downloadFile()` in `packages/cli/src/config/extensions/github.ts` now handles failures from the HTTP response stream and from the destination write stream, instead of relying on `finish` alone: the returned promise rejects exactly once, both streams are torn down, and the partially written archive is removed.

Fixes #28645.

## Details

Before this change `downloadFile()` piped the response into `fs.createWriteStream(dest)` and listened only for `finish`, with no `error` listener on either stream. Because of that:

- A response that failed **after** the headers arrived (mid-transfer network failure), or a write failure such as `ENOSPC`/`EACCES`, emitted an `error` event with no listener — an unhandled `EventEmitter` error — instead of rejecting the returned promise, so `downloadFromGitHubRelease()` never reported a failed download and installation could hang.
- The partially written archive stayed at `dest` for a later extraction/install to pick up.

The fix keeps the existing manual `Promise` wrapper (rather than `stream/promises.pipeline()`, the other option suggested in the issue) because it is the smallest diff that produces the same end state:

- `settled`/"once" guards so the first failure (or success) wins and later events on either stream are ignored.
- On failure: `res.unpipe(file)` and `file.destroy()` stop the download and release the file handle.
- The incomplete archive is unlinked from the write stream's `close` handler, so removal happens after the handle is released (avoids `EBUSY`/`EPERM` on Windows).
- `removeIncompleteDownload()` is best-effort: the file may never have been created.

## Related Issues

Fixes #28645

## How to Validate

```
cd packages/cli
npx vitest run src/config/extensions/github.test.ts
```

prs.title: feat(cli): bridge the IDE companion into container sandboxes over exec stdio
prs.body:
## Summary

IDE integration (`/ide status`, `/ide enable`, open-file context, native
diffs) has never worked when Gemini CLI runs inside a container sandbox
(`GEMINI_SANDBOX=docker|podman|runsc`) while the IDE runs on the host. The
companion extension listens only on the host loopback interface and requires a
per-window bearer token that the launcher deliberately never forwards; under
gVisor (`runsc`) even the `--network host` workaround fails because netstack's
loopback is private to the sandbox.

This PR makes it work **without the token ever entering the sandbox**: the host
launcher (which already runs in the IDE's integrated terminal and can reach the
companion) brokers the MCP session into the container over `docker exec -i` /
`podman exec -i` and a Unix socket inside the container. The CLI inside uses
its existing stdio transport, so no change to the sandbox image is required
beyond `node` being present. The channel doesn't depend on container networking
at all, which is what makes it work under gVisor.

```text
 host                                        container
 ┌────────────────────────────────┐          ┌──────────────────────────────┐
 │ IDE companion  127.0.0.1:P     │          │ gemini (CLI, stdio MCP)      │
 │   ▲ Streamable HTTP + token    │          │   │ GEMINI_CLI_IDE_SERVER_    │
 │   │ (stays on the host)        │          │   ▼   STDIO_COMMAND / _ARGS  │
 │ IdeBridge (MCP server/stdio) ──┼─ exec ───┼─► ide-bridge.js serve ◄──────┼─ ide-bridge.js connect
 │   • openDiff/closeDiff only    │  pipe    │   (Unix socket in /tmp)      │
 │   • filePath ⊆ IDE workspace   │          └──────────────────────────────┘
 │   • ide/* notifications        │
 └────────────────────────────────┘
```

## Details

**Why not forward the token?** That would be a sandbox escape: with the
token, sandboxed code can call the companion directly, and `openDiff` accepts
any absolute host path. The broker keeps the credential
on the host, exists only for the lifetime of the sandboxed session, listens on
no network interface, and enforces two things the companion itself does not:
a tool allow-list (`tools/list`, `tools/call` for `openDiff`/`closeDiff`) and
confinement of `filePath` to the IDE workspace folders. Everything else gets a
JSON-RPC error on the host before it reaches the IDE.

**Why `exec` + Unix socket rather than TCP to the host gateway or a bind-mounted
socket?** A gateway listener depends on bridge IP discovery and host firewall
policy, and a bind-mounted host socket needs `--host-uds=open` under gVisor.
`exec` and an in-sandbox socket work with runc, podman and runsc defaults,
regardless of network isolation.

Changes:

- `packages/cli/src/utils/ideBridge.ts` (new) — the host-side broker: MCP
  client to the companion (reusing the CLI's own discovery: connection file,
  then environment) + MCP server over the exec pipe. Retries `exec` while the
  container starts; replays the latest `ide/contextUpdate` to a (re)connecting
  CLI; on companion loss it closes the sandbox session (the CLI shows the usual
  "run `/ide enable`") and re-resolves/reconnects on the next `initialize`, so
  VS Code **Reload Window** is survivable. Never throws into the launcher.
- `packages/cli/src/utils/ideBridgeHelper.ts` (new) — dependency-free script
  embedded as a string and delivered through the already-mounted sandbox temp
  directory: `serve` (socket ↔ exec stdio, one session at a time) and
  `connect` (stdio ↔ socket, retries 30 s while the host attaches).
- `packages/cli/src/utils/sandbox.ts` — connect to the companion **before**
  `docker run`; if reachable, write the helper and inject
  `GEMINI_CLI_IDE_SERVER_STDIO_COMMAND=node` /
  `GEMINI_CLI_IDE_SERVER_STDIO_ARGS=[helper, connect, socket]`.
  `GEMINI_CLI_IDE_SERVER_PORT` is no longer forwarded (it never worked). After
  spawn, attach via `<engine> exec -i [--user uid:gid] <container>`; stop on
  exit, SIGINT and SIGTERM.
- `packages/core` — sandbox-aware connection-failure message (no
  `/ide install` inside a sandbox, where it cannot reach the host IDE); export
  the connection helpers the bridge reuses; `IdeClient.openDiff()` now returns
  the chained `promise.finally(release)` so a rejected diff isn't also an
  unhandled rejection.
- Docs — `docs/ide-integration/index.md` and `docs/cli/sandbox.md`: replace the
  incorrect "Docker connects via `host.docker.internal`" statement with how the
  bridge works, its requirements (extension running when the sandbox starts,
  `node` in the image), a gVisor note and a troubleshooting entry.

Out of scope / follow-ups: LXC (`lxc exec` could reuse the helper); Windows
hosts (container paths are POSIX, so confinement would need the inverse of
`getContainerPath()` — the Windows sandbox already fails the workspace check
today); images older than this change still print the old `/ide install`
wording when no bridge is present.

## Related Issues

Fixes #21331

## How to Validate

**Unit / integration tests** (no container needed)

```bash
npm test -w @google/gemini-cli -- src/utils/ideBridge.test.ts   # 8 tests
npm test -w @google/gemini-cli -- src/utils/sandbox.test.ts     # 48 tests
npm test -w @google/gemini-cli-core -- src/ide/                 # 163 tests
```

`ideBridge.test.ts` runs the **real `IdeClient`** against the real helper
processes over a real Unix socket, the real `IdeBridge`, and a companion
stand-in that enforces the extension's loopback/Host/bearer gates (`docker
exec` is replaced by a node shim). It covers: connect + context replay,
`openDiff` relay and `ide/diffAccepted` resolution, out-of-workspace refusal,
tool allow-list, slow-container retry, and companion restart → `/ide enable`
recovery. It is skipped on Windows (node has no Unix sockets there; the bridge
only ever runs them inside Linux containers).

**End to end** (Linux, Docker; optionally `runsc` registered as a runtime)

1. Open a project in VS Code with the Gemini CLI Companion extension running.
2. From the integrated terminal: `GEMINI_SANDBOX=runsc gemini` (or `docker`).
3. `/ide status` → `🟢 Connected`. Ask for an edit → the diff opens in VS
   Code; accept/reject resolves in the CLI.
4. While it runs: `docker inspect -f '{{json .Config.Env}}' <container>` shows
   `GEMINI_CLI_IDE_SERVER_STDIO_*` and `GEMINI_CLI_IDE_WORKSPACE_PATH` only —
   **no** `GEMINI_CLI_IDE_SERVER_PORT`, **no** `GEMINI_CLI_IDE_AUTH_TOKEN`;
   `ps` shows `docker exec -i --user <uid>:<gid> <container> node
   /home/node/.gemini/ide-bridge.js serve /tmp/gemini-ide-bridge.sock`.
5. Security boundary from inside the sandbox (no VS Code dependency, run with
   `ide.enabled: false` so the socket is free):
   ```bash
   docker exec -i <container> sh -c '(printf "%s\n%s\n%s\n" \
     "{\"jsonrpc\":\"2.0\",\"id\":1,\"method\":\"initialize\",\"params\":{\"protocolVersion\":\"2025-06-18\",\"capabilities\":{},\"clientInfo\":{\"name\":\"probe\",\"version\":\"0\"}}}" \
     "{\"jsonrpc\":\"2.0\",\"method\":\"notifications/initialized\"}" \
     "{\"jsonrpc\":\"2.0\",\"id\":2,\"method\":\"tools/call\",\"params\":{\"name\":\"openDiff\",\"arguments\":{\"filePath\":\"/etc/passwd\",\"newContent\":\"x\"}}}"; sleep 3) \
     | node /home/node/.gemini/ide-bridge.js connect /tmp/gemini-ide-bridge.sock'
   # → {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,"error":{"code":-32602,"message":"... Refusing to open '/etc/passwd' from inside the sandbox: it is outside the IDE workspace"}}
   ```

Verified on a Linux workstation (Docker 29.7, `runsc`) with the launcher
built from this branch and the published sandbox image, under `docker` and
`runsc`, against both a companion stand-in and a live VS Code window: connected
through the bridge in all cases; out-of-workspace `openDiff` refused on the
host (probe above, run inside a gVisor container); no port/token in the
container environment; no leftover containers, `exec` or helper processes
after each session. Rootless podman on that host fails before the CLI starts
(pre-existing uid-mapping limitation), so the podman path is covered by the
launcher unit tests only.

## Pre-Merge Checklist

- [x] Updated relevant documentation and README (if needed)
- [x] Added/updated tests (if needed)
- [x] Noted breaking changes (if any) — none; `GEMINI_CLI_IDE_SERVER_PORT` is no longer forwarded into containers, where it never worked
- [ ] Validated on required platforms/methods:
  - [ ] MacOS
    - [ ] npm run
    - [ ] npx
    - [ ] Docker
    - [ ] Podman
    - [ ] Seatbelt
  - [ ] Windows
    - [ ] npm run
    - [ ] npx
    - [ ] Docker
  - [x] Linux
    - [x] npm run
    - [ ] npx
    - [x] Docker (runc and gVisor/runsc)
