type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, improvement, or new functionality

issues.body:
### Describe the feature or problem you'd like to solve

When Copilot CLI executes a shell command, the output is collapsed by default in the timeline (showing "2 lines..."). Users have to manually press  Ctrl+O / Ctrl+E to expand all results. This creates friction when reviewing what commands actually did.

### Proposed solution

Add a user setting in settings.json (e.g. "expandTimelineByDefault": true) that automatically expands all shell command outputs in the conversation timeline.
 
This would benefit users who want full visibility into every command execution without needing to manually expand each result, improving transparency and trust in the agent's actions.

### Example prompts or workflows

1. User asks: "install the latest .NET 8 SDK" → Copilot runs `winget install` 
    → output is collapsed, user cannot see if install succeeded without pressing Ctrl+O
 
 2. User asks: "list installed .NET SDKs" → Copilot runs `dotnet --list-sdks` 
    → result hidden by default, user misses the actual SDK versions returned
 
 3. User asks: "what is my default .NET version?" → Copilot runs `dotnet --version` 
    → answer is collapsed, user has to manually expand to see "10.0.202"
 
 4. During a multi-step task (build, test, deploy), each command result is collapsed 
    → user loses track of what succeeded or failed without manually expanding each step

### Additional context

The current workaround is Ctrl+O / Ctrl+E to expand all timeline entries manually, but this needs to be repeated every session. A persistent setting like "expandTimelineByDefault": true in ~/.copilot/settings.json would solve this cleanly without changing the default behavior for users who prefer the compact view.

issues.title: Bash commands that `cd` into a directory created in the same command are hard-denied without a prompt ("unusable session working directory") since 1.0.99-0

labels.name: area:permissions
labels.description: Tool approval, security boundaries, sandbox mode, and directory restrictions

issues.body:
### Describe the bug

Since 1.0.99-0, the agent's `bash` tool denies, without showing a prompt, any command that `cd`s into a directory created earlier in the same command and then does something that needs a permission check (a write redirect, `git status`, `git log`, …). It returns:

```
Permission denied and could not request permission from user. Copilot needed the user's approval and no one could answer. This is not an OS or sandbox error.
```

This happens in an interactive session with `/allow-all` on, with the user at the terminal. The process log attributes it to the permissions engine:

```
[WARNING] [rust:permissions_engine::orchestrator] permission request denied: unusable session working directory
```

The denial happens before execution: none of the command runs, not even the leading `mkdir`.

It breaks common agent flows such as `git worktree add <dir> <ref> && cd <dir> && git log` (e.g. creating a worktree to review a PR) and `gh repo clone owner/repo <dir> && cd <dir> && …`. The agent then abandons the approach (for example, reviewing from `gh pr diff` instead of a worktree) because the error says approval was impossible.

### Affected version

GitHub Copilot CLI 1.0.100-1 (also 1.0.99-0, 1.0.99-1, 1.0.99-3, 1.0.100-0)

### Steps to reproduce the behavior

In an interactive session with `/allow-all` on, ask the agent to run each command as a single `bash` tool call:

| Command | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `mkdir -p /tmp/A && cd /tmp/A && echo hi > f.txt` | **Denied** |
| `cd /tmp && git init -q C && cd /tmp/C && git status --short` | **Denied** |
| `mkdir -p ~/tmp-B && cd ~/tmp-B && echo hi > f.txt` | **Denied** |
| `cd /tmp/existing-dir && echo hi > f.txt` (dir already exists) | OK |
| `mkdir -p /tmp/D && cd /tmp/D && pwd` | OK |
| `mkdir -p /tmp/E && cd /tmp/E && touch x && pwd` | OK |
| `d=$(mktemp -d); cd "$d"; touch f.txt` | OK |
| `git init -q /tmp/F && git -C /tmp/F status --short && echo hi > /tmp/F/f.txt` | OK |

Workaround: create the directory in one tool call and `cd` into it in the next, or avoid `cd` by using absolute paths and `git -C <dir>`.

### Expected behavior

With allow-all on, the command should run. If the CLI can't evaluate the command's paths before execution (because the `cd` target doesn't exist yet), it should ask the user rather than hard-deny. The error shouldn't say no one could answer when an interactive user is present.

### Additional context

- **Regression boundary**, from my local session history, counting `bash` calls shaped like `<mkdir -p | git init | git clone | gh repo clone | git worktree add> … && cd …`:

  | Versions | Such calls | Denied |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | 1.0.95 – 1.0.98-2 | ~64 | 0 |
  | 1.0.99-0 – 1.0.100-0 | ~57 | 24 |

- **Not caused by hooks:** my configured hooks return no permission decision for these commands, and the log line above comes from `permissions_engine::orchestrator`.
- **Likely cause:** pre-execution shell path analysis appears to resolve the `cd` target before the command runs. It can't resolve a directory that doesn't exist yet, and it hard-denies instead of falling back to a prompt.
- **Environment:** macOS 26.7.1, arm64. Terminal: iTerm2. User shell: zsh; the agent's bash tool uses `/bin/bash`.

issues.title: Copilot exfiltration protection is too agressive and block legitimate spec content.
issues.body:
### Describe the bug

I have a spec file that contains the following line

```
- Rover's `supergraph.yaml` supports Router-style variable expansion (e.g. `Authorization: "Bearer ${env.AUTH_TOKEN}"`), so the token can be injected via an environment variable at compose time without hand-editing the config file per run.
```

The security feature redact the `Bearer ${env.AUTH_TOKEN}`, to `******` causing agent to get confused.

That's really not ideal. It prevent reading completely valid specification. As you can see, no actual secret are being exfiltrated.

I understand why the feature exists,  clearly the PII protection should be on by default but it would be nice to be able to configure the level of redaction. Certain type of task demand that we edit Authorization Header code, it is part of programming. The current security settings make this impossible.

That's quite blocking for my current work 

### Affected version

GitHub Copilot CLI 1.0.69

### Steps to reproduce the behavior

Use plan mode or similar to create a markdown file containing specification on how to construct an Authorization Header
In a fresh session, ask the agent to review the file and see if there is ambiguities

The agent will complain about the ******. Sometime he will be smart about it and use xxd to read the ****** , meaning the secrets aren't really protected.

### Expected behavior

With a precise, not on by default workaround, the agent can be made to see the full specification so he can review the file and work on it.

### Additional context

_No response_

issues.title: Windows: with --sandbox, shell commands can't list or stat directories when the working directory is on a non-system drive
issues.body:
## Summary

On Windows, when Copilot CLI's command sandbox is enabled and the working directory is on a drive other than the system drive (for example `D:\`), sandboxed shell commands cannot list, stat or change into directories on that drive. `Get-ChildItem`, `Test-Path`, `cmd /c dir` and git repository discovery fail with **Access is denied**, and the shell does not start in the working directory: `Get-Location` reports `C:\WINDOWS\System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0`.

Reading a file by its full path still works, and so does .NET `[IO.Directory]::GetFiles`. The same commands work when the working directory is on `C:\`, and everything works on `D:\` without `--sandbox`.

## Environment

- Windows 11 Enterprise 26H1, OS build 28000 (x64)
- GitHub Copilot CLI 1.0.101-0 (installed with WinGet)
- Windows PowerShell 5.1 as the sandboxed shell
- Volumes that reproduce it:
  - `D:` NTFS, fixed disk;
  - `E:` ReFS Dev Drive (trusted);
  - a freshly created 2 GB NTFS VHDX mounted as `T:`.
- Works: `C:` (NTFS, system drive).
- No sandbox settings beyond `--sandbox`.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Create a test folder on a non-system drive:

   ```powershell
   New-Item -ItemType Directory D:\sandbox-probe | Out-Null
   Set-Content D:\sandbox-probe\existing.txt 'hello'
   cd D:\sandbox-probe
   ```

2. Run the CLI with the sandbox enabled and ask it to run this probe:

   ```powershell
   copilot --sandbox --allow-all --no-ask-user -s -p @'
   Run exactly this PowerShell, once, then print its raw output verbatim:
   $w = 'D:\sandbox-probe'
   "location=$((Get-Location).ProviderPath)"
   try { (Get-ChildItem -LiteralPath $w -ErrorAction Stop).Name } catch { "Get-ChildItem: $($_.Exception.Message)" }
   try { Test-Path -LiteralPath $w -ErrorAction Stop } catch { "Test-Path: $($_.Exception.Message)" }
   cmd /c "dir /b D:\sandbox-probe"
   try { [IO.File]::ReadAllText('D:\sandbox-probe\existing.txt') } catch { "ReadAllText: $($_.Exception.Message)" }
   try { [IO.Directory]::GetFiles($w) } catch { "GetFiles: $($_.Exception.Message)" }
   '@
   ```

3. Run the same command **without** `--sandbox` as a control.
4. Optionally, repeat steps 1–3 with a folder under `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Temp` on `C:` (adjust `$w`).

(`Set-Location` is left out of the probe because in `-p` mode it triggers a CLI approval prompt, which is unrelated to the sandbox. In our runs through the Copilot SDK with the same sandbox, `Set-Location D:\sandbox-probe` also fails with Access is denied.)

## Expected

The sandboxed shell starts in the working directory and can list and stat it, as it does on `C:`. `copilot help sandbox` says sandboxed commands can access the allowed paths, and the working directory is allowed by default. The sandbox's PowerShell setup is meant to make the working directory's drive enumerable when it isn't the system drive.

## Actual

With `--sandbox`, working directory `D:\sandbox-probe`:

```text
location=C:\WINDOWS\System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0
Get-ChildItem: Access is denied
False
Test-Path: Access is denied
Access is denied.
hello

D:\sandbox-probe\existing.txt
```

Without `--sandbox` (control), same folder:

```text
location=D:\sandbox-probe
existing.txt
True
existing.txt
hello

D:\sandbox-probe\existing.txt
```

With `--sandbox`, working directory on `C:`: every probe succeeds, and `location` is the working directory.

Summary across volumes (sandbox on):

| Working directory | Get-ChildItem | Test-Path | cmd dir | git status | Read by full path | .NET GetFiles |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| C: NTFS (system) | OK | True | OK | OK | OK | OK |
| D: NTFS | Access denied | Access denied | Access denied | "not a git repository" | OK | OK |
| E: ReFS Dev Drive | Access denied | Access denied | Access denied | "not a git repository" | OK | OK |
| T: new NTFS VHDX | Access denied | Access denied | Access denied | "not a git repository" | OK | OK |

## Diagnostics

- **Engagement:** the sandbox reports itself as engaged (`process_container` backend), and host support reports filesystem enumeration as supported.
- **Policy:** the effective sandbox policy includes an enumeration grant for both the system drive and the working directory's drive (for D:, the roots `C:\` and `D:\`), and the working directory is in the read-write paths.
- **Not drive-specific:** a freshly created NTFS VHDX fails the same way, so this isn't about one drive's history or permissions. Dev Drive filter policy isn't the cause either, since plain NTFS volumes fail too.
- **ACLs:** the volume roots have ordinary default ACLs. One difference: the `C:\` root carries an extra capability ACE (`S-1-15-3-65536-…`) that the other roots lack. Copying that ACE to `D:\` did not fix it (since reverted).
- **Filters:** `fltmc instances` shows `bindflt` attached to `C:` only, and `bfs` attached to `C:` and `D:`. Attaching `bindflt` to `D:` did not fix it (since reverted).
- **Process Monitor:** a trace of a failing run showed no ACCESS DENIED result on the test folder. The denial may happen at a layer Process Monitor doesn't observe, such as the sandbox's own brokering. Raw traces are available on request.
- **Partial enumeration:** .NET `Directory.GetFiles` succeeds where `Get-ChildItem` and `cmd dir` fail. So enumeration is not blocked outright; some directory-open or metadata queries are denied while others succeed.

## Workarounds tried

- Working directory on `C:`: works.
- Adding the `C:\` root's capability ACE to `D:\` and `E:\`: no change (reverted).
- Attaching `bindflt` to `D:`: no change (reverted).

## Impact

On machines where repos live on a data drive or a Dev Drive (which Windows recommends for development), turning on the sandbox makes the working directory unusable for ordinary shell commands and git, even though the CLI reports the sandbox as engaged. The failure looks like the agent "can't see the repo", not like a sandbox restriction, so it's hard to diagnose.

## Suspected component

The Windows `process_container` sandbox (MXC): the drive-root enumeration grant for a non-system working-directory drive appears not to take effect, or to cover only some directory operations. We have not confirmed the exact denied operation.

issues.title: macOS sandbox blocks Gradle daemon connection despite local networking being allowed

labels.name: area:permissions
labels.description: Tool approval, security boundaries, sandbox mode, and directory restrictions

issues.body:
### Describe the bug

Gradle cannot execute even an offline `help` task inside the Copilot CLI macOS sandbox when outbound and local networking are configured as allowed.

The Gradle daemon starts successfully and listens on localhost, but the Gradle client cannot connect to it:

```text
java.net.SocketException: Operation not permitted
```

The identical command succeeds with the Copilot sandbox disabled. Restarting Copilot with the sandbox enabled does not resolve the failure.

### Affected version

Copilot CLI `1.0.95`; also observed on `1.0.93`.

### Steps to reproduce the behavior

1. On macOS, enable the Copilot CLI sandbox and allow both outbound and local networking. The configured network settings are:

   ```json
   {
     "allowOutbound": true,
     "allowLocalNetwork": true,
     "allowedHosts": [],
     "blockedHosts": []
   }
   ```

   `/sandbox policy` reports outbound and local networking as allowed.

2. In a Gradle 9.1.0 wrapper project with Java 21 selected, ask Copilot to execute:

   ```bash
   ./gradlew --offline --no-daemon --console=plain --stacktrace help
   ```

3. Gradle launches a single-use daemon to honor the project's JVM settings. The daemon binds a localhost port, but the client connection fails with `Operation not permitted`, before any task executes.

4. Disable the Copilot sandbox and repeat the identical command. It succeeds, executing only `help`.

### Expected behavior

When local networking is explicitly allowed, Gradle should be able to connect to its localhost daemon.

If that setting intentionally excludes host-loopback connections, the policy display should make this distinction clear and document a supported way to permit the required connection without disabling the entire sandbox.

### Additional context

**Environment:** macOS `26.6.2`, ARM64; Gradle wrapper `9.1.0`; Java Amazon Corretto `21.0.6.7.1`.

The command uses offline mode, so dependency downloads are not involved. `--no-daemon` still launches a single-use daemon in this project.

**Kernel-confirmed denial**

In one sandbox-enabled run, the daemon listened on `127.0.0.1:53774`. The macOS kernel log recorded:

```text
Sandbox: java(5913) deny(1) network-outbound remote:*:53774
```

**Effective policy from a separate failing run**

Copilot's debug log identified the generated policy used for the command. Its network section was:

```json
{
  "network": {
    "egress": {
      "default": "deny"
    },
    "ingress": {
      "default": "allow",
      "hostLoopback": "deny"
    },
    "runtimeConfig": {
      "networkProxy": "http://127.0.0.1:55437"
    }
  }
}
```

In that run, the Gradle daemon listened on `127.0.0.1:55438`, not the proxy port `55437`.

This appears consistent with the client being denied a direct host-loopback connection despite `allowLocalNetwork: true`. Gradle's daemon protocol uses raw TCP, so the HTTP proxy cannot carry that connection.

Please investigate whether `allowLocalNetwork` is being mapped correctly to the effective macOS policy, or whether a separate supported host-loopback permission is required.

**Related reports**

- [github/copilot-cli#4854](https://github.com/github/copilot-cli/issues/4854): a Windows `/sandbox policy` display issue. Unlike that report, the display here says networking is allowed, while the generated policy and kernel denial demonstrate an actual blocked connection.
- [github/copilot-cli#4516](https://github.com/github/copilot-cli/issues/4516): JVM filesystem-grant failures on macOS, with a recent comment also describing remote-repository/proxy problems. This report concerns the local Gradle daemon connection, without dependency downloads.

Only sanitized excerpts are included here; no project source, credentials, or full conversation/debug logs are attached.

issues.title: Autopilot repeatedly retries write_agent for completed non-resumable agent with conflicting selectors
issues.body:
## Describe the bug

When a background agent has completed as blocked and is non-resumable, the coordinator can repeatedly call `write_agent` instead of replacing it. In the observed failure, the model also supplied all three mutually exclusive selectors (`agent_id`, `agent_ids`, and `scope`) on every retry, so each call failed schema validation before the runtime could report the target agent's terminal lifecycle state.

The result was a long Autopilot loop displaying repeated `Write <agent-id>` calls with no recovery.

Observed sequence:

1. A background general-purpose agent was launched successfully.
2. The agent completed with a blocked result because it started from the wrong working directory. Its launch metadata reported `resumable: false`.
3. The coordinator attempted to steer/resume the completed agent repeatedly.
4. Every generated `write_agent` call contained all three selectors:

   ```json
   {
     "agent_id": "<agent-id>",
     "agent_ids": ["<agent-id>"],
     "scope": "children",
     "message": "Resume..."
   }
   ```

5. The tool returned:

   ```text
   Provide exactly one of "agent_id", "agent_ids", or "scope"
   ```

6. Autopilot retried the same malformed operation many times instead of inspecting lifecycle state and starting a replacement.

The old agent had no durable resumable session. Starting a fresh agent with the original objective, preserved worktree, and absolute project root recovered the work.

## Affected version

```text
1.0.100
```

## Steps to reproduce the behavior

1. Start a background agent with `mode: "background"`.
2. Have the agent finish with a blocked result and a terminal/non-resumable lifecycle state.
3. Ask the main agent to resume or steer that completed agent.
4. Observe the main model call `write_agent` repeatedly.
5. In the failing case, inspect the tool calls and observe that `agent_id`, `agent_ids`, and `scope` are all populated.
6. Observe every call fail with `Provide exactly one of "agent_id", "agent_ids", or "scope"`.
7. Observe Autopilot continue retrying the dead agent instead of launching a replacement.

## Expected behavior

The tool and orchestrator should defend against both failure modes:

1. The generated `write_agent` call should contain exactly one selector.
2. When the target is completed, failed, cancelled, missing, or non-resumable, the tool should return a structured actionable result, for example:

   ```text
   agent_not_resumable:
   Agent <id> is completed/blocked and cannot accept messages.
   Do not retry write_agent. Start a new task agent using the original objective and preserved context.
   ```

3. Autopilot should treat that response as terminal for the old agent ID and automatically start a fresh replacement with the original objective and durable context.
4. After an invalid-selector response, the coordinator should retry at most once with only `agent_id`, not loop indefinitely.

## Additional context

- OS: macOS, arm64
- Interface: interactive TUI, Autopilot
- Agent: background general-purpose agent
- Model: `gpt-6.1-sol`, accessed through a custom OpenAI-compatible gateway
- API subtype: OpenAI Responses (`/v1/responses`)
- The replacement-agent workaround was successful when explicitly given the original objective, absolute worktree/project root, approved plan, constraints, and known progress.

Related open issues:

- #5143 — follow-ups to idle agents can be delayed; its documented workaround is starting a fresh agent.
- #4101 — `write_agent` may block while waking an idle agent.
- #4911 — background subagent stream failures can end without a failure status.
- #2595 — completed agents can disappear and become unrecoverable.

Those issues cover adjacent delivery, status, and retention failures, but I could not find one covering the exact combination of malformed selector retries plus failure to replace a terminal/non-resumable agent.

Suggested lifecycle handling:

- Permit `write_agent` only for agents currently reported as `running` or `idle`.
- Reject terminal/non-resumable agents with a dedicated error code and replacement guidance.
- Persist enough final metadata/result for the coordinator to seed a replacement safely.

issues.title: Linux sandbox: shell commands are killed after ~10 s (bwrap parent-death signal bound to an exited thread)

labels.name: area:platform-linux
labels.description: Linux-specific: Wayland, X11, Ubuntu, Fedora, Alpine, ARM, terminal emulators

labels.name: area:permissions
labels.description: Tool approval, security boundaries, sandbox mode, and directory restrictions

issues.body:
### Describe the bug

On Linux with the sandbox enabled, a shell command that runs longer than ~10 s is killed
with SIGKILL. The tool reports `exit code -1`. There is no error message. The same command
passes without the sandbox, and it also passes with plain `bwrap` outside the CLI.

### Affected version

1.0.98 (Linux x64). Ubuntu 24.04, kernel 6.8, bubblewrap 0.9.0.

### Steps to reproduce the behavior

1. Enable the sandbox (`/sandbox`, or `"sandbox": {"enabled": true}` in settings).
2. Run:
   ```
   copilot -p 'Run this exact shell command once: date +%T; sleep 30; date +%T' --allow-all-tools
   ```
3. Result: only the first `date` prints, then `Failed with exit code -1` after ~10 s.

In `-p` mode it fails every time. In interactive sessions it fails only on some runs.

### Expected behavior

The command runs to the end (exit 0 after ~30 s).

### Additional context

Cause, from `strace -f` of the CLI:

```
<bwrap>   11:58:37.324667 prctl(PR_SET_PDEATHSIG, SIGKILL) = 0
<thread>  11:58:47.432660 exit(0)
<bwrap>   11:58:47.433353 +++ killed by SIGKILL +++
```

The CLI starts `bwrap --die-with-parent` from a worker (pool) thread. On Linux,
`PR_SET_PDEATHSIG` fires when the thread that forked the child exits, not when the
process exits. The runtime stops that thread after ~10 s idle, so the kernel kills bwrap
and the command. There is no `kill()` syscall and no OOM event.

Possible fixes: spawn bwrap from a long-lived thread, or watch the CLI process (for
example with a pidfd) instead of using `--die-with-parent`.

Workaround: put a small `bwrap` wrapper first in `PATH`. The wrapper starts the real bwrap
from its own process and kills it when the CLI process exits.

issues.title: Explicit-approval requests silently denied in resumed sessions: 'could not request permission from user' / orchestrator 'permission request denied: unusable session working directory'
issues.body:
## Describe the bug

In interactive sessions that have been **resumed**, any tool action requiring explicit approval is silently denied instead of prompting the user, even though allow-all ("yolo") elevation is active for the session. Two records appear for each denial:

1. Tool result: `Permission denied and could not request permission from user. Copilot needed the user's approval and no one could answer. This is not an OS or sandbox error.` (error code `denied`)
2. CLI log: `[rust:permissions_engine::orchestrator] permission request denied: unusable session working directory`

Auto-approval of judge-clean actions still works, so the failure masquerades as a targeted block on specific commands (e.g. `sudo pacman …`). `sudo` itself is not special: in one affected resumed session `/usr/bin/sudo -n true && echo sudo-ok` and `sudo -n git --version` were auto-approved and ran, while other escalated commands in the same time window were denied.

Denied actions all involve destructive/privileged operations or file effects **outside the session working directory**; read-only / in-cwd / trivially safe commands in the same turns auto-approve:

| Denied (exact events) | Auto-approved in the same session/turn |
|---|---|
| `mkdir -p ~/Workspace/pkgcache && sudo pacman -Sw --cachedir ~/Workspace/pkgcache …` | `/usr/bin/sudo -n true && echo sudo-ok` |
| `systemd-inhibit --what=idle --mode=block --who=… sleep 3 & INH=$!; loginctl show-session …` | `v4l2-ctl -d /dev/video0 --info …` |
| `rm -rf /tmp/… && mkdir -p /tmp/… && cd /tmp/… && git init …` | `sed -n '411,500p' crates/…/index.rs` |
| `cp -a /run/media/…/build/… /tmp/… && cd /tmp/…` | `echo ok && ls /tmp \| head -3` |
| `cd /tmp && GIT_CONFIG_COUNT=0 git clone -q … && cd …` | `grep -n … …` |

All observed denials occurred in **resumed** sessions (one session resumed several times across 4 days; another resumed after a pause). Fresh sessions approve the same class of actions.

Onset: **2026-10-16 on 1.0.99-2** (prerelease channel, auto-update). No occurrences under 1.0.99-0 despite the same usage pattern. Still reproduces on 1.0.100-1 and 1.0.101-0. 24 denial events across `~/.copilot/logs/process-*.log` since 10-16.

## Affected version

`GitHub Copilot CLI 1.0.101-0` (first seen on 1.0.99-2; also reproduced on 1.0.100-1)

## Steps to reproduce the behavior

1. Use an interactive session with `defaultPermissionMode: "allow-all"` active (session events show `allowAllPermissions: true`), do some ordinary work in a project subdirectory, then end the session.
2. `/resume` (or relaunch the CLI and resume) that session later.
3. In the resumed session, run a command with privileged components or file effects outside the session cwd, e.g. `mkdir -p ~/Workspace/pkgcache && sudo pacman -Sw --cachedir ~/Workspace/pkgcache <pkg>` or `systemd-inhibit --what=idle --mode=block --who=test sleep 3`.
4. Observe the denial above; the orchestrator warning `permission request denied: unusable session working directory` appears in the process log at the same timestamp.
5. Control: the same command in a **fresh** session succeeds; a simple `sudo -n true` in the same resumed session also succeeds.

## Expected behavior

Escalated actions in an interactive session should present an approval prompt the user can answer, or the allow-all elevation (which the session state still reports as active) should cover them. At minimum, the denial should say why the request could not be raised — `unusable session working directory` is currently visible only in the log file, and it is unclear what makes the working directory unusable.

## Additional context

- `~/.copilot/settings.json`: `"defaultPermissionMode": "allow-all"`, `"sandbox": {"enabled": false}`. No managed policy: logs report `[managedSettings] effective policy resolved: source=none, bypassDisabled=false`.
- OS: Linux x86_64 (CachyOS), shell fish (CLI processes run with /bin/bash), terminal Ghostty.
- `copilot help config` says of `defaultPermissionMode`: *"Any value is ignored on resumed sessions, outside interactive runs, and when `--allow-all`/`--yolo` already elevated the session."* The runtime also contains the string `the session-claim bypass requires force=true (omitting the flag is treated as a refusal to escalate)`. If resume intentionally drops the bypass, the session state is misleading: `session.permissions_changed` events still show `allowAllPermissionMode: "on"` and `/yolo on` appears effective.
- Possibly related recent changes (bundled changelog): 1.0.98 *"Resuming a session now respects abandoned pending-permission work and continues only active permission requests."*; 1.0.99-0 / 1.0.100 assisted-permission judge routing for bash commands; 1.0.96 timeline attribution of "unattended fallback" permission decisions.
- Ruled out:
  - **Command concurrency**: ~61% of 4,550 successful tool calls in the most-affected session overlapped another in-flight call; only 5 of 18 denials had an overlapping sibling.
  - **OS/sudo policy**: `sudo whoami` / `sudo -n whoami` run fine in fresh sessions (and simple sudo probes auto-approve even in affected sessions).
  - **Sandbox**: disabled in settings and in effect.
- Evidence is available in `~/.copilot/session-state/<session-id>/events.jsonl` (tool.execution_start/_complete pairs with exact commands and error payloads) and `~/.copilot/logs/process-*.log`; happy to attach sanitized extracts on request.

Questions: what condition produces `unusable session working directory` for a session whose cwd exists and is writable? And can the approval path recover (surface the prompt) instead of falling through to the unattended deny?

issues.title: Context window rollover fails: "checkpoint.md is absent for this agent; write it before requesting rollover"
issues.body:
# Context window rollover fails: "checkpoint.md is absent for this agent; write it before requesting rollover"

### Describe the bug
Long-running agent sessions crash when the context window fills and the runtime attempts a rollover:

```
Execution failed: Failed to start a fresh context window: checkpoint.md is absent for this agent; write it before requesting rollover
```

The turn ends and the session (or sub-agent) is effectively dead; it recurs on subsequent turns in the same session.

### What we observed
- The agent **had** written a `checkpoint.md` to the session's `files/` folder (via a normal file write / patch) ~7 minutes before the first failure, yet the runtime still reported it as absent "for this agent".
- The native runtime contains related errors ("Replacing checkpoint.md requires expected_revision; read or stat it first, or use append", "Stale checkpoint writer…"), which suggests checkpoints must be written through a runtime-managed store/tool rather than a plain file write. In our sessions the model did not appear to have any tool exposed for that store, so it could never satisfy the precondition.
- Seen repeatedly across multiple sessions/sub-agents (custom agents and the main agent), mostly in long tool-heavy sessions (builds, test runs, large tool outputs).

### Expected behavior
Either the runtime writes/derives the checkpoint itself before rollover, or the agent is given (and prompted to use) the tool needed to create it. Failing that, it should fall back to normal compaction instead of terminating the turn.

### Environment
- GitHub Copilot CLI 1.0.100 (also seen on 1.0.98)
- Windows 11 x64, PowerShell
- Models: GPT-6.1 Sol and Claude Opus 5.5 sessions

### Workaround
Manual `/compact` before the context fills avoids it.

### Describe the bug

The banner shows `Selected custom agent: my-agent`, then `MCP Servers reloaded: 1 server connected`, and the agent disappears from the status bar; the session falls back to the default agent.

It looks like a race between the startup agent selection and the agent/MCP refresh after sign-in. `events.jsonl` of an affected session (no user input in between):
```
14:59:11.603 subagent.selected {"agentName":"my-agent"}
14:59:11.765 subagent.selected {"agentName":"my-agent"}
14:59:11.717 subagent.selected {"agentName":"my-agent"}   <- out of order, concurrent re-selection
14:59:12.400 subagent.deselected {}
```
The deselect follows `Signed in to https://github.com` and the MCP client re-init in the process log (`Service initialized as client` -> `task cancelled` -> `Service initialized as client`).

### Affected version

1.0.95

### Steps to reproduce the behavior

1. Have a custom agent available (user-level `~/.copilot/agents/my-agent.md`, or plugin-provided).
2. Start interactively: `copilot --agent my-agent`
3. Don't type anything; watch the banner and status bar for ~2 s.
4. Agent is gone from the status bar; `events.jsonl` shows `subagent.deselected`.

### Expected behavior

The agent passed via `--agent` stays selected for the whole session.

### Additional context

- Frequency (automated pty launches, no input, 15 s each): dropped **5/6** with a user-level agent (`--agent my-agent`), **4/6** with a plugin agent (`--agent myplugin:my-agent`).
- When MCP startup failed (`Failed to start MCP Servers: session not found`), the agent was **never** dropped, which points to the MCP reload / agent-list refresh path clearing the selection.
- Workaround: run `/agent my-agent` after startup.
- macOS (Apple Silicon, arm64), zsh, launched via shell alias with `--allow-all` and several `--deny-tool` flags.

issues.title: MCP OAuth tokens for HTTP servers not reliably reused across sessions — duplicate cache-key entries force repeated re-auth

labels.name: area:authentication
labels.description: Login, OAuth, device auth, token management, and keychain integration

labels.name: area:mcp
labels.description: MCP server configuration, discovery, connectivity, OAuth, policy, and registry

issues.body:
### Describe the bug

For an HTTP-type MCP server that uses OAuth (PKCE, public client — `clientSecret: null`), Copilot CLI appears to mint a new token-cache entry under a different cache-key hash more often than expected, instead of finding and reusing the one still-valid cached token for that server.

Over about 3 weeks of normal use, I have **13 separate `<hash>.tokens.json` files** in `~/.copilot/mcp-oauth-config/` that are all for the exact same server URL + OAuth scope, when I'd expect at most one entry that gets updated/refreshed in place. Only **1 matching `<hash>.json` client-registration file** exists for that server, so the token-cache key and the client-registration key appear to diverge over time.

Two of the 13 token files were written in the same second and contain **byte-identical `expiresAt` epoch values**, which strongly suggests a single OAuth completion got persisted under two different cache-key hashes rather than one canonical entry being reused.

Separately (possibly independent, possibly compounding): none of the 13 cached tokens contain a `refreshToken` field — only `accessToken` + `expiresAt`. Observed access-token lifetime is consistently ~75–90 minutes. Since there's no refresh token, once it expires there is no silent-refresh path and the full interactive browser consent flow must run again. Combined with the cache-key issue above, the net effect looks like "the token expires in under an hour and I constantly have to re-authenticate," when it's really a mix of (a) a genuinely short-lived, non-refreshable token, and (b) the client sometimes failing to locate a still-valid cached token for the same server.

### Affected version

1.0.80

### Steps to reproduce the behavior

1. Configure an HTTP MCP server that requires OAuth (registered in `~/.copilot/mcp-config.json` with `"type": "http"`, pointing at a server behind an internal API gateway).
2. Authenticate once via the interactive browser flow.
3. Use the tool across multiple CLI sessions (including separate worktree-backed sessions) over several days.
4. Inspect `~/.copilot/mcp-oauth-config/*.tokens.json` — instead of a single file per server updated in place, multiple files accumulate for the identical server URL/scope. Some have `expiresAt` values identical to the second with another file.
5. In practice this surfaces as being prompted to re-authenticate noticeably more often than the access token's actual ~75–90 minute lifetime would suggest, i.e. sessions don't always find/reuse an already-valid cached token.

### Expected behavior

- A given MCP server's OAuth token cache entry should be looked up and updated using a single, stable cache key (e.g., derived only from server/resource URL + client ID), not one that can vary across otherwise-identical auth attempts for the same server.
- When a still-valid, non-expired cached token already exists for a server, any session should find and reuse it rather than triggering a fresh interactive login.
- If a variable value (such as the randomly chosen local loopback redirect port used during the OAuth flow) is unintentionally being folded into the persisted cache-key, that would explain the duplicate-key behavior observed above.

### Additional context

- OS: Windows 11 (Windows_NT)
- MCP server type: `http`, OAuth with PKCE, public client
- Token cache directory (`~/.copilot/mcp-oauth-config/`) is per-user/global, not per-session, so in principle tokens should already be shareable across sessions/worktrees on the same machine — but the duplicate cache-key entries above show that reuse isn't happening reliably.
- Observed access-token lifetimes across 13 samples for the same server: consistently ~75–90 minutes.
- No `refreshToken` field present in any of the 13 cached token files for this server.
- Docs describe `mcp-oauth-config/` as file-based storage used "when keychain-backed storage is unavailable." On this machine (Windows 11 with Credential Manager available) it may be worth confirming why the file-based fallback path is being used at all, since that could be related to the cache-key inconsistency.

issues.title: Remote MCP (OAuth): expired access token forces interactive re-auth instead of silent refresh_token grant

labels.name: area:authentication
labels.description: Login, OAuth, device auth, token management, and keychain integration

labels.name: area:mcp
labels.description: MCP server configuration, discovery, connectivity, OAuth, policy, and registry

issues.body:
## Summary

When a remote OAuth-protected MCP server's cached **access token** is expired at session start, the Copilot CLI treats the server as needing a fresh **interactive** OAuth login and drops its tools — even though a valid **refresh token** is cached. It never attempts an [RFC 6749 §6](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6749#section-6) `refresh_token` grant. In non-interactive/automation sessions the interactive flow can't complete, so the server's tools silently never load.

## Environment

- GitHub Copilot CLI `1.0.71`, running inside VS Code
- macOS (Darwin); credential store = Apple Keychain (`copilot-mcp-oauth`)
- MCP transport: `rmcp` streamable HTTP (`rmcp::transport::worker` / `::streamable`), `reqwest 0.13.4`

## Configuration

- Remote HTTP MCP server in `~/.copilot/mcp-config.json`:
  ```json
  "notion": { "type": "http", "url": "https://mcp.notion.com/mcp" }
  ```
- Cached grant in Keychain (`service copilot-mcp-oauth`, account `<hash>`) and `~/.copilot/mcp-oauth-config/<hash>.tokens.json` — contains `accessToken`, `expiresAt`, `refreshToken`.
- Server authorization-server metadata ([RFC 8414](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8414)) advertises refresh support:
  `token_endpoint: https://mcp.notion.com/token`, `grant_types_supported: ["authorization_code", "refresh_token"]`

## Steps to reproduce

1. Authenticate a remote OAuth MCP server (e.g. Notion) so a valid access+refresh grant is cached.
2. Let the **access** token expire while the **refresh** token stays valid (Notion access tokens last ~8h — e.g. leave it overnight).
3. Start a new Copilot CLI session (especially a non-interactive/scheduled one).
4. Observe: the server's tools are absent from the session.

## Observed behavior

From `~/.copilot/logs/process-<...>.log` (redacted):

```
[ERROR] Starting remote MCP client for notion with url: https://mcp.notion.com/mcp
[ERROR] Connecting MCP client for notion...
        -> connects to mcp.notion.com:443 using the cached (expired) access token
[ERROR] [rust:rmcp::transport::worker] worker quit with fatal: Transport channel closed,
        when Client(OAuthChallenge { www_authenticate_header:
        "...OAuth, resource_metadata=\".../.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/mcp\",
        error=\"invalid_token\", error_description=\"Mis...\"" })
[ERROR] Server notion requires authentication, initiating OAuth flow
[ERROR] OAuth authentication required for notion
```

The runtime then reads the cached OAuth entry from Keychain but still ends at **"OAuth authentication required."**

### Evidence that no refresh was attempted

Grep of the entire session-start process log:

```
POSTs to mcp.notion.com/token : 0
```

Zero `refresh_token` grants were sent, despite a valid refresh token being cached.

## Expected behavior

On a `401` / `WWW-Authenticate: … error="invalid_token"` for a server that has a cached refresh token:

1. Silently POST `grant_type=refresh_token` (+ `client_id`) to the discovered `token_endpoint`.
2. Persist the rotated access/refresh tokens.
3. Reconnect and load the server's tools.
4. Only fall back to the interactive OAuth flow if the refresh itself fails (`invalid_grant`, expired/revoked).

## Impact

- Any remote OAuth MCP server silently loses its tools once the access token expires, until a manual re-auth — even though the refresh token is valid and the whole point of storing it is to avoid exactly this.
- Breaks unattended/scheduled sessions (e.g. a daily automation), where the interactive prompt can never be completed.

## Likely root cause / where to look

- The `rmcp` streamable transport surfaces the OAuth challenge as a **fatal** transport error ("worker quit with fatal … `OAuthChallenge`"), and the CLI's handler maps "auth required" directly to the interactive flow without first attempting a token refresh.
- Secondary: the session's tool list appears to be snapshotted at startup, so even a later successful (re)auth doesn't surface the tools into an already-running session.

## Suggested fix

- Insert a refresh step in the auth-challenge path: if a `refresh_token` is cached for the server, perform the refresh grant against the discovered `token_endpoint`, persist rotated tokens, and reconnect **before** considering interactive auth.
- Optionally refresh **proactively** when `expiresAt` is at/near expiry before the first connect.
- Consider re-syncing tools into active sessions after a late auth success.

## Workaround

- Manually perform the `refresh_token` grant against the `token_endpoint`, write the rotated tokens back into the cache; or re-run the CLI's interactive auth for the server before starting the session.

---

cc @connor4312 (VS Code team)

<sub>Filed with assistance from GitHub Copilot CLI.</sub>

issues.title: Regression: Manual Approval no longer prompts for repository-mutating Git commands after Copilot harness migration

labels.name: area:permissions
labels.description: Tool approval, security boundaries, sandbox mode, and directory restrictions

issues.body:
### Describe the bug

## Critical Facts

1. **Regression introduced with the October 2026 Copilot agent harness migration.**
   - Before the migration, VS Code Copilot Chat consistently requested explicit approval before executing repository-mutating Git commands.
   - This included `git add`, `git commit`, `git push`, `git checkout -b`, `git branch -D`, merges, rebases, and similar operations.
   - After the migration to the new Copilot agent harness, some of these commands execute without approval.
   - The developer did not request or authorize a change to this approval behavior.

2. **Reproduced in both Copilot CLI and VS Code Copilot Chat.**
   - Both environments exhibit inconsistent approval behavior.
   - This suggests the problem may originate in the shared Copilot CLI agent harness or its permission-handling implementation.

3. **Manual Approval mode is explicitly enabled.**
   - Both Copilot CLI and VS Code Copilot Chat are running in Manual Approval mode.
   - Neither environment was intentionally configured to allow unrestricted tool execution.
   - The observed behavior is inconsistent with the developer's expectation that repository-mutating Git commands require approval.

4. **Controlled reproduction demonstrates inconsistent authorization.**
   - Executed `git branch -D nope` through Copilot CLI.
   - The command executed without requesting approval.
   - Git reported `error: branch 'nope' not found`, confirming the command was actually executed.
   - In the same Copilot CLI session, deleting `PR_DESCRIPTION.md` through PowerShell triggered an explicit approval request.
   - Therefore, the approval mechanism is operational but is not consistently applied to potentially destructive Git commands.

5. **VS Code terminal auto-approval is explicitly disabled.**
   - `chat.tools.terminal.enableAutoApprove` is set to `false`.
   - `chat.agent.sandbox.allowAutoApprove` is set to `false`.
   - `chat.agent.sandbox.network.allowNetwork` is set to `false`.
   - File-edit auto-approval is also explicitly disabled.
   - Investigation suggests that the new harness may execute commands through a `powershell` tool rather than VS Code's traditional terminal tool, potentially bypassing the VS Code terminal approval configuration.
   - This execution-path explanation remains a hypothesis, not a confirmed root cause.

6. **No evidence of a persisted blanket approval.**
   - `%USERPROFILE%\.copilot\permissions-config.json` does not exist in the inspected configuration directory.
   - Extensive configuration analysis has not identified an intentional authorization for automatic execution of destructive Git commands.
   - The absence of this file does not conclusively exclude other permission sources.

7. **Related existing issue.**
   - GitHub Copilot CLI issue #4156 describes `git branch -D` executing without approval.
   - https://github.com/github/copilot-cli/issues/4156
   - However, this report concerns the broader regression in Git operation approvals observed after the October 2026 harness migration.

## Expected Behavior

In Manual Approval mode, repository-mutating Git operations should require explicit authorization before execution, consistent with the behavior of VS Code Copilot Chat before the October 2026 agent harness migration.

This includes commands such as `git add`, `git commit`, `git push`, branch creation/deletion, merges, and rebases.

## Actual Behavior

Some repository-mutating Git commands execute without requesting authorization, despite Manual Approval mode being active.

Other destructive operations, such as deleting files through PowerShell, correctly request approval.

The resulting permission behavior is inconsistent and difficult for developers to predict.

## Impact

This regression undermines human-supervised, non-autonomous coding workflows.

Previously, developers could depend on the IDE to mediate repository-mutating Git operations. After the harness migration, that authorization boundary is no longer consistently enforced.

This is particularly concerning for operations such as `git push`, forced branch deletion, resets, merges, and rebases, where an unintended operation can have significant consequences.

**This is not a request for a new feature. It is a report of an established authorization behavior that regressed during the Copilot agent harness migration.**

## Environment

- OS: Windows 11
- VS Code: 1.140.0
- Copilot CLI: Manual Approval mode
- Copilot CLI version: 1.0.98
- VS Code Copilot Chat: New Copilot agent harness (October 2026 migration)
- Chat : Agent: Sandbox Enabled: off

## Requested Resolution

Restore reliable, explicit approval for repository-mutating Git operations in Manual Approval mode.

Ideally, approval enforcement should be deterministic and independent of the agent model's judgment about whether a command is safe.

At minimum, developers need a supported configuration that guarantees approval before executing Git commands that modify repository state.

### Affected version

GitHub Copilot CLI 1.0.98

### Steps to reproduce the behavior

1. Manual Permissions mode is on. 
2. No auto approval settings for repo-mutating git commands
3. ask GH CLI or VS Code copilot chat to execute `git branch -D nope` and it executes it without prompting for approval. 
4. `git push` commands and many other repo-mutating commands also execute without first requesting approval via the built-in terminal approval mechanism. 

### Expected behavior

Repo-mutating `git` commands should prompt for approval via the built-in terminal approval mechanism as it did before the October 2026 update. 

### Additional context

## Environment

- OS: Windows 11
- VS Code: 1.140.0
- Copilot CLI: Manual Approval mode
- Copilot CLI version: 1.0.98
- VS Code Copilot Chat: New Copilot agent harness (October 2026 migration)
- Chat : Agent: Sandbox Enabled: off

issues.title: [ACP] Support mid-turn steering in --acp mode (parity with interactive CLI and SDK mode: "immediate")

type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, improvement, or new functionality

issues.body:
### Describe the feature or problem you'd like to solve

_No response_

### Proposed solution

[ACP] Support mid-turn steering in --acp mode (parity with interactive CLI and SDK mode: "immediate")
中文版见下方 / Chinese version below.

Summary
In copilot --acp mode there is no way for an ACP client to deliver a message into a turn that is already running. Sending a second session/prompt while a turn is in progress cancels the running turn (stopReason: "cancelled"), kills the in-flight tool, and starts a new turn, so the model re-runs the interrupted work.

The same capability already exists elsewhere in Copilot: - The interactive CLI treats input typed while Copilot is working as steering ([Steering agents in GitHub Copilot CLI](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/copilot-cli/use-copilot-cli/steer-agents)). - The SDK / --headless protocol supports session.send(..., mode: "immediate") ([Steering and queueing](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/copilot-sdk/features/steering-and-queueing)).

Only the ACP surface lacks it. We’d like ACP to expose steering (and ideally queueing) so ACP hosts get the same behavior.

Environment
Copilot CLI 1.0.100 (@github/copilot via npm, linux-x64), copilot --acp --allow-all-tools, stdio transport
ACP protocolVersion: 1
Comparison: github-copilot-sdk 1.0.23 (Python) → copilot --headless --stdio
Reproduction
initialize → session/new
session/prompt: Run the shell command `sleep 25 && echo DONE1`, then reply with its output.
After the tool_call for bash starts, send a second session/prompt on the same session: The secret word is 9527. Include it in your final reply.
Observed (ACP): - The first session/prompt resolves immediately with {"stopReason": "cancelled"}; the running sleep is killed. - The second prompt runs as a new turn. The model says the earlier run was interrupted and re-runs the command. - Adding _meta: {"mode": "immediate"} (or "enqueue") to the second session/prompt has no effect. - Extension-method guesses all return -32601 Method not found: _session/steering, _session/steer, session/steer, _copilot/session/steer, _session/inject, session/send, session/enqueue, etc. - initialize → agentCapabilities.sessionCapabilities is {close, list}. Nothing advertises steering or queueing.

Observed (same task via SDK --headless, mode: "immediate"): - The running bash tool keeps running in the background and is not killed. - The steering message is inserted into the current session immediately, and the model acknowledges it. - When sleep finishes, the model replies with both DONE1 and 9527 without re-running the command. session.idle fires only once, at the very end.

Expected / Proposal
Expose steering over ACP as an extension method until the ACP spec covers it. The ACP v2 prompt RFD currently says it “does not specify queueing, steering, or whether agents insert new prompts while busy”. For example:

Method: _session/steering with { sessionId, prompt: ContentBlock[] } (or message: string), returning { queued: true, messageId }, with semantics equivalent to SDK mode: "immediate".
Advertise it in initialize, e.g. agentCapabilities._meta.copilot.steering: true, so clients can detect support instead of probing.
Emit a session/update when the steering message is actually injected (with the same messageId), so clients can reconcile pending messages.
Optional: a queue mode, i.e. hold the message until the current turn ends instead of cancelling.
Keep the current “second session/prompt cancels” behavior, or document it explicitly.
Precedents in the ACP ecosystem that use the same naming: - claude-agent-acp added _session/steering (agentclientprotocol/claude-agent-acp#871, PR #919, shipped in v0.64.0). - Kimi Code: MoonshotAI/kimi-code#2370 proposes mapping _session/steering to Session.steer(). - Kiro CLI 2.32.0 ships an equivalent private method (_session/steer).

Related issues
#4555: session/prompt unconditionally aborts the session, cancelling running background sub-agents (the interactive TUI does not).
#4743: end_turn precedes background-shell completion; autonomous follow-up output arrives after the prompt RPC completes, with no idle signal. A steering/queue API would likely need a clear “session idle” notification as well.
Why it matters
We embed Copilot CLI as an agent engine in a multi-engine platform via ACP. Users routinely send follow-ups while the agent is working. Today our only choices over ACP are to cancel and lose in-flight work, or to buffer client-side until end_turn, which is unreliable because of #4743. So we have to use the --headless SDK protocol instead of ACP for Copilot, even though we use ACP for other engines.

【ACP】--acp 模式支持盘中插入（steering），与交互式 CLI 和 SDK mode: "immediate" 对齐
概述
copilot --acp 模式下，ACP 客户端没有办法把消息送进正在进行的 turn。turn 进行中再发一次 session/prompt，会直接取消当前 turn（stopReason: "cancelled"），杀掉正在执行的工具，再开一个新 turn，模型随后会把被打断的工作重做一遍。

Copilot 的其他入口已经有这个能力： - 交互式 CLI 中，工作期间输入的内容默认按 steering 处理（[Steering agents in GitHub Copilot CLI](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/copilot-cli/use-copilot-cli/steer-agents)）。 - SDK / --headless 协议支持 session.send(..., mode: "immediate")（[Steering and queueing](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/copilot-sdk/features/steering-and-queueing)）。

只有 ACP 缺这个能力。希望 ACP 也能提供 steering（最好同时提供排队），让 ACP 宿主获得一致的体验。

环境
Copilot CLI 1.0.100（npm 安装 @github/copilot，linux-x64），copilot --acp --allow-all-tools，stdio 传输
ACP protocolVersion: 1
对照：github-copilot-sdk 1.0.23（Python）→ copilot --headless --stdio
复现步骤
initialize → session/new
session/prompt：Run the shell command `sleep 25 && echo DONE1`, then reply with its output.
待 bash 的 tool_call 开始后，在同一会话再发一次 session/prompt：The secret word is 9527. Include it in your final reply.
实际现象（ACP）： - 第一个 session/prompt 立刻以 {"stopReason": "cancelled"} 返回，正在跑的 sleep 被杀。 - 第二条作为新 turn 执行，模型表示前一次运行被中断，于是重新执行命令。 - 在第二次 session/prompt 上加 _meta: {"mode": "immediate"}（或 "enqueue"）没有任何效果。 - 尝试的扩展方法名全部返回 -32601 Method not found，包括 _session/steering、_session/steer、session/steer、_copilot/session/steer、_session/inject、session/send、session/enqueue 等。 - initialize 返回的 agentCapabilities.sessionCapabilities 只有 {close, list}，没有任何 steering 或排队相关的能力声明。

同一任务改用 SDK --headless 的 mode: "immediate"： - 正在执行的 bash 转到后台继续运行，没有被杀。 - 插入的消息立刻进入当前会话，模型确认收到。 - sleep 结束后，模型的回复同时包含 DONE1 和 9527，命令没有重跑。session.idle 只在全部结束时触发一次。

期望 / 建议
在 ACP 规范覆盖之前，先用扩展方法暴露 steering。ACP v2 prompt RFD 目前写明“does not specify queueing, steering, or whether agents insert new prompts while busy”。例如：

方法：_session/steering，参数 { sessionId, prompt: ContentBlock[] }（或 message: string），返回 { queued: true, messageId }，语义与 SDK mode: "immediate" 一致。
在 initialize 中声明能力，例如 agentCapabilities._meta.copilot.steering: true，客户端不必靠探测判断是否支持。
消息实际注入时发一条 session/update（带同一个 messageId），方便客户端对账待注入的消息。
可选：提供排队模式，即消息挂起到当前 turn 结束后再处理，而不是取消当前 turn。
现有的“第二次 session/prompt 会取消当前 turn”的行为可以保留，但请在文档中写明。
ACP 生态中已有同名先例： - claude-agent-acp 已新增 _session/steering（agentclientprotocol/claude-agent-acp#871、PR #919，v0.64.0 发布）。 - Kimi Code：MoonshotAI/kimi-code#2370 提议把 _session/steering 映射到 Session.steer()。 - Kiro CLI 2.32.0 提供了等价的私有方法 _session/steer。

相关 issue
#4555：session/prompt 会无条件中止会话，取消正在运行的后台子代理（交互式 TUI 不会）。
#4743：后台 shell 还没结束就先返回 end_turn，之后的自主输出出现在 prompt RPC 完成之后，而且没有 idle 信号。steering / 排队 API 大概率也需要一个明确的“会话空闲”通知。
影响
我们通过 ACP 把 Copilot CLI 作为引擎接入一个多引擎平台。用户经常在 agent 工作时追加消息。目前走 ACP 只有两个选择：取消当前 turn 并丢失进行中的工作，或者在客户端缓存到 end_turn，而后者受 #4743 影响并不可靠。所以虽然其他引擎都走 ACP，Copilot 只能改用 --headless SDK 协议。

### Example prompts or workflows

_No response_

### Additional context

_No response_

issues.title: Voice server segfaults (signal 11) on WSL2 after updating to 1.0.100; /voice stuck on 'Fetching voice models'

labels.name: area:input-keyboard
labels.description: Keyboard shortcuts, keybindings, copy/paste, clipboard, mouse, and text input

issues.body:
## Summary
After updating to Copilot CLI 1.0.100 (which also pulled a new voice runtime), voice input no longer works on WSL2. The voice server process segfaults (signal 11) a few seconds after starting, so `/voice` stays on "Fetching voice models" and no model can be downloaded.

## Environment
- Copilot CLI: 1.0.100 (linux-x64), latest at time of report
- OS: Ubuntu (glibc 2.39) on WSL2, kernel 6.18.33.2-microsoft-standard-WSL2
- CPU: x64 with AVX2, 8 cores, 16 GB RAM
- Audio: WSLg PulseAudio available (`/mnt/wslg/PulseServer`)
- Voice worked on earlier versions (e.g. 1.0.98) with the older runtime (`Microsoft.AI.Foundry.Local.Core.so`, ~645 MB)

## Steps to reproduce
1. Update to 1.0.100; the update installs a new voice runtime (`libfoundry_local.so`, ~85 MB).
2. Start `copilot` and run `/voice`, choose Continue.
3. Status shows "Fetching voice models" indefinitely.

## Actual behaviour
Process log:
```
[INFO]  voice server: boot pid=1708 endpoint=/run/user/1000/copilot-voice/<id>.sock
[INFO]  voice server: connected to spawned voice server pid=1708
[WARNING] [VoiceEngine] connection error: read ECONNRESET
[ERROR] [VoiceEngine] fatal: Engine connection closed.
[WARNING] [VoiceEngine] start failed: Engine connection closed.
```
WSL kernel log (repeated on every attempt, ~6-15s after the voice server starts):
```
copilot: MainThread: potentially unexpected fatal signal 11.
WSL (CaptureCrash): Capturing crash for pid: 1708, executable: .../@github/copilot-linux-x64/copilot, signal: 11
```

## Already tried
- Removed stale `/run/user/$UID/copilot-voice/*` socket/pid files
- Deleted `~/.cache/copilot/foundry` and `~/.github-copilot-cli/cache/models`, then re-ran `/voice` to reinstall the runtime. The crash still occurs with the freshly downloaded runtime.
- `ldd` on `libfoundry_local.so` reports no missing libraries.

## Expected behaviour
The voice server stays running, the model list loads, and dictation works.

Possibly related: #4024

issues.title: File links not clickable in VS Code Remote-SSH terminal (Windows client, macOS remote): UriError / file not found

labels.name: area:terminal-rendering
labels.description: Display and rendering: flickering, scrolling, line wrapping, output formatting

issues.body:
### Describe the bug

In a VS Code Remote-SSH terminal (Windows client, macOS remote), Ctrl/Cmd+click on file links printed by Copilot CLI does not open the file. Quick Open (Ctrl+P) with the same path works.

### Environment
- VS Code on Windows, Remote-SSH to a macOS host
- Copilot CLI running in the integrated terminal on the remote
- Related but distinct: #4885 (local Windows drive-letter paths)

### Observed
1. Link with a relative target (hover tooltip shows `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-19-...-design.md (ctrl + click)`): clicking logs in Developer Tools:

Links open the file on the remote host. The CLI should emit link targets VS Code's remote terminal can resolve (for example, absolute paths, or plain paths with no OSC 8 wrapping when `TERM_PROGRAM=vscode` in a remote session), or offer a setting to disable OSC 8 hyperlinks.

issues.body:
### Describe the bug

With tool search enabled, MCP tools are deferred and `/context` shows "MCP Tools 0" for the default agent for the whole session.

When a custom agent is selected (`--agent` or `/agent`), deferral only holds for the first model call. From the second call on, every tool of every configured MCP server is loaded into context. In my case that is 26.9k tokens (one server with ~100 tools), added to every request.

Side effect: `tool_search_tool` then returns "No tools found" because the tools are already loaded (same symptom as #4773, different cause).

It happens with a minimal custom agent that has no `tools:` list, so it is not specific to the agent content.


### Affected version

1.0.98

### Steps to reproduce the behavior

1. Configure an MCP server with many tools in `~/.copilot/mcp-config.json`, with `"toolSearch": true` and `"dynamicRetrieval": { "mcp": true }` in settings.json.
2. Create a minimal custom agent (name + description + one line of instructions, no `tools:` list).
3. Run `copilot --agent "<agent name>"`.
4. Send `hi`, then run `/context` -> MCP Tools: 0.
5. Send any second prompt, then run `/context` -> MCP Tools: 26.9k (all tools of the server listed).
6. Repeat without `--agent` -> MCP Tools stays 0 for the whole session.

Same in non-interactive mode: `copilot -p "Hi" --agent "<agent name>"`. In `~/.copilot/session-state/<id>/events.jsonl`, the `session.usage_record` events show:
- call 1: toolTokenCount=11485, inputTokens=27051
- call 2: toolTokenCount=40069, inputTokens=66329, cacheReadTokens=0 (prompt cache invalidated)
- requestBodyBytes unchanged (~170 KB) on both calls
Without `--agent`, toolTokenCount stays constant (11207) on every call.

### Expected behavior

Custom agents keep deferred MCP tool loading like the default agent: MCP tools are loaded only when found via tool search, and the tool list does not change between calls (so the prompt cache is not invalidated).


### Additional context

Windows, Claude Opus 5.5 (also seen with Claude Sonnet 5.5).
Impact: ~27-39k extra tokens on every call of every custom-agent session, plus a prompt cache miss on the second call.
Workaround: `--disable-mcp-server <name>` for servers the agent does not need.
Related: #4773 ("Found 0 tools" for an already-loaded namespace).

A local stdio MCP server that holds a credential must keep it out of the agent's reach. Copilot's local sandbox can provide that. The server can only rely on it if it can learn, at call time, which session is calling and what that session's sandbox allows.

### Proposed solution

Copilot CLI 1.0.95, used through VS Code, already appears to provide both: each session starts its own MCP server process with COPILOT_AGENT_SESSION_ID in its environment, and the runtime writes the enforced policy to ~/.copilot/session-state/<id>/policies/*.json. labels.name: area:non-interactive

labels.name: area:mcp

issues.body:
### Describe the bug

In ACP mode (`copilot --acp`), the OAuth token for a remote HTTP MCP server is never written to disk or the OS keychain after a successful sign-in. Each new ACP session (for example, each new thread in an ACP client) starts unauthenticated, gets a 401, and opens the browser authorization page again.

Evidence from a successful sign-in (macOS, Atlassian remote MCP `https://mcp.atlassian.com/v2/mcp`):

```
14:32:47.301Z [INFO] [rust:acp::mcp_oauth] opened the MCP OAuth authorization page {"server_name":"atlassian-cloud"}
14:32:47.302Z [WARNING] [rust:copilot_runtime::session::mcp::agent_host] HTTP 401 challenge (...) {"server":"atlassian-cloud"}
14:32:59.348Z [INFO] [rust:rmcp::service] Service initialized as client {...}
```

- The tools work for the rest of that session. No log line shows a token being stored.
- `~/.copilot/mcp-oauth-config/` does not exist. #4695 says this is where tokens are cached (`<hash>.tokens.json`). `COPILOT_HOME` is unset and HOME is the default.
- A scan of files modified in the two minutes after sign-in found only browser profile files. Nothing changed under `~/.copilot`, `~/.config`, `~/Library/Application Support` (excluding the browser), or the project directory.
- The keychain has no MCP or OAuth item. Only the `copilot-cli` GitHub login entry exists.
- The next ACP session, started about 50 minutes later, got a 401 and opened the authorization page again:

```
15:22:30Z [WARNING] [rust:copilot_runtime::session::mcp::agent_host] HTTP 401 challenge (...) {"server":"atlassian-cloud"}
15:22:30Z [INFO] [rust:acp::mcp_oauth] opened the MCP OAuth authorization page {"server_name":"atlassian-cloud"}
15:23:48Z ... timed out after 60s
```

So the token appears to be held only in memory for the lifetime of the ACP process.

### Affected version

1.0.98 (installed by an ACP client, macOS arm64)

### Steps to reproduce the behavior

1. Configure a remote OAuth MCP server, e.g. in the project's `.mcp.json`:
   `{"mcpServers":{"atlassian-cloud":{"type":"http","url":"https://mcp.atlassian.com/v2/mcp"}}}`
2. Start `copilot --acp` from an ACP client and open a session. The browser opens; complete the sign-in. The MCP tools work.
3. Close the session or process, then start a new ACP session in the same project.
4. The browser authorization page opens again. `~/.copilot/mcp-oauth-config/` still does not exist.

### Expected behavior

- After a successful sign-in, the token (and refresh token) is persisted, either in `~/.copilot/mcp-oauth-config/` or in secure storage per #2783.
- Later ACP sessions reuse it silently, as the 1.0.90 release notes describe ("reuses a still-valid cached token").
- Ideally, when no valid token exists, the browser opens only when an MCP tool is actually used, not at session start.

### Additional context

- Related to #4994 (the auth page opens on every ACP session since 1.0.89). This issue covers the underlying cause: nothing is persisted, so there is never a cached token to reuse.
- Also related: #4695 (duplicate cache keys preventing reuse) and #2783 (secure credential storage).
- Older 1.0.8x logs show the server only marked as "needing auth", with no browser opened.

labels.name: area:input-keyboard
labels.description: Keyboard shortcuts, keybindings, copy/paste, clipboard, mouse, and text input

issues.body:
## Description

Using Ctrl+G from the normal composer to edit a long prompt in Vim can result in the saved prompt text being missing when control returns to Copilot CLI. This has occurred repeatedly but is not deterministic.

## Environment

- Copilot CLI: 1.0.98
- OS: macOS arm64
- Editor: Vim

## Observed workflow

1. From the normal composer, press Ctrl+G.
2. Enter a long prompt in Vim.
3. Save and exit with `:wq`.
4. Return to the composer.

The newly entered text is missing. In an occurrence, the two temporary prompt files were no longer present afterward, and the session draft/history did not contain the text. No visible failure was reported.

## Expected behavior

A successful editor save should populate the composer. If the editor exits unsuccessfully or the file cannot be read back, Copilot CLI should retain a recoverable copy and show an error with its recovery location rather than silently discarding the text.

## Actual behavior

Prompt text was missing after returning from Vim, with no visible failure report and no remaining temporary copy available for recovery.

## Investigation notes

A read-only local investigation indicates that the normal composer imports content only when the external editor operation succeeds, does not surface a nonzero editor exit as an error, and cleans up the temporary file. The incident exit code is unknown; this does not establish the exact cause.

An isolated Vim `:wq` test using harmless text and `-i NONE` succeeded with exit code 0, so the exact user trigger was not deterministically reproduced.

## Workaround

Before `:wq`, save a separate permanent copy with `:write <backup-path>`.

## Suggested diagnostics and test

Please consider recording sanitized editor exit status/signal, readback outcome, and the composer state update, and retaining a recovery copy until import is confirmed.

Hypothesis-only maintainer test idea (not executed): use an editor wrapper that writes the prompt file and then exits nonzero; verify that the composer reports the failure and retains the content for recovery.

Related: #5004 concerns Ctrl+G cancelling an `ask_user` question. This report concerns the normal composer and saved prompt text loss.

issues.title: Attaching a 3840x2160 PNG wedges the TUI and kills all terminal sessions
issues.body:
### Description

# Bug report: Large payloads into TUI input wedge opencode and kill all terminal sessions

## Summary

Two distinct repros, same failure mode: pushing a large blob (image attach or clipboard paste)
through the opencode TUI wedges the whole box — all terminal windows die, keyboard rescue
(SysRq) needed. Long-running background jobs survive (launched with setsid), but every
interactive session is lost.

## Environment

- OS: Linux (Arch-ish), kernel with xe Intel GPU driver
- Terminal: multiple terminals open (kitty/gnome-term), several tmux-style workflows
- opencode TUI session running alongside heavy GPU training job (31GB RAM box, ~19GB in use)

## Repro 1 — attaching a 4K image

1. Attach a 3840x2160 PNG (phone screenshot) to a TUI message
2. opencode logs: `using resized image ... from=3840x2160 to=2000x1125`
3. ~90 seconds later the system is wedged; all terminals dead; SysRq required

Log evidence (~/.local/share/opencode/log/opencode.log):

```
timestamp=2026-10-21T02:44:16.392Z level=INFO run=a979b0c1 message="using resized image" from_mime=image/png to_mime=image/png from=3840x2160 to=2000x1125
timestamp=2026-10-21T02:52:53.520Z level=ERROR run=a979b0c1 message=process session.id=ses_ea5bca27cffer5Tr9dvNKbM42l messageID=msg_15c5f952e00117trwoJuZB0CKi error=Aborted stack=undefined
```

Kernel journal (same window):

```
Oct 21 12:45:47 ares kernel: sysrq: HELP : loglevel(0-9) reboot(b) crash(c) ...
```

## Repro 2 — pasting large text

1. Copy a large block of text to clipboard
2. Paste into the opencode TUI input
3. Same wedge: all terminals die, system unresponsive, recovery required

(Repro 2 has no log capture yet — box was wedged before a log pull was possible.)

## Suspected common cause

Both paths push a multi-MB payload through the TUI input handling (base64 image data /
multi-hundred-KB paste text). Memory spike or blocking encode in the resize/paste path
appears to take down the TUI and its terminal children. The `error=Aborted` suggests a
Go runtime abort (possibly OOM) in the session process.

## Frequency

Image crash: reproduced multiple times over several days (user reports "sometimes" —
correlates with 4K screenshots). Paste crash: reproduced at least once.

## Workarounds

- Large text: write to a file and reference the path (`@/tmp/notes.txt`) instead of pasting
- Screenshots: save to disk first, attach by path
- Long jobs: always launch with `setsid`/`nohup` — they survive the carnage

## Impact

High: total loss of all interactive terminal sessions on the machine; rescue requires
SysRq or hard reboot. Data in running sessions is lost.

issues.title: Windows: GET /api/skill returns an empty array with skill roots configured (2.0.32)
issues.body:
## Summary

On Windows, `GET /api/skill` returns `{"data": []}` even with skill roots configured, while the same request on macOS returns 48 entries. A session that already had the skill catalogue (recorded 2026-10-18) no longer receives one, so no skill can be loaded on either Windows machine.

## Environment

- opencode version: `2.0.32` on both Windows machines; `2.1.1` on macOS (same call returns 48 entries there)
- OS: Windows 11, `Microsoft Windows [Version 10.0.26300.9711]`; macOS Darwin 27.0.0 arm64
- Terminal: OpenCode desktop app (Windows); `cmd.exe` for the headless checks
- Shell: `cmd.exe` (Windows), `zsh` (macOS)
- Install/channel: release build. Windows uses the CLI shipped with the desktop app, copied to `%APPDATA%\npm\opencode.exe`; macOS uses the app's own CLI
- Active plugins: `C:/Users/usaki/.opencode/plugins/graphify/index.ts` (one machine); the other machine has no plugins. The failure is identical on both

## Reproduction

1. On Windows, configure two skill roots in `opencode.jsonc`:

   ```jsonc
   "skills": [
     "C:/Users/usaki/.config/opencode/agent-skills/skills",
     "C:/Users/usaki/.config/opencode/claude-video/skills"
   ],
   ```

2. Run `opencode api --standalone GET /api/skill`. The private service reads the current config.
3. Repeat with each of these variants, restarting the standalone service each time:
   - `"skills": []`
   - `"skills": ["C:/Users/usaki/.config/opencode/claude-video/skills"]` (one root, one skill inside)
   - backslash paths: `"C:\\Users\\usaki\\.config\\opencode\\agent-skills\\skills"`
   - tilde paths: `"~/.config/opencode/agent-skills/skills"`
4. Run the same request on macOS with the equivalent config.

## Expected Behavior

`/api/skill` lists the skills found under the configured roots, as it does on macOS (48 entries with the same packs and the same package version), and the agent receives them in its system prompt.

## Actual Behavior

Every Windows variant returns an empty list:

```json
{"data": []}
```

No skill-related lines appear in the service log, and an agent turn on that machine has no skills to load. The same packs, copied to the same relative layout, work on macOS.

## Additional Context

- The directory contents are not the cause: each root contains `SKILL.md` files with frontmatter, and the identical tree returns 48 entries on macOS.
- The config is not the cause: an empty array, a single-root array, and three path styles all return `[]`, so the loader is not reaching the configured roots at all on Windows.
- It worked on the same Windows machine before: session data from 2026-10-18 contains the model counting its `available_skills` list ("Counting the skills in the available_skills list..."), so the catalogue was delivered by an earlier build.
- Workaround tried: pointing the CLI's working directory at the config directory (rejected: `--dir` is not accepted before the subcommand), and using `--standalone` so no cached service state is involved. Neither changed the result.
- Frequency: consistent, both Windows machines, every run since the update.
- Version scope: these checks used the CLI copy at `%APPDATA%\npm\opencode.exe` reporting `2.0.32`. The desktop app on that machine was updated on 2026-10-20; the shipped CLI copy was not replaced, so the report is against 2.0.32.

issues.title: Delegated subagent write silently denied on "ask" permission (works on v1, broken on v2)
issues.body:
### Description

## Description

A primary agent delegating a write to a subagent whose permission for that path is set to `ask` silently fails on OpenCode 2.0 — no prompt is shown anywhere (checked both the main session view and any secondary/subagent view in Desktop), and no approval occurs. The subagent simply reports it cannot write, with no further detail. On OpenCode 1.x, the identical config and identical delegated write succeeds with no prompt shown either — but the write actually lands.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Configure a subagent with `edit` permission set to `ask` for a specific path (e.g. `"**/findings/**": "ask"`).
2. From the primary agent, delegate a write to that subagent, targeting a file under that path, using explicit delegation syntax (`@subagent-name — create a file at <path> containing <content>`).
3. Observe the result.

## Expected behavior

Either:
- The subagent's write succeeds (matching v1's observed behavior for the same config), or
- A permission prompt is shown somewhere in the session (main view or subagent view) that the user can approve, per the `ask` effect.

## Actual behavior

- On OpenCode 2.0 (CLI and Desktop, same config, same box): the delegated write is denied. No prompt appears in the main session view or any subagent-specific view in Desktop. The subagent reports it cannot obtain write approval.
- On OpenCode 1.x (same machine, same opencode.json, same permission rule): the identical delegated write succeeds silently — no prompt shown, but the write lands correctly.
- A write to the same path made directly by the primary agent (no delegation) succeeds silently with no prompt on v2.
- Tested three times across different, never-before-written file paths under the same `ask`-gated directory, to rule out a stale per-path approval. All three delegated attempts were denied identically; all three primary-agent direct writes succeeded identically.

## Environment

- CLI v2: 2.0.32
- CLI v1: 1.19.3
- Desktop: 2.0.32 (matches CLI exactly on this box — no version skew)
- OS: Windows 11
- Relevant permission config:
```json
  { "action": "edit", "resource": "**/findings/**", "effect": "ask" }
```

## Additional notes

This may be related to #4078 (subagent permission prompts not surfaced in the primary agent's view) — but in this case no prompt is generated at all, in any view, rather than being generated and simply hidden. It's also possibly related to the documented behavior of headless OpenCode auto-rejecting unattended permission asks — if that default now also applies to subagent sessions spawned from an interactive Desktop/CLI session, that would explain this, but that hasn't been confirmed from source.

Net effect: any `ask`-gated permission rule intended to gate a subagent's delegated writes is currently non-functional on v2 — it neither prompts nor silently allows, it just fails the write unconditionally.
