prs.title: fix(acp): treat missing cwd as stale bound session
prs.body:
## Summary

- Problem: a bound ACP session can stay attached after its persisted runtime working directory disappears, so retries keep failing against a dead session and the conversation stays wedged.
- Why it matters: affected conversations remain wedged until the stale binding state is manually cleared.
- What changed: during ACP dispatch, treat a generic `ACP_SESSION_INIT_FAILED` as stale when the bound session's persisted `runtimeOptions.cwd` can no longer be resolved on disk (`ENOENT`/`ENOTDIR`), then unbind the dead conversation. The signal is folded into the existing `isStaleSessionInitError` classifier and the existing `maybeUnbindStaleBoundConversations` dispatch helper — no new module, no parallel helper.
- Scope: dispatch-only. Two files: `src/auto-reply/reply/dispatch-acp.ts` and its test.

## Change Type

- [x] Bug fix
- [ ] Refactor required for the fix
- [ ] Feature
- [ ] Docs
- [ ] Security hardening
- [ ] Chore/infra

## Scope

- ACP stale-session classifier (`isStaleSessionInitError`) extended to accept the bound session's persisted cwd.
- Auto-reply ACP dispatch stale-binding cleanup (`maybeUnbindStaleBoundConversations`) passes the persisted cwd at the `runTurn` catch.
- Regression tests: generic `ACP_SESSION_INIT_FAILED` + missing persisted cwd unbinds; generic init failure + existing cwd does not.

## Linked Issue/PR

- Related #60720
- [x] This PR fixes a bug or regression

## Root Cause

The dispatch path already removes stale ACP bindings for selected ACP session init failures, but it classified staleness from the error message only. The live missing-cwd case surfaces as a generic spawn `ENOENT` wrapped as `ACP_SESSION_INIT_FAILED`, whose message does not match the stale-message set. The reliable signal is the bound session's persisted `runtimeOptions.cwd`: when it no longer resolves to a directory, the binding is unrecoverable. Without checking it, the stale bound conversation survives the failed dispatch and keeps routing future turns into the dead ACP session.

## Implementation Notes

- Rebased onto current `main` after the `@openclaw/acp-core` runtime extraction. The fix now extends `main`'s existing in-file `maybeUnbindStaleBoundConversations`/`isStaleSessionInitError` instead of introducing a separate `src/acp/runtime/stale-session.ts` helper (which no longer fits the post-extraction layout). The earlier `extensions/memory-core` test shim is dropped — current `main` carries that mock contract natively.
- Staleness now requires **filesystem-confirmed** absence of the persisted cwd. The unbind cannot be triggered by an error-message string alone, which removes an over-removal vector (e.g. a transient tool error whose text mentions a missing working directory). `ENOENT` and `ENOTDIR` count as missing; a present-but-unreadable cwd (`EACCES`) is treated as present so a transient permission/mount issue never severs a live conversation.

## Maintainer Decision (session-state semantics)

This removes persisted bound-conversation state when a generic `ACP_SESSION_INIT_FAILED` is paired with a filesystem-confirmed missing cwd — the recovery is correct for a permanently gone cwd, but it is session-state behavior worth explicit maintainer acceptance (per ClawSweeper's `merge-risk: session-state`). Two residual, deliberately out-of-scope behaviors to weigh:

- A transient filesystem outage (mount briefly returning `ENOENT`) on a still-valid cwd would unbind a live session. Mitigated by treating only `ENOENT`/`ENOTDIR` (not `EACCES`) as missing, but not eliminated.
- `unbind({ targetSessionKey })` removes all bindings for that session (pre-existing helper scope). For a shared-cwd session that is arguably correct, since the cwd is shared by all its bindings.

## Real behavior proof

- Behavior or issue addressed: A bound ACP session whose persisted runtime `cwd` no longer exists should be treated as stale during dispatch cleanup, unbinding the affected conversation instead of keeping retries stuck on the same dead session.
- Real environment tested: Disposable local OpenClaw gateway from this PR checkout on NixOS Linux, Telegram DM via staging bot `@kesslerClawBot`, loopback gateway port `18794`, cron/heartbeats disabled. Gateway was stopped after the proof run.
- Exact steps or command run after this patch: Started the disposable staging gateway from PR head `1ad568ba1e0db9051904eacee025ee36ec2f06ee`, sent a Telegram DM to `@kesslerClawBot` that routed through a bound ACP conversation whose persisted `runtimeOptions.cwd` pointed at `/home/art/.local/state/openclaw-staging/disposable/missing-cwd-pr68843`, let ACP dispatch fail with generic `ACP_SESSION_INIT_FAILED`, then inspected the post-run binding state.
- Evidence after fix (screenshot, recording, terminal capture, console output, redacted runtime log, linked artifact, or copied live output): Redacted public proof artifact: https://gist.github.com/kesslerio/dbefdac0c5d5a5849997b6bf702047c6. Follow-up proof comment: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/68843#issuecomment-4558022819.

  ```txt
  2026-05-27T12:18:57.491-07:00 telegram: routed via bound conversation 8352721935 -> agent:niemand-code:acp:binding:telegram:default:ecf1b7272077d0d1
  2026-05-27T12:18:57.520-07:00 telegram inbound: chatId=8352721935 ... preview="[...] PR68843 patched missing cwd cleanup proof"
  2026-05-27T12:19:06.365-07:00 [plugins] embedded acpx runtime backend ready
  2026-05-27T12:19:06.400-07:00 dispatch-acp: removed 1 stale bound conversation(s) for agent:niemand-code:acp:binding:telegram:default:ecf1b7272077d0d1 after ACP_SESSION_INIT_FAILED: Failed to spawn agent command: /run/current-system/sw/bin/codex-acp-openclaw
  2026-05-27T12:19:06.404-07:00 acp-dispatch: session=agent:niemand-code:acp:binding:telegram:default:ecf1b7272077d0d1 outcome=error code=ACP_SESSION_INIT_FAILED latencyMs=327 queueDepth=0 activeRuntimes=0
  ```

  Post-run binding state:

  ```json
  {
    "bindingCount": 0,
    "sessionKey": "agent:niemand-code:acp:binding:telegram:default:ecf1b7272077d0d1",
    "acpState": "error",
    "runtimeOptions": {
      "cwd": "/home/art/.local/state/openclaw-staging/disposable/missing-cwd-pr68843"
    }
  }
  ```

- Observed result after fix: the staging Telegram DM routed through the stale bound ACP conversation, ACPX reached the runtime backend, dispatch failed with generic `ACP_SESSION_INIT_FAILED`, and the stale bound conversation was removed because the persisted ACP cwd was missing. Post-run binding state showed `bindingCount: 0`.
- What was not tested: Production AlphaClaw was not used. This proof uses the disposable staging gateway and staging Telegram bot to avoid disrupting the live Telegram poller. A broader channel-neutral ACP proof was not run because the Telegram staging proof exercises the dispatch cleanup path directly.
- Proof limitations or environment constraints: the raw local `/home/art/...` gateway log is retained only as an operator audit pointer because it contains unnecessary routing identifiers and machine-specific details. Public proof is the redacted gist and copied transcript above.
- Before evidence (optional but encouraged): current `main` only treated selected ACP init-failure messages as stale and did not inspect persisted ACP session `cwd` metadata for a generic `ACP_SESSION_INIT_FAILED`; ClawSweeper confirmed the source-level pre-fix path in its review comment.

## Tests and validation

Commands run on rebased head `79c9e2392d` (worktree off current `origin/main`):

```sh
pnpm exec oxfmt --check --threads=1 src/auto-reply/reply/dispatch-acp.ts src/auto-reply/reply/dispatch-acp.test.ts
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/auto-reply/reply/dispatch-acp.test.ts -t "stale|cwd"
node scripts/run-tsgo.mjs -p test/tsconfig/tsconfig.core.test.json --incremental --tsBuildInfoFile .artifacts/tsgo-cache/core-test.tsbuildinfo
```

Results: formatting passed; focused stale/cwd dispatch suite passed (5 passed, 50 skipped — including the new missing-cwd-unbinds and existing-cwd-does-not-unbind cases); core test typecheck passed (exit 0).

## Security Impact

No new permissions, secrets handling, network calls, command execution surface, or data access scope. The behavioral expansion is limited to unbinding stale ACP conversations after an ACP init failure when the persisted ACP cwd is filesystem-confirmed missing.

## Compatibility / Migration

No config or migration required. The change affects only stale ACP init failure recovery.

## AI Assistance

AI-assisted rebase onto current `main`, fold-in to the existing dispatch helper, structural/correctness/adversarial review hardening, validation, and PR-body update. The live staging proof above remains valid: it unbound via the generic `Failed to spawn agent command` failure plus the missing-cwd probe, which is exactly the path this rebased head preserves.

prs.title: fix: show primary failures alongside fallback login errors
prs.body:
Closes #165135.

## What Problem This Solves

A failed primary attempt disappears from the channel reply when the fallback model also fails while refreshing its OAuth login. The shared formatter already receives the ordered attempts but returns only the final provider's login guidance.

## User Impact

The reply distinguishes the primary failure from the failed fallback. A provider-matched hard refresh deadline is reported as a timeout, without claiming that the login expired or exposing raw runtime diagnostics or channel profile IDs. Explicit expired/invalid-login recovery and single-attempt wording remain unchanged.

## Why This Change Was Made

The existing reply formatter now prefixes OAuth guidance with safe classified primary-attempt copy, and includes the failed-fallback count for longer chains. Unknown failures use generic copy and direct operators to logs. The broad failover timeout category also includes DNS/transport failures, so it alone cannot establish a refresh timeout.

This fixes reporting. It does not change credential storage, refresh/retry policy, permissions, or the underlying MCP cleanup/OAuth incident.

## Evidence

Current candidate: `02061fc69e117cd80d8ada456087bf1cc124e15f`, a normal merge of official main `131b59288f32d478f9cef689b03ca417e309a17a` into the existing PR. The upstream diff remains the original three files (+144/-3); no new production or test behavior was authored in this maintenance.

- The original real `executeAgentTurn` → error-handler → formatter reproduction failed without the patch (1 failed/25 unselected; 97.491 s including import/wrapper work). Its five regressions cover the deadline, longer chains, invalid login, ordinary transient failure, and transport failure that must not be called a timeout, with private-diagnostic controls.
- On the current merged tree, all **15 execution authentication cases and 21 formatter cases pass**. The native two-file command took **199.514 s**, including a **65.851 s** compiled-worker rebuild; Vitest reported 85.26 s and 35.76 s for the two files. The existing execution fixture runs actual reply settlement and formatting with an injected embedded-runner failure; this is not a live provider/channel proof. Most execution-file time is existing transformation/import work; this boundary also proves caller error precedence and reply settlement beyond formatter-only cases.
- The two current queued-followup custody cases pass, with 243 unrelated cases unselected. The native focused command took **756.599 s**, including native E2E build preparation; Vitest reported **157.15 s**. These are existing main tests, with unchanged deadlines, assertions, and fixtures.
- Targeted production/test types, type-aware lint, formatting, line-cap, mock-export and assertion-safety guards, docs sanity and diff checks pass. Fresh independent P0–P2 CLI review is scoped-clean; its final pass contains the complete three-file patch (earlier passes carry source/status context).

### Previous CI failure and current lifecycle contract

[Old CI 37245417264](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/37245417264) remains a failed run on `6594310b304534a26a2e780fcd255456ba6ddbeb`: the old 224-case runner file had 223 passing cases and failed `releases a queued followup after the pending tool delivery idle bound`. The same original file/order failed with this OAuth patch absent on CI base `dc518bf` and producer `605bd1` (1994.334 s including first compiled-subprocess preparation; 409.69 s Vitest). That checkout also contained a separately reviewed Doctor resolution, so the replay is not pristine-main or published-package proof.

[Shakker's merged fixture repair #165250](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/165250), commit `75b8ce01b85ea0fc777f4b5deac572bd1a5e89f6`, synchronizes the clock advance with the real drain and awaits terminal completion before inspecting the old registry. Later, [the accepted session-controller migration #175837](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/175837), commit `36e277d76147ab839a5068f4d8bc0c5254f1d05a`, changed ownership: pending delivery retains the physical session at both 29,999 and 30,000 ms until settlement. This merge preserves that current contract and its authorship. Passing the current cases does **not** mean the retired release-at-30,000-ms assertion was replayed or restored.

**Current-head broad CI:** [Natural CI 39339198467](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/39339198467) completed **success** on `02061fc69e117cd80d8ada456087bf1cc124e15f`: **67 jobs, with 38 successful executions and 29 skipped**. Observed workflow elapsed time was **3019 s**, including waiting; successful jobs sum to **6044 job-seconds**. These workflow/job wall times are separate from local file/case timings and are not billing. This result does not satisfy the shipped chat-entry-point proof request below. No workflow rerun or dispatch was requested. The old workflow took 457 s wall time / 6599 summed executed job seconds; those are prior-head historical measurements, not new-head CI time or billing.

### Remaining proof

Actual delivery of this failure through a shipped chat entry point, provider credentials/refresh behavior, and the original cleanup incident remain unverified. The existing review asks for shipped chat / Telegram Test Server proof; this focused native proof does not satisfy that request. Successful reauthentication elsewhere does not validate this candidate. No real Gateway, paid provider, installed upgrade, or permission change was used for this maintenance.

prs.title: refactor(extensions): remove private helper controls
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Private extension helpers still exposed arguments and dependency bags that no production caller used.

## User Impact

No user-visible change, migration, new configuration, or SDK/protocol change. Existing authorization, credential persistence, cancellation, retry/flood limits, and audio backpressure remain. The standalone Phase E memory backend and all associated machinery/tests are untouched.

## Why This Change Was Made

Inline the actual production values, call the canonical dependencies directly, and remove an unread private result member. Tests use existing module spies, real clocks under scoped test control, and the actual production limits instead of smaller injected limits.

This is the extension area split from the widely imported core/plugin helper family in #178807. The campaign's area-split exception applies; this is not a terminal residue or a 500-line claim. Current reduction: **77 production lines**, with **28 test lines added**, across **20 paths**. No dependency, schema, persisted-data, config key, CLI flag, or public SDK export changed.

## Best-effort tradeoffs accepted

- Browser's platform override only supported a fabricated Windows-on-POSIX test path. Real Windows validation, binding, framing, and pairing checks remain; the host now always uses its actual platform.
- Managed Codex's private probe bag was supplied only by tests. The completed installed-binary selection feature from #168228 keeps its real version/handshake probes, lazy import, deadlines, fallback, desktop exclusion, and native-path guards. Tests spy the same dependencies rather than inject alternate implementations.
- Discord's question authorization/resolver substitutions had no runtime suppliers. Native questions from #109922 still parse, await current authorization, acknowledge, resolve, and report in the same order. No authorization guard is removed.
- Reef's notifier clock and Telegram's chat-action clock were test substitutions. The same live clock is read at the same effect points; expiry, bounded tracking, scheduling, and cancellation remain.
- Telegram's only runtime chat-action caller selected a 4-second interval and the default ten-failure suspension. Those values are fixed now. The real bot-deletion protection associated with #27092, transient cooldown, retry-after handling, and topic coalescing are retained; tests exercise the actual limits.
- Voice-call's only runtime pacer used the default 960,000-byte queue cap. Keep that bound and overflow/backpressure behavior; its test now crosses the real cap instead of requesting a smaller one.
- Zalo credential capture's three callers used the process environment. The same captured state root, supervisor mode, revocation/CAS, setup authority, and durable completion from #156003 remain; arbitrary private environment substitution is gone.
- Google Chat's payload suppression clock was never supplied. The lower text helper still checks the live expiry and allowed decision from #89502. Empty/structured payloads no longer evaluate an unused clock before returning; no clock-count contract exists.
- iMessage's retry-map byte override was never supplied. The 48,000-byte and 512-entry limits, deterministic selection, and persisted cursor shape from #88797 remain; no durability or retention behavior changes.
- Telegram's forum-cache getter clock was never supplied. The real General-topic repair from #126656 / #126655 keeps cached false versus absence, TTL, capacity, explicit hints, and routing. The independently used setter clock remains.
- Copilot's private auth result `source` had no reader. Credential validation, the returned key/base URL, error behavior, and all external credential/security contracts remain.

These are unused private controls, not removal of incident fixes or security/durability guards. No live failure scenario is intentionally discarded.

## Evidence

- Whole-tree caller checks include extensions, core, packages, UI, scripts, SDK/barrel and manifest escapes. Introducing changes and in-flight activation work were checked before adoption.
- The original 16-file slice is byte-identical to individually reviewed/proved collector files; focused owner/sibling suites and selected native graphs are reused for those unchanged inputs. Real Codex probe, native Windows, transport, flow receipt, Telegram flood/coalescing, and playback assertions remain.
- Fresh selected native typecheck of the final extension roots and relevant consumers passed. Fresh independent area review found no actionable P0–P2 issue.
- Fresh additional channel proof passed 50 selected cases across five files: real Zalo credential worker/persistence, Google Chat approval suppression, Telegram helpers/routing, and iMessage's count/byte bounds. No assertions or test cases were changed for these four new source cuts.
- Final 20-file typed lint, formatting, whitespace, all 14 lint-suppression cases, and cycle checks passed (runtime and Madge both zero cycles).
- Tests run serially with one worker and isolated HOME/OpenClaw/XDG state. No live account, operator Gateway, build, E2E, broad local suite, or whole-graph typecheck was used. Exact-head PR CI is the broad gate.

prs.title: fix(gateway): finish config save responses before restart
prs.body:
Related: #120408. The non-restart config response work from #129321 is already on main.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes config.patch/config.apply restart writes losing their success response during auth rotation, and an unfinished response preventing forced restart after the deferral deadline.

## User Impact

Restart-required writes acknowledge restart admission before the initiating connection closes. An unfinished response shares the existing bounded restart deferral; at the deadline, forced restart can proceed. Clients should reconnect and use config.get to confirm the running configuration. No migration or new configuration option is required.

## Why This Change Was Made

The managed reloader now carries response settlement with the existing write receipt and counts it as pending work in the native restart coordinator. It does not await that response inside restart preparation, so the existing forced deadline remains effective. Superseded requests preserve outstanding responses, and stopping cancels the deferred restart. Auth revocation and successor-readiness checks retain their existing owners.

Integrated main at 72330e21dbf53dab4457014881a5e8cbcdd8d35a, resolved conflicts against the current reloader/dispatcher contracts, and removed superseded polling/test-support changes. Extracted the existing receipt lifecycle helpers to satisfy the source growth guard.

## Evidence

Pushed head: 0962faa2cbc70ac6d4ddf56d85f27566aedf58a3. [Exact-head CI](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/39363548855) is running; no merge or auto-merge was requested.

- Before: both stalled-response regressions fail against the unbounded preparation wait: no restart emission at 300,000 ms.
- After: 333 focused tests pass across nine suites. The fake-clock regressions verify forced emission at the deadline, ordinary response ordering, supersession, and cancellation. Real loopback WebSocket tests cover both config methods with simultaneous auth rotation.
- Final-source reruns: all six changed test files pass; the reloader's 133 tests pass after extraction. Unchanged-input restart infrastructure and reload-handler proof was retained.
- Built runtime profile qaRuntime passes (78.9 seconds). Through pnpm openclaw, both config.patch and config.apply with gateway.controlUi.basePath changes plus token rotation receive success before auth closure and production restart emission; the successor reaches ready and authenticated config.get confirms the final configuration. Temporary Gateway state/processes were cleaned up.
- Formatting, scoped lint (zero warnings/errors), core typecheck, whitespace, line-growth, and timeout-race guards pass. Independent full-candidate review and extraction-delta review are scoped-clean for P0-P2.
- Verification gap: an earlier isolated port-change probe acknowledged and restarted correctly, but the in-process CLI successor retained the original listener port; new-port reconnection failed. Port relocation is not claimed fixed by this PR.
- Full check:changed is not green: three UI max-lines suppressions and core test-shard root budgets (gateway-root 725; plugins-platform 726; cap 720) reproduce on clean pinned main. No baseline/suppression exceptions were added. The broad typegraph continuation was stopped after core and Gateway graphs passed; full PR CI remains separate evidence.

prs.title: feat(googlechat): add sessionThread option to bind OpenClaw sessions to Google Chat threads
prs.body: AI-assisted: yes (Claude Opus 4.7). ## Summary - Problem: In Google Chat, all messages in a space shared a single OpenClaw session. Starting a new thread to change topic still inherited memory from prior threads, and replies did not reliably land in the user's inbound thread. - Why it matters: Chat threads are the natural topic boundary in Google Chat. Leaking context across threads produces confusing replies ("why does the bot remember something from a different thread?"), forces multiple concurrent threads to queue sequentially on one session, and breaks the mental model users already have from Slack. Requested in #13373. - What changed: Added an opt-in `sessionThread` channel option. When `true`, the OpenClaw session peer id is derived from the inbound thread name, so each Google Chat thread is its own conversation. Replies are now threaded via `thread.name` + `messageReplyOption=REPLY_MESSAGE_FALLBACK_TO_NEW_THREAD`, so bot responses land in the user's thread. - What did NOT change (scope boundary): Default behavior is unchanged (`sessionThread: false` keeps space-scoped sessions). No changes to auth, allowlists, webhook routing, DM flow, reactions, or attachments. No slash commands / `/focus`-style bindings added (see "future work" below). ## Change Type (select all) - [x] Bug fix - [x] Feature - [ ] Refactor required for the fix - [x] Docs - [ ] Security hardening - [ ] Chore/infra ## Scope (select all touched areas) - [ ] Gateway / orchestration - [ ] Skills / tool execution - [ ] Auth / tokens - [ ] Memory / storage - [x] Integrations - [ ] API / contracts - [ ] UI / DX - [ ] CI/CD / infra ## Linked Issue/PR - Closes #13373 (per-thread session mode feature request) - Closes #41788 (Google Chat replies creating new threads instead of staying in the existing one) - Related #44347 — resolves the first of the two requests in that issue - [x] This PR fixes a bug or regression ### Note on naming vs the issue's proposal The issue proposes `threadSessionMode: "per-thread" | "per-space"`. This PR ships the same behavior under a boolean flag `sessionThread: boolean` (default `false` = per-space, `true` = per-thread). Rationale: - A boolean matches the two-state nature of the option and is simpler to document. - The name aligns with the existing session-scoping vocabulary in the codebase. - Happy to rename to `threadSessionMode` with a string enum if maintainers prefer the issue's exact wording, it's a straightforward rename. ## Root Cause (if applicable) - Root cause: The Google Chat channel used the space id as the session peer id and did not pass the inbound thread name back on outbound messages. That coupling meant (a) all threads in a space mapped to one session, and (b) replies could fall back to a new thread instead of the user's. - Missing detection / guardrail: No peer-id unit coverage for Google Chat; Slack already has `prepare.thread-session-key.test.ts` as prior art for this exact pattern, but nothing equivalent existed for Google Chat. - Contributing context (if known): Google Chat threads were less prominent historically in OpenClaw flows; the space-scoped default was acceptable until users started relying on threads to separate topics. ## Regression Test Plan (if applicable) - Coverage level that should have caught this: - [x] Unit test - [ ] Seam / integration test - [ ] End-to-end test - [ ] Existing coverage already sufficient - Target test or file: `extensions/googlechat/src/monitor.session-thread.test.ts` - Scenario the test should lock in: `resolveGoogleChatPeerId` returns the thread name when `sessionThread` is enabled and an inbound thread is present; falls back to `spaceId` otherwise; and produces distinct peer ids for distinct threads so sessions do not cross. - Why this is the smallest reliable guardrail: The peer id is the single point where "which session does this message belong to?" is decided for Google Chat. Locking its behavior at the helper boundary catches the regression without pulling in the full monitor stack. - Existing test that already covers this (if any): None for Google Chat. Slack's `prepare.thread-session-key.test.ts` covers the analogous primitive. ## User-visible / Behavior Changes - New opt-in config: `channels.googlechat.sessionThread` (default `false`). - `false` (default): space-scoped sessions, prior behavior unchanged. - `true`: one OpenClaw session per Google Chat thread; a new thread starts a fresh conversation. - Outbound messages now consistently target the inbound thread via `thread.name` + `messageReplyOption=REPLY_MESSAGE_FALLBACK_TO_NEW_THREAD`, so replies land in the user's thread more reliably. This applies regardless of `sessionThread`. ## Diagram (if applicable) ```text sessionThread: false (default, unchanged) space S, thread A -> session(peer=S) space S, thread B -> session(peer=S) # shared memory sessionThread: true space S, thread A -> session(peer=A) space S, thread B -> session(peer=B) # isolated memory space S, no thread -> session(peer=S) # falls back to space-scoped ``` ## Security Impact (required) - New permissions/capabilities? No - Secrets/tokens handling changed? No - New/changed network calls? No (same Chat API endpoints; only request payload now sets `thread.name` and `messageReplyOption`) - Command/tool execution surface changed? No - Data access scope changed? No (in fact, `sessionThread: true` narrows memory scope per thread) ## Repro + Verification ### Environment - OS: macOS - Runtime/container: Node 22 / local gateway (`pnpm openclaw gateway restart`) - Model/provider: any (provider-agnostic) - Integration/channel (if any): Google Chat - Relevant config (redacted): ```jsonc { "channels": { "googlechat": { "enabled": true, "serviceAccountFile": "/path/to/service-account.json", "sessionThread": true } } } ``` ### Steps 1. In a Google Chat space, mention the bot in thread A and ask an identifying question (e.g. "remember the color red"). 2. Start a new thread B in the same space and ask "what color did I mention?". 3. Reply again inside thread A and ask the same question. ### Expected - `sessionThread: true`: in thread B, the bot has no memory of thread A. In thread A, the bot still remembers "red". Replies land in the thread the user messaged in. - `sessionThread: false` (default): behavior is unchanged from prior releases. ### Actual - Matches expected for both modes. ## Evidence - [x] Failing test/log before + passing after ``` pnpm test extensions/googlechat/src/monitor.session-thread.test.ts ✓ resolveGoogleChatPeerId returns spaceId when sessionThread is disabled ✓ resolveGoogleChatPeerId returns spaceId when sessionThread is undefined (default) ✓ resolveGoogleChatPeerId returns thread name when sessionThread is enabled and inbound has a thread ✓ resolveGoogleChatPeerId falls back to spaceId when sessionThread is enabled but inbound has no thread ✓ resolveGoogleChatPeerId produces distinct peer ids for distinct threads so sessions don't cross Test Files 1 passed (1) Tests 5 passed (5) ``` - [ ] Trace/log snippets - [x] Screenshot/recording - When disabled(previous behavior): - When enabled: - [ ] Perf numbers (if relevant) ## Human Verification (required) - Verified scenarios: - Manually verified in a real Google Chat space against a local gateway: - Bot replies land inside the user's inbound thread (both existing threads and thread-starter messages). - With `sessionThread: true`: new thread = fresh session; prior thread keeps its own context; no cross-thread memory leakage. - With `sessionThread: false`: unchanged, space-scoped memory. - Edge cases checked: - Inbound message with no thread (thread-starter): falls back to space-scoped session as designed. - Two concurrent threads in the same space maintain separate sessions. - What you did **not** verify: - Bot-initiated outbound into a space with no prior inbound thread context (no webhook-origin thread). This PR intentionally does not introduce a `threadKey` fallback for that case; the follow-up work below can add richer binding if demand emerges. - DM flow (no behavior change expected; DM scope is already per-channel-peer). ## Review Conversations - [x] I replied to or resolved every bot review conversation I addressed in this PR. - [x] I left unresolved only the conversations that still need reviewer or maintainer judgment. ## Compatibility / Migration - Backward compatible? Yes - Config/env changes? Yes, additive only: new optional `channels.googlechat.sessionThread` boolean (default `false`). - Migration needed? No. Existing configs continue to behave as before. - If yes, exact upgrade steps: N/A. To opt in, set `channels.googlechat.sessionThread: true`. ## Risks and Mitigations - Risk: Users relying on cross-thread memory in a space would lose that if they set `sessionThread: true` without realizing the implication. - Mitigation: Default is `false`; docs call out the per-thread isolation explicitly; the name `sessionThread` signals the intent. - Risk: `resolveGoogleChatPeerId` is a new exported helper surface from the plugin's `monitor.ts`. - Mitigation: Kept it narrow (one pure function) and it is only consumed inside the extension itself; no public SDK subpath added. ## Future Work (non-blocking) This PR adds the minimal primitive, matching Slack's auto thread-scoped session behavior, just gated behind an opt-in flag for Google Chat. A follow-up could align with the Telegram/Discord `session.threadBindings` model (`/focus`, `/unfocus`, `/session idle`, `/session max-age`) on top of this primitive. That work requires registering slash commands in the Chat API app config and wiring `SLASH_COMMAND` events, which is out of scope here.

prs.title: fix(memory): prevent duplicate Gemini batch jobs after timeouts
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Gemini native embedding-batch creation is non-idempotent. If a create response is lost or times out after the provider accepted it, an immediate retry can create a second paid remote job. The provider assigns the batch name only in the response and does not expose a caller-supplied idempotency key.

- https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/batch-api#best-practices
- https://ai.google.dev/api/batch-api#method:-models.asyncbatchembedcontent

## What Changed

This version treats batch submission as a crash-recoverable ownership protocol:

- Memory Core persists an exclusive reservation in the published memory database before Gemini's non-idempotent create call.
- Acknowledged provider batch names are attached to that reservation as soon as they are returned.
- Each request set has a deterministic SHA-256 fingerprint; manifests retain content-independent custom IDs and chunk hashes, not source text, credentials, or vectors.
- Restarted managers adopt an acknowledged job only when its exact request fingerprint matches.
- Completed output is reconciled by stable chunk hash and published idempotently to the shared embedding cache, including when source enumeration has drifted since submission.
- Ambiguous create outcomes remain quarantined. Definitive non-ambiguous 4xx rejections (except 408) release the reservation.
- The reservation is cleared only after local cache/index publication commits.
- Closing a manager aborts local polling without cancelling or duplicating an accepted remote job.
- Gemini's native-batch failure mode remains fail-closed instead of fanning a large migration into synchronous paid requests.
- Status output exposes the submission, provider job, timestamps, and recovery state.
- Deliberate quarantine clearing requires both `--force` and `--clear-batch-quarantine`.

The ownership record lives in the published database while a shadow rebuild remains isolated. Independent managers serialize reservation changes through SQLite immediate transactions.

## User Impact

Interrupted Gemini memory migrations can resume acknowledged work without resubmitting already accepted requests. Operators get an explicit quarantine for genuinely ambiguous remote ownership instead of hidden duplicate spend or an uncontrolled synchronous fallback.

## Evidence

Exact candidate head: `ca2a3d6a9bcb7215a9dfba22f8407b06ab116206`

Candidate base at construction: `044cf2e6e027591e6361dbd2784a8b9c68959e18` (`upstream/main` at the time)

- Focused Google provider/lifecycle tests: **67/67 passed**.
- Memory integration tests: **235/235 passed**.
- Plugin contract suite: **1,117/1,117 passed**.
- Total: **1,419 tests passed**.
- Core and extension production/test TypeScript checks passed.
- Changed-file structural, dependency, formatting, documentation, SDK, and extension-boundary gates passed.
- Documentation validation passed: 1,294 MDX files, 13,239 internal links with 0 broken, and 1,224 config examples.
- Full production build passed, including 91 external plugins, 152 public SDK subpaths, CLI bootstrap, and Control UI performance gates.
- `git diff --check` passed.
- A secrets/logging audit found no credentials, request text, vectors, or authorization values added to logs.

The implementation has also been exercised against a real authenticated Gemini migration outside CI: completed jobs were reconciled, cache entries advanced, and a subsequent quota rejection occurred before a new provider job ID was assigned. Completed fingerprints were not replayed. No provider identifiers or credentials are included here.

## Scope

This PR intentionally adds no quota-size, parallelism, or retry-policy configuration. It does not alter production deployment files. Provider transport remains in the Google extension; Memory Core owns durable publication and recovery state.

## Required Before Ready/Merge

- Upstream CI must pass on this exact head.
- An independent exact-head review must complete; the author-side GCP environment does not currently have an independent Codex reviewer identity, so this is not being bypassed.
- Maintainers must approve the fail-closed ambiguity/quarantine contract and its operator-recovery tradeoff.

This PR is kept as a draft until those gates are satisfied.

prs.title: fix(prompt): unbounded channel context arrays and objects flood the model prompt
prs.body:
Related: #119213 — the review feedback there flagged this exact spot (the unbounded `sanitizeContextJsonValue` in `channel-prompt-context.ts`); this PR addresses that feedback directly.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users whose channels or plugins attach structured context to inbound messages — group directories, member lists, reply chains, or other channel-supplied payloads — would have the entire array or object serialized into the model prompt with no size limit: thousands of entries and hundreds of kilobytes in a single context block. The prompt grows far beyond what the operator expects, token spend inflates, and useful context gets crowded out of the window.

The affected surface is the user-role context blocks built on the inbound reply path (`Conversation info:`, `Reply chain of current user message:`, and one block per structured-context entry), plus the equivalent user-message boundary block in the embedded agent runner.

## Why This Change Was Made

The prompt-context sanitizer already capped every string at 2,000 chars, but it mapped arrays and objects through with no bound on entry or key counts, so one channel payload could carry unlimited repeated entries into the prompt. Two budgets now apply, each measured against the largest first-party payloads:

- **Per-block, inside the JSON sanitizer** (`channel-prompt-context.ts`): arrays cap at 20 entries and objects at 50 keys (50 leaves headroom over the largest first-party payload, the Conversation info block at ~25 keys) — these bound fan-out. On top of them, one **cumulative serialized-character budget of 50,000 chars per block** is shared across the whole recursion through a mutable counter: the per-container caps alone cannot bound the total (50 keys × 20 entries × 2,000 chars passes every per-level cap yet serializes ~2 MB). 50k is ~2.6× the largest measured first-party block (a 10-link reply chain at ~19k serialized chars, each body already at the 2,000-char string cap). Nesting is capped at **depth 8** (4× the deepest measured first-party payload, which nests 2 levels). Key text is channel-controlled too, so keys are now capped and neutralized like string values and charged to the budget. When the budget runs out, the walk stops adding siblings and appends an explicit `…[truncated: context budget exhausted]` marker; the depth cut emits `…[truncated: max depth reached]` — the serialized block stays valid, parseable JSON in every case.
- **Per-message, in the inbound context assembly** (`buildInboundUserContextPrefix` in `inbound-meta.ts`): one **cumulative budget of 150,000 chars** covers labels plus every emitted block — Conversation info, reply chain/target, forwarded, location, chat-window and one block per structured-context entry (whose count is unbounded), chat history, goal, and current-message blocks. The largest measured first-party assembly (group Conversation info + 10-link reply chain + forwarded/thread-starter blocks + 20-entry chat history) totals ~43k chars, so 150k leaves ~3.5× headroom. When it is spent, later blocks are dropped behind a single `…[truncated: inbound context budget exhausted]` marker line, stamped with the same `⟦openclaw:ctx⟧` provenance marker as every other injected header so strippers recognize it.

Non-goals: no change to the per-string cap, the history bound, or the chat-window formatter.

## Response to round-3 review

Both findings were correct; both fixes live in `channel-prompt-context.ts` and no new constant or export was added.

**String channel-context path bounded.** The canonical `ChannelPromptContext` string array reaches the prompt through `appendChannelPromptContext` (called from `prompt-prelude.ts`), a body join that never passes through the inbound context assembly — the assembly budget covers the runtime-only context prefix, not the command body these strings are appended to, so the bound belongs at the append point rather than in the assembly. The string form is one model-visible context block exactly like the fenced JSON blocks, so it now shares the same per-block cumulative budget (`MAX_CONTEXT_JSON_BLOCK_CHARS`, 50k — the measured justification carries over unchanged: one block is one block, whichever form it takes). Entries are kept whole while the budget lasts; the first entry that would overflow is head-truncated with `…[truncated]` (same convention as `truncateContextJsonString`) and the drop is flagged with the same `…[truncated: context budget exhausted]` marker as the JSON path, so both forms now cross one bounded, uniformly-marked boundary. The envelope-level regression builds a full `buildReplyPromptEnvelope` with 5,000 × 2,000-char channel strings: `prefixedCommandBody` was ~10 MB and is now < 51k chars ending in the marker.

**Escaped keys charged by their JSON size.** Raw key length undercounted exactly as described: a key of N raw chars emits ~2N once quotes and backslashes are escaped. The object walk now reserves each property's serialized size — the `JSON.stringify` length of the escaped key plus the serialized value — before appending it; a property that would cross the remaining budget is dropped behind the budget marker instead of overshooting, so the emitted block can no longer approach twice the budget while the counter reads under it. The covering test mixes backslashes, quotes and a control char in every key: raw key text totals 40,140 chars (the old counter stayed under 50k and accepted the block) while the emitted keys total 70,290; the emitted JSON now stops at 49,657 chars, carries the marker, and parses cleanly.

## Response to the P1 review

The review was correct: per-level count caps bound fan-out, not total size — a 50-key object of 20-element arrays of 2,000-char strings passed every limit and emitted ~2 MB, and nesting depth and key text were unrestricted. The rework follows the suggested shape: the inbound context assembly now owns one cumulative serialized-character budget (150k) spanning labels and all structured entries, while the JSON sanitizer enforces a per-block cumulative budget (50k, shared across the recursion) and a depth cap (8), always preserving valid JSON with an explicit `…[truncated: …]` marker. The saturated nested payload from the review (2,014,851 chars raw) now serializes to 40,099 chars with the marker and parses cleanly; the per-container caps (20/50) stay because they bound fan-out within the budget. All budget values are measured against the largest first-party payloads (see Evidence), not picked arbitrarily.

## Response to round-4 review

The nested-budget finding was correct, and the repair is split into two reviewable commits at the same sanitizer owner boundary.

- `062cd6316d9` (`fix(prompt): avoid double-charging nested context`) sanitizes candidates against a scratch copy of the remaining budget at both recursive retain edges (object property and array element), then charges the parent exactly once for the serialized value it actually keeps. This preserves the exact ClawSweeper object → array repro (`{ payload: Array(20).fill("x".repeat(2_000)) }`, 40,073 JSON chars) and the sibling array → objects shape (40,269 chars) byte-for-byte, without a marker.
- Review of that commit found one remaining acceptance gap: the array parent retained a sanitized candidate even when its serialized size exceeded the remaining parent budget. `e090a2a82e2` (`fix(prompt): enforce nested array budget`) mirrors the object acceptance check: measure the sanitized candidate, omit it when it does not fit, set budget exhaustion, and commit its cost only when accepted.

### [P1] Preserve the current reply target before exhausting the budget — fixed

Its cost is now **reserved up front**, the same way the exhaustion marker already reserves its own, and released when the block is emitted.

prs.title: fix(whatsapp): bound deferred ingress handoffs
prs.body:
## Summary

- Keep the shared ingress watchdog bounded before and after explicit deferred handoff.
- Preserve the original claim-time deadline for every caller that does not configure a distinct deferred window.
- Let opted-in owners reset the watchdog at handoff so healthy scheduler waits receive their own bounded adoption window.
- Give WhatsApp a deliberately long seven-day operational bound instead of the generic five-minute bound.
- Fail closed with `handler-timeout` when a deferred scheduler never adopts or abandons, aborting late work and releasing the conversation lane.
- Close the shared state database before Windows test cleanup so SQLite-backed owner tests remove their temporary directories reliably.
- Keep core reply-queue lifecycle helpers out of the Plugin SDK test surface; exercise the WhatsApp owner proof through the supported `turnAdoptionLifecycle` contract.

Related to #120265 and #116547. This fixes the WhatsApp owner path without introducing an unbounded scheduler-owned deferral mode.

## What problem this solves

The generic ingress watchdog is appropriate while a claimed message is dispatching, but WhatsApp may legitimately defer adoption while its debounce and reply scheduler waits behind an active turn. Applying the same five-minute clock across both phases can dead-letter healthy queued work.

Clearing the watchdog after handoff is also unsafe: WhatsApp's scheduler has terminal callbacks but no independent liveness timeout, so a never-settling scheduler promise could refresh the durable claim and block the conversation lane forever.

This revision uses two bounded policies:

1. the generic watchdog starts at claim time and remains unchanged for callers that do not opt in;
2. an explicit `deferredAdoptionStallTimeoutMs` resets the watchdog only when deferral actually occurs;
3. WhatsApp opts into a seven-day operational safety bound for that second phase;
4. a missing terminal callback aborts and dead-letters the claim, rejects late adoption as guillotined, and lets the next same-lane message proceed.

The seven-day value is an operational recovery policy, not a scheduler-derived semantic maximum. A renewable scheduler heartbeat remains the stronger future refinement if arbitrarily long healthy waits must be supported.

## Safety and public contract

- No unbounded scheduler-owned deferral mode remains.
- Callers without an explicit post-handoff timeout keep the original claim-time deadline.
- The post-handoff clock resets only for an owner that explicitly configures it.
- Adoption and abandonment cancel the post-handoff watchdog.
- Timeout preserves claim-token fencing, abort, `handler-timeout`, and failed-tombstone behavior.
- Late adoption after timeout fails loudly instead of replaying work.
- The Plugin SDK channel documentation explains omission, explicit deferral reset, timeout behavior, the WhatsApp seven-day policy, and the renewable-lease alternative.
- Internal reply-queue admission helpers remain core-owned and are guarded by a negative SDK source-contract regression.
- Production configuration, services, queues, credentials, and WhatsApp traffic were not touched.

## Review verdict and scope

- Best-fix verdict: the distinct opt-in deferred watchdog is the narrowest compatible seam. A core-wide reset would change every channel, while clearing the watchdog would make lost scheduler ownership unbounded.
- Production TypeScript: **+38 / -11**.
- Tests: **+362 / -8**.

- Focused behavior proof: **61/61 tests passed** across four files and two Vitest shards covering WhatsApp durable receive, the mock-socket inbox owner path, the core deferred watchdog, and the core drain contract.
- SDK-boundary repair proof: the new negative source-contract regression failed before the fix with exactly the two leaked queue helpers, then passed after their removal; the complete affected WhatsApp file passed **17/17**, the complete SDK contract file passed **18/18**, and the focused core lifecycle-owner slice passed **3/3**.
- Windows cleanup regression: the first run's only failures were ten `EBUSY` removals of open SQLite temp files; the repository's test-only database closer was added before cleanup, after which all focused tests passed.
- Core production types passed: `pnpm tsgo:core`.

- Plugin SDK surface check passed: 336 total entrypoints, 7,738 total exports, 151 public entrypoints, 4,847 public exports, and zero forbidden package subpaths.
- Exact changed-file type-aware lint, formatting, and `git diff --check` passed.
- Mandatory trusted exact-final-branch autoreview completed with **0 accepted/actionable findings** and **0.99 correctness confidence** (254,237-byte one-pass bundle).
- TruffleHog's exact committed branch scan passed clean against frozen `main`, including the review runner's independent 7.5-second scan.

## Owner-path proof available today

The current automated proof reaches the real OpenClaw ownership seams but uses an ephemeral durable queue and mock Baileys socket. It does not use credentials or send live traffic.

```json

Core-owner tests separately prove queue admission behavior, reset-at-handoff timing, timeout dead-lettering, late-adoption fencing, and adoption/abandonment timer cancellation.

## Outstanding acceptance — do not merge yet

1. Maintainers must explicitly accept the seven-day WhatsApp delivery-versus-recovery tradeoff. This PR documents the proposed operational policy but does not assume that product decision.
2. The mandatory real Baileys/WhatsApp lost-adoption trace is still missing. The mock-socket path above must not be represented as live external-account proof, and no synthetic external traffic should be created to satisfy it.

prs.title: fix(ui): model provider card buttons do not name their provider
prs.body:
Closes #178261

## What Problem This Solves

On Settings > Model providers, every provider card has Connect provider, Test connection, Set API key and Remove key buttons that are named only by their visible text, so with two providers a screen reader's button list or voice control hears "Remove key, Remove key" with no provider (repro in the issue). Remove key deletes the saved key without a confirmation.

## User Impact

Screen reader and voice control users hear "Remove key: OpenAI", "Test connection: Anthropic" and so on, and can tell which provider a button acts on. The visible text and layout do not change.

## Why This Change Was Made

The four buttons in `ProviderActions` (`ui/src/pages/model-providers/view.tsx`) now get an `aria-label` built from four new English keys next to the existing ones (`login.actionNamed`, `probe.testNamed`, `apiKey.setNamed`, `apiKey.removeNamed`, each `"<existing label>: {name}"`) with the card's `displayName`, the same name the card heading shows. This is the same pattern as #178140 (`<label>: <row>` form) and #178162 (named keys beside the existing ones, label left off while the button shows a busy text). Each name starts with the visible text, so the visible label stays inside the accessible name (WCAG 2.5.3). While a probe runs, Test connection reads "Testing…"; the label is left off in that state so the accessible name is the visible "Testing…" rather than a stale "Test connection: OpenAI". The names use a colon after the visible text ("Remove key: OpenAI"); the existing `*Named` keys in this UI use a space ("Remove {name}"). Both keep the visible label first, which is what WCAG 2.5.3 needs; the colon reads more clearly when the visible text is itself two or three words and the provider name follows. Either form is a one-string change per key if maintainers prefer the space form.

The regression test is a sibling file, `view.provider-actions.test.ts`, because `view.test.ts` is at the 1000-line test cap. E2E specs that matched these buttons by their old exact name now use the full name, and three card-scoped `getByLabel("API key")` lookups became exact, since that substring now also matches the "Set API key: OpenAI" button.

Contract:

| Case | Outcome |
|---|---|
| Card with no account and a sign-in option | Connect provider named "Connect provider: {name}"; visible text "Connect provider" |
| Card with credentials | Test connection named "Test connection: {name}" |
| Card that supports API keys | Set API key named "Set API key: {name}" |
| Card with a config or removable API key | Remove key named "Remove key: {name}" |
| Two or more providers | Every card action has a distinct name (measured with `openai` "OpenAI" and `anthropic` "Anthropic") |
| Probe in flight | That card's Test button reads "Testing…", disabled, named "Testing…" (no label); other cards unchanged |
| Probe finished | Name returns to "Test connection: {name}" |
| Key editor open | All four names unchanged |
| Key save or Remove key in flight | That card's Set API key and Remove key are disabled and keep their named labels |
| Key write finished | Names unchanged; after Remove key the card's Remove key and Test connection are gone and the other card keeps "Remove key: OpenAI" |
| Sign-in dialog open | Every Connect provider is disabled and keeps its named label |
| Not handled here | A per-provider busy name such as "Testing OpenAI"; the page-level Connect provider button in the section header (not per provider); focus after Remove key |

## Evidence

All of the following ran on one machine at the staged tree, base `82919eb7cc1`.

**Build.** `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` (exit 0). The browser runs use the repo's Control UI E2E harness (`pnpm test:ui:e2e`), which builds this tree's Control UI and answers Gateway requests with `installMockGateway`: two synthetic providers, `openai` ("OpenAI") and `anthropic` ("Anthropic"), each with an API key in config (`[redacted]`), an OAuth login option, and `apiKeySupported: true`. `models.probe`, `models.authSetApiKey` and `models.authLogout` are held pending with `deferNext` to capture the busy state, then resolved the way the Gateway does (for Remove key, `config.get` and `models.authStatus` first return the provider without its key). BEFORE = this branch with only `view.tsx` and `en-settings.ts` reverted to base (tests kept); AFTER = this branch. Same spec in both arms, both exit 0. The UI sent the same writes in both arms: `models.authSetApiKey {"provider":"openai","agentId":"main","apiKey":"synthetic-cui23-key"}` and `models.authLogout {"provider":"anthropic","agentId":"main","credentialType":"api_key"}`.

**Behaviour, Settings > Model providers**, headless Chromium, 1280x1000, dark. Nine states per arm, in order: idle; Test connection on OpenAI clicked with the probe pending (busy) and then resolved (settled); Set API key on OpenAI clicked (editor open), Save with the write pending (busy) and resolved ("Secret saved.", settled); Remove key on Anthropic with the write pending (busy) and resolved ("Saved API keys removed.", settled); Connect provider on Anthropic clicked (sign-in dialog open). Each record lists every button in the two cards' action rows (provider, aria-label, visible text, disabled), `getByRole("button", { name, exact: true })` counts inside the provider list (the section header has its own page-level Connect provider button, so counts are scoped to the list that holds both cards), then each card's actions `ariaSnapshot` and the buttons' `outerHTML`, read from the DOM. Playwright quotes a snapshot name that contains a colon, so `'button "Remove key: OpenAI"': Remove key` is button, accessible name, then visible text. In every state the BEFORE and AFTER `outerHTML` lines differ only by the `aria-label` attribute (checked by script: removing `aria-label="…"` from each AFTER line gives the BEFORE line byte for byte). Screenshots of the provider list are byte-identical between arms in all nine states (`cmp`); the proof is the accessibility tree.

prs.title: fix(google): report embedding batch lifecycle statistics
prs.body:
Related: #120889

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an observability gap where operators running Gemini native embedding batches could not see the provider-reported request totals, success/failure/pending counts, lifecycle timestamps, elapsed time, or whether downloaded results fully reconciled with submitted requests.

The Gemini embedding API exposes `createTime`, `updateTime`, `endTime`, `batchStats`, state, and output metadata, but the adapter previously discarded those fields.

- https://ai.google.dev/api/embeddings#method:-models.asyncbatchembedcontent
- https://ai.google.dev/api/embeddings#embedcontentbatch

## Why This Change Was Made

The Google adapter now normalizes both current top-level Batch fields and the legacy Operation-metadata shape, with top-level terminal fields taking precedence over stale metadata. It emits structured subsystem events when a job is created, reaches a terminal state, and reconciles output.

Successful events report provider counts/timestamps plus separate provider and locally observed durations. Terminal failures report only structured provider codes. Output transport, HTTP, parse, record, missing-response, and unusable-metadata paths emit sanitized failure classes and reconciliation counts.

Durable events never include request text, provider error text, authentication, file URLs, response bodies, request IDs, or embedding vectors. Existing thrown error behavior and debug callbacks are unchanged.

This PR intentionally adds no configuration or quota claims. Public numeric batch knobs were deliberately retired upstream, and a real concurrency ceiling requires one shared admission semaphore across both file scheduling and group submission. That design remains separate follow-up work.

## User Impact

Operators can diagnose Gemini batch progress and failures from durable, structured evidence without enabling payload-level debug logging or exposing user content. The counts distinguish returned embeddings, provider record errors, genuinely missing responses after clean EOF, and unreconciled responses after transport/parse failure.

## Evidence

- Exact refreshed head: `2f67cd46baaaf29072427f27c5588cabd481fd3d`.
- The branch was refreshed by a normal merge from validated upstream `main` at `e97c3450a2724a6189762fa0d6c76284b9b83071`; no rebase or force-push was used.
- 27/27 focused Gemini batch tests pass, including the disposable loopback HTTP lifecycle.
- Regression coverage includes current and legacy API shapes, canonical top-level output precedence over stale legacy aliases, fail-closed rejection when conflicting legacy output aliases lack a canonical field, provider statistics/timestamps, terminal failure/cancel/expire states, output HTTP/parse/record errors, full-stream reconciliation after a record error, missing output metadata, fallback and provider timing semantics, and log-content secrecy.
- All four TypeScript surfaces pass: core production, core tests, extensions production, and extensions tests.
- Plugin SDK API baseline, export synchronization, and public-surface checks pass; no SDK regeneration was required.
- Targeted formatting, direct type-aware extension lint on both changed files, and `git diff --check` pass.
- The repository lint wrapper was attempted twice and timed out during broad plugin-boundary artifact preparation after 124 seconds and 304.1 seconds without a diagnostic. It is not counted as green; the underlying repository `oxlint` binary completed the equivalent type-aware two-file lint cleanly in 70.1 seconds.
- Mandatory isolated autoreview passed on the final branch against the frozen validated base: TruffleHog v3.95.9 reported the exact patch clean in 3.6 seconds, and Codex `gpt-5.6-sol` with high reasoning reviewed one complete 27,812-byte bundle and returned no accepted/actionable findings (`patch is correct`, confidence 0.98).
- Exact-head CI [run 31476497307](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/31476497307) is terminal with 29 successful and 15 skipped jobs; its only underlying failure is [`build-artifacts`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/31476497307/job/93731653297), followed by the aggregate gate. prs.title: fix(agents): yield between restart-recovery store probes
prs.body:
Closes #149935

## What Problem This Solves

On a multi-agent install, restart-recovery discovery probes every configured store synchronously — an admission-refusal read plus a status read per store — so gateway startup blocked for the combined length of all probes (reporter: 237 agents ≈ 63.6s startup freeze; their measured maxGap 31,020ms × 2 → 1,372ms after a two-point yield change).

## What Changed

- Discovery probes stores in the same order but yields one macrotask between targets (`setImmediate`), so timers queued before the scan run mid-scan while eligibility and ordering stay identical (`main-session-restart-recovery-shared.ts`).
- The recovery loop runs stores one macrotask apart for the same reason (`main-session-restart-recovery-runtime.ts`).

## Evidence

- New regression (`main-session-restart-recovery-yield.test.ts`): a timer queued before discovery runs while the scan is still probing, and both stores still come back eligible and sorted. Red on `origin/main` (the blocking chain never yields), green on this head.
- Suites: recovery 223/223, `session-accessor.readonly` 26/26, `server-startup-post-attach` 115/115, `check-changed` clean (all tsgo lanes + ratchets).
- Per the sweeper's acceptance note, the shared `resolveAllAgentSessionStoreTargetsSync` and the eligibility/`toSorted` ordering are untouched.


## Update — 2026-09-29 (Rev 1 follow-up: interleaving proof pinned)

- The regression now observes from a queued immediate **while the scan is unsettled** and counts the probes: with two stores the observation must land **between probe 1 and probe 2** (`observedProbes === 1`), so a single yield before all probes — or none — fails the test (`main-session-restart-recovery-yield.test.ts`). Red on `origin/main` (no yields: the observer runs post-settle).
- Measured runtime: the new test file runs in ~0.25 s (`pnpm test <file> --maxWorkers=1` wall ~2 s including boot).
- Still open: an after-fix multi-store Gateway observation for the body — the local verification above is the rerunnable artifact for the interleaving itself.


## Update 2 — 2026-09-29 (Rev 2 follow-up: cancellation recheck)

- The recovery loop now rechecks `shouldContinue` **immediately after the inter-store yield** (`main-session-restart-recovery-runtime.ts`): a stop landing during the yield no longer lets `recoverStore` synchronously load the next store before its own cancellation check.
- Regression: with two running stores and cancellation landing at the post-yield recheck, `recoverStore` is never invoked (0 calls, empty counts) — on the previous head it still ran once for the first store. Red-checked against `origin/main`.
- Still open: the after-fix multi-store Gateway observation (environment-dependent).


## Update 3 — 2026-09-29 (Rev 3 follow-up: discovery cancellation)

- Discovery now threads the runtime's `shouldContinue` through (`main-session-restart-recovery-shared.ts`) and breaks between store probes, mirroring the recovery loop's post-yield recheck: a stop landing during a discovery yield skips the remaining probes.
- Regression: with two running stores and cancellation landing after the first probe, discovery returns one target and `hasSessionEntriesByStatusReadOnly` runs exactly once — red on the previous head.
- The recovery loop passes its `shouldContinue` through the existing params spread, so shutdown now stops both phases between probes.


## Update 4 — 2026-10-02 (Rev 4 follow-ups)

- **Cancellation test pinned to the recovery yield**: the shared `shouldContinue` callback also serves discovery now, so the previous counter let cancellation land during the second discovery probe — the post-yield recheck went unpinned. The test now queues the cancellation when discovery finishes (call 9 on this fixture), landing it inside the first inter-store recovery yield: with the guard the store is skipped entirely (`recoverStore` never runs, counts stay zero); without it `recoverStore` loads the store synchronously and the test fails/hangs. Red-checked with the guard removed.
- **Main merged** (`cc77b17c6f8`, main `b72a95e3f75`): main's async status-probe discovery kept as the structure; this PR's per-target macrotask yield and the shared-cancellation threading layered on top. Discovery + recovery suites green on the merged head (150 + 3/3).
- Still open: after-fix multi-store Gateway timing evidence (environment-dependent).


## Update 5 — 2026-10-05 (Rev 5 test retune)

Retuned the three regressions for the worker-backed inventory (call cadence and probe timing changed):
- The mid-scan timer observation now chains off probe 1's completion and requires the scan to be unsettled at that moment.
- The recovery-yield guard pin now lands cancellation at the first recovery pre-check (call 7 of 8 on the two-store fixture), asserting `recoverStore` never runs.
- Entry cancellation (already-cancelled at discovery entry) pins discovery stopping before any probe.
- The between-probe discovery cancellation timing is environment-dependent with worker-backed probes; it is covered by inspection and noted here rather than pinned flakily.


## Update 6 — 2026-10-05 (rationale after main's worker cutover)

Main's worker-backed inventory moved the status reads off the Gateway thread, which changes what this PR is for. The remaining synchronous main-thread chain in discovery is the per-store admission-refusal probe, and the recovery loop still runs real recovery work per store. This PR now guarantees:

- One macrotask boundary between stores in both phases, bounding the remaining synchronous chain (admission refusal in discovery; recovery work in the recovery loop) so timers queued before startup recovery run mid-scan.
- Both phases honor `shouldContinue` at those same boundaries — cancellation stops the scan/recovery before the next store is touched.
- The regressions pin each boundary (mid-scan timers, recovery-yield cancellation, entry cancellation, discovery-stop).

prs.title: docs: correct container gateway bind defaults
prs.body:
Follow-up to #61818.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: standalone-container guidance says the Gateway defaults to loopback even though detected-container startup defaults to `auto` and resolves to `0.0.0.0`.

## User Impact

User impact: container operators can distinguish listener reachability from host port publication, and EasyRunner deployments get the external browser origin required by their Caddy hostname.

## Why This Change Was Made

The Dockerfile and Gateway docs now describe the detected-container default, fail-closed authentication requirement, container-network reachability, and the fact that the image creates no host port mapping. The EasyRunner example keeps an explicit `--bind lan` to pin proxy intent and adds the matching `gateway.publicOrigin`. Runtime behavior is unchanged.

## Evidence

Real container proof ran from the repository Dockerfile at exact head `db4a4dcfb0a76b3dc148a5242e7d970d47e2e072` on Docker Engine 28.5.2 (Linux amd64). The image build metadata reported the same commit. Its default command was `["node","openclaw.mjs","gateway"]`, with no bind flag. The task-owned config omitted `gateway.bind` and `gateway.controlUi.allowedOrigins`, set Tailscale to `off`, required token auth, and set `gateway.publicOrigin` to `https://gateway.example.test`.

- Startup/listener: the Gateway emitted `[gateway] http server listening`; `lsof` reported `TCP *:18789 (LISTEN)`.
- No host publication: the image reported `ExposedPorts={}`; the running Gateway reported `PortBindings={}` and `NetworkPorts={}`; `docker port` produced no output. No `-p` or `--publish` option was used.
- Container-network reachability and auth: an authenticated OpenClaw peer on the task-only bridge connected with protocol 4. The same route with an intentionally wrong synthetic token was rejected with `unauthorized: gateway token mismatch`.
- Caddy/public-origin trace: task-only Caddy served `https://gateway.example.test/healthz` as `{"ok":true,"status":"live"}`. A paired client from the exact-head image identifying as `openclaw-control-ui` connected over WSS with `Origin: https://gateway.example.test`, protocol 4, and `operator.read`; the same client and valid token with `Origin: https://mismatch.example.test` was rejected with `origin not allowed`.

<details>
<summary>Selected redacted runtime output</summary>

```text
[gateway] http server listening (14 plugins; 9.0s)
openclaw-   7 node 78u  IPv4 <redacted> 0t0 TCP *:18789 (LISTEN)

Gateway.Cmd=["node","openclaw.mjs","gateway"]
Gateway.PortBindings={}
Gateway.NetworkPorts={}
Gateway.docker-port=<no output>
```

```json
{"scenario":"peer-authenticated-final","result":"connected","protocol":4,"authMode":null,"grantedScopes":[]}
{"scenario":"peer-wrong-token-final","result":"rejected","error":"unauthorized: gateway token mismatch (provide gateway auth token)"}
{"scenario":"caddy-origin-match-final","result":"connected","protocol":4,"authMode":null,"grantedScopes":["operator.read"]}
{"scenario":"caddy-origin-mismatch-final","result":"rejected","error":"origin not allowed (use gateway.publicOrigin with allowedOrigins omitted, or allow this origin in gateway.controlUi.allowedOrigins)"}
```

</details>

The Caddy container had no host-published ports. Its exact task-private source address was listed in `gateway.trustedProxies`, and Caddy overwrote the forwarded client headers. The TLS CA, credentials, network, containers, state, and browser identity were synthetic and task-owned; secrets, private addresses, IDs, and ephemeral ports were redacted. This exercised the production browser protocol over real WSS through Caddy rather than a GUI browser session. Task-only Docker resources and secret-bearing state were removed after capture; the repository remained clean at the exact head.

Focused validation also passed:

- Docker build/cache/digest/Dockerfile unit specs: 12 passed
- Docker install-script specs: 71 passed
- `pnpm check:docs` (15,734 internal links, zero broken)
- `git diff --check`
- Codex Security immutable patch-risk assessment: `merge` / `human_review_required`; its initial Tailscale exception finding was corrected and the amended commit was reassessed clean
- Repository autoreview: no accepted/actionable findings (`patch is correct`, confidence 0.93); TruffleHog clean

The aggregate test wrapper compiled its shared worker but exited before emitting a Vitest diagnostic in this environment. The same 83 requested specs passed directly through their owning unit and tooling Vitest configurations.

prs.title: fix(diagnostics-otel): gateway stalls after every model call when content capture is on
prs.body:
Closes #158116

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: with `diagnostics.otel.captureContent: true`, the gateway blocks its event loop for minutes after each model call once a session's prompts carry a lot of text, tool output or image data.

## User Impact

User impact: a gateway with content capture enabled stays responsive on large sessions, and it still exports redacted, size-bounded content attributes.

On one gateway running a busy Telegram group session (prompts well over 1M characters), the main thread blocked for ~150 s after every model call. All three bots on that gateway stopped answering for 40 minutes: Telegram polling stalls, `/readyz` timeouts, liveness heartbeats overdue by ~150,000 ms. Setting `captureContent: false` cleared it immediately.

Gateways that set `logging.redactPatterns` still redact every captured string whole, as main does, and export the same attributes as main. They get a smaller speedup: 32.2 s -> 3.5 s for the slowest model call measured below.

Content small enough to export untruncated is now also redacted string by string before serialization. Before, it was only redacted as serialized JSON, where escaping turns a line break into `\n` and hides a line-start `password=...` from the text rules, so the value was exported unmasked.

A value whose JSON is over the 128 KiB attribute budget but fits once its secrets are masked is exported whole, as on main, for JSON up to 4x the budget (`a98c2d54130`), and past that when what made it large is a secret the export window cut open, such as a JWT with a 600,000-character payload (`3425a53b077`). The price is one whole-value redaction pass for every captured value between 1x and 4x the budget, including those that then still have to be truncated: up to 8x the budget, measured below.

## Why This Change Was Made

`safeJsonString` redacted the whole serialized value only to find it was over the 128 KiB attribute budget. It then tried up to 63 truncation budgets, and every attempt redacted each string in full before cutting it. That ran once each for `gen_ai.input.messages`, `input.value` and `openclaw.content.input_messages` (and again for outputs and tool definitions), so redaction work grew with prompt size x attempts x attributes, all on the main thread.

With this change:

- The truncation budget is chosen from unredacted sizes; only the candidate that gets exported goes through the redactor.
- A clipped string is redacted over its kept prefix plus a lookahead: 4,096 characters, or the longest registered secret when that is longer. A secret that starts before the cut and ends inside the lookahead is masked as it would be in the full text. Registered secrets only match whole, so the longest one always fits; core reports its length through a new `getLongestRegisteredSecretLength()` in `openclaw/plugin-sdk/logging-core`, counting the URL-encoded and JSON-escaped forms it registers with each value.
- Some secrets need a part the lookahead can cut off: a private key block without its END line, a quoted secret without its closing quote, a JWT without its signature, a URL password without the `@` after it, an Atlassian `ATATT` or `ATCTT3xFfG` token without its `=` suffix, and a form first pair's value without the `&key=` after it. When the window ends inside one of these, the string is redacted whole by the shared redactor instead, while its export can afford it: 8x the export's size, so 1,048,576 characters for a content attribute and 32,768 for a log body. For a JSON value past 4x the attribute, the strings redacted whole are then substituted, and the value is exported whole if it fits. Past the budget, the window masks the secret from its start, after masking registered values whole the way the shared redactor does first.
- Core tells whether the window ends inside such a secret, through a new `findTruncatedSecret(text)` in `openclaw/plugin-sdk/logging-core` (`src/logging/redact-open-secret.ts`). For the rules that run as linear matchers (the Atlassian tokens, JWTs, both URL password rules, form first pairs and private keys) it runs the shared matcher itself over the window's last run of non-whitespace characters (the whole window for private keys) with a closing appended: `=AAAAAAAA`, a JWT payload and signature, `@`, the rest of a form pair's `&key=` (`&a=`, or `a=` after a bare `&`, or `=` after the start of a key), an END line. A match that runs into the closing, or that the window alone does not hold, is open, and is masked from where the redactor would start its mask. So the check follows each rule's prefixes, letter case, boundaries and `;base64,` exemption. For quotes, it asks the redactor whether the key before the last quote of each kind, a stand-in value and the closing quote would be masked; the probe skips whitespace between the key and the quote, starts its key context on a non-word character, looks only at its own stand-in, and stays under 512 characters. A quoted value that a form rule also reads (`api_key="...`) keeps its closing quote.
- Configured `logging.redactPatterns` replace the default string rules, and a configured rule can need any amount of text after the start of its match. When they are set, every string is redacted whole and the 8x cap below is off, as on main. Core reports this through a new `hasConfiguredRedactPatterns()` in `openclaw/plugin-sdk/logging-core`, which reads the same logging config the redactor does.
- Masks shorten a redacted window, so the export could reach the window end and show part of a fixed-length secret the cut split. A window its masks shorten is redacted once more, wider.
- Clipped text sent to the redactor is capped at 8x the attribute budget per JSON candidate; a candidate over the cap falls through to the next, smaller budget. When the cap rules out every candidate that would fit the attribute, the export keeps 16, then 4, then 1 object fields, so fewer strings are clipped and each keeps more text. Only when that also fails is the export `{"truncated":true,"reason":"max_redaction_work",...}` instead of `max_attribute_size`.
- `normalizeOtelLogString` (log bodies, log attributes, string content) uses the same bounded prefix.
- `input.value` and `output.value` reuse the `gen_ai.*` serialization instead of producing it a second time.
- JSON up to 4x the attribute budget is redacted whole first (each string, then the serialized JSON) and exported whole if the result fits. A credentials dump shrinks by about half when masked, so main exported such values complete and this branch used to truncate them. The pass sends at most 8x the budget to the redactor, the cap a truncated candidate already has; past 4x, and when the result still does not fit, truncation runs as before. Since #161480 the redactor's built-in rules scan the whole text, so the pass masks a token wherever it falls in a long string.

Without configured `logging.redactPatterns`, redaction work per content attribute is now bounded by the attribute budget plus the longest registered secret, instead of the prompt size. Masks and quote probes can make a clipped string cost up to about five windows, so a JSON attribute's work can exceed the 8x budget it is chosen by: 6.3M characters for a model call with 200 tool results full of masked secrets, against 248.6M on main's code for the same input (Evidence). A value between 1x and 4x the budget adds its whole-value pass on top: at most 17x the budget per attribute when it does not fit. Strings redacted whole because their window ended inside a secret add at most 8x more, and the substituted pass for a value past 4x at most 8x again. With configured rules, work still grows with the prompt, but only the exported candidate is redacted.

## Evidence

<!-- remediation-2026-10-20:start -->
