prs.title: fix(channels): honor Telegram 429 retry_after via shared per-token flood gate
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master`
- **What changed and why:**
  - Telegram Bot API 429 responses were treated like formatting failures: `sendMessage` retried immediately as plain text (a markdown→plain double-hit), draft edits kept their cadence, and the typing loop never noticed — so a rate-limited token got hammered, its penalty escalated, and finalized replies were lost (issue #11615).
  - This adds a flood-control gate (`TelegramRateLimiter`) shared **by the clones of one channel instance** (channel fields, spawned typing loop, approval paths) — it is *not* a registry keyed by bot token: separately constructed channels on the same token, including repeated one-off announcement factories, keep independent windows. Gated surface: the channel's text traffic — `sendMessage` (final answers, draft creation, approval prompts), `editMessageText` (draft updates, finalize), and `sendChatAction` in the recurring typing loop. Initial inbound typing hints, model-picker sends and text/markup edits, approval-resolution text edits, acknowledgement reactions, media uploads, `deleteMessage`, and `answerCallbackQuery` still post directly and are not covered by this gate.
  - Droppable calls (typing, draft edits) skip silently while the window is open. Deliver calls wait the window out bounded by a caller-side budget (`rate_limit_max_wait_secs`), **re-check the shared gate after sleeping**, and stop with a distinguishable budget-exhausted outcome if the window is still active — the budget bounds how long the caller waits, never the server deadline, so nothing is sent into an active window. On a fresh 429 a Deliver call retries once; a second 429 contributes its own (possibly longer) `retry_after` to the shared window and stops the formatting/resume/resend fallbacks — a 429 is not a formatting failure.
  - The recorded deadline keeps the later of the active and new values, so out-of-order concurrent 429 responses cannot shorten the window; an unrepresentable delay is rejected rather than clamped into permission to send sooner.
  - Honors `retry_after` from the JSON envelope (`parameters.retry_after`), with a `retry after <N>` description fallback and a 5s fallback when nothing is parseable.
  - Partial deliveries still suppress the orchestrator's full-answer resend via `FinalizePartialDelivery`, and flood-control exhaustion now stops the chunk-resume path as well instead of burning the wait budget twice. The pending-narration loop in multi-message finalization also stops on the terminal gate outcome: instead of burning three narration retries plus a final-answer wait on fresh budgets, it propagates the gate error, so the outer resend is suppressed without reporting an undelivered final answer as delivered.
  - Two new optional telegram channel config keys: `rate_limit_max_wait_secs` (default 60; `0` restores the default — it is not a disable switch) and `typing_refresh_interval_secs` (default 4, previously hardcoded). Both resolve from the live config authority at each use, including per-tick in the typing loop, so a published change applies to a running channel without a rebuild.
- **Scope boundary:** adaptive draft throttling and any listener-side changes are explicitly out of scope (per maintainer triage on #11615); no behavior change when no 429 occurs — the pre-send gate is a no-op on `Clear`.
- **Blast radius:** Outbound paths of the Telegram channel only (`send_text_chunks`, `send_draft`, `update_draft`, `finalize_draft`, `start_typing`, approval send) plus one guard in the orchestrator's finalize-fallback arm. No change to inbound/listener logic, other channels, or the agent loop. Defaults keep today's behavior for well-behaved tokens.
- **Linked issue(s):** Related #11615. Related #11608.

### What this does, simply

Telegram tells throttled bots exactly when to come back (`retry_after` in the 429 body), but the channel ignored that and fired again immediately — markdown attempt, then plain attempt, then more draft edits and typing ticks. Each ignored window made the next one longer, and when the final reply finally hit the limit it was dropped: users saw drafts vanish mid-sentence. Now the channel records "blocked until N seconds" per channel instance (shared by its clones) the moment a gated call sees a 429, keeping the longest active deadline. Gated cosmetic traffic (recurring typing indicator, live draft edits) stays silent during the window; user-visible sends wait out the server-directed window up to a bounded caller budget and try again once. When the window clears within budget, the reply is late instead of dropped. When the window outlasts the budget, nothing is sent into it: the answer is held and an error is returned — this slice has no durable delivery queue or automatic later redelivery, so such a reply can go undelivered (WARN-logged) until the sender retries; the gated callers stop retrying inside the recorded window and suppress blind resends of accepted chunks. The direct-call exclusions listed above still apply.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** `N/A` — the rate-limit interaction is fully covered by mock-server tests (429-then-success, repeated limiting with escalating deadlines, blocked-window skipping, budget expiry without resend, mid-wait window extension, cancelled waiter, cross-chat window sharing, gated draft creation, live-config resolution, pending-narration finalize stop with zero and nonzero accepted prefixes); a live 429 cannot be induced reliably without flooding a real bot token.

### How I tested

```sh
cargo fmt --all -- --check
cargo clippy -p zeroclaw-channels --all-targets --no-deps -- -D warnings
env -u HTTP_PROXY -u HTTPS_PROXY -u ALL_PROXY cargo test -p zeroclaw-channels telegram
env -u HTTP_PROXY -u HTTPS_PROXY -u ALL_PROXY cargo test -p zeroclaw-channels finalize
```

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** channels/config unit and integration tests cover the changed surface (telegram channel + config schema).
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` at workspace level shows pre-existing warnings in platform-conditional code outside this diff (unix-gated code on a Windows host, Windows-only service code); none originate from this change, and the channels crate itself is `-D warnings` clean. Two pre-existing `zeroclaw-config` test failures reproduce on unpatched master (`agent_bundle::…outside_shared_is_dropped_with_its_content`, `platform::native::…powershell_full_scripts_execute_with_native_semantics`).
- **Commands run and tail output (head `fe42c5d30`):** `cargo test -p zeroclaw-channels telegram` → `test result: ok. 429 passed; 0 failed`; `cargo test -p zeroclaw-channels finalize` → `test result: ok. 23 passed; 0 failed` (including the two new `finalize_stops_on_flood_gate_with_{zero,nonzero}_accepted_narration_prefix` regressions and the retained transient-retry controls).
- **Beyond CI, what did you manually verify?** Author-reported live observation (distinct from CI signals): ran an earlier revision of this change as a production Windows service against live Telegram for 24h — 3 real 429s observed (previously 7+ per incident), zero `failed to reply` events, every post-429 turn delivered after the gate window. This predates the review-round semantics tightening; the current head's budget/no-resend and pending-narration-stop behavior is covered by the mock-server regressions above, not by live observation.
- **Visual interface evidence:** `N/A` — no presentation change.
- **Tested revision, interface, and evidence path:** `fe42c5d30` on branch `fix/telegram-429-retry-after`; terminal test output above.
- **If any command was intentionally skipped, why:** the full `cargo test -p zeroclaw-channels --lib` run from the previous round was not repeated at this head; the changed surface (pending-narration finalization, flood gate) is covered by the `telegram` (429 tests) and `finalize` (23 tests) filters above. `cargo test --test integration telegram_` remains un-run locally (link step needs more free disk than this host currently has); the equivalent behavior is covered by the in-crate wiremock tests.

## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? (`No`)
- New external network calls? (`No`)
- Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? (`No`)
- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? (`No`)
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? (`No`)

## Compatibility (required)

- Backward compatible? (`Yes`)
- Config / env / CLI surface changed? (`Yes`)
- Rust/MSRV/toolchain floor changed? (`No`)
- Upgrade steps: none required. The two new telegram channel keys are optional with defaults matching prior behavior (`rate_limit_max_wait_secs = 60`, `typing_refresh_interval_secs = 4`). Existing configs load unchanged.

## Rollback (required for medium/high-risk PRs)

- **Fast rollback command/path:** `git revert <merge-sha>` of this PR's merge commit.
- **Feature flags or config toggles:** none — `rate_limit_max_wait_secs = 0` restores the default 60s wait budget; it is not a disable/rollback switch. Rollback is reverting the PR.
- **Observable failure symptoms:** grep runtime trace for `failed to reply` or `Telegram sendMessage failed` reappearing, or users reporting vanished drafts/answers again.

prs.title: fix(deps): patch Wasmtime 48.0.7 for RUSTSEC-2026-0375..0379
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master`
- **What changed and why:**
  - Bump `wasmtime`, `wasmtime-wasi` and `wasmtime-wasi-http` from 48.0.6 to 48.0.7 in `crates/zeroclaw-plugins/Cargo.toml`, and re-lock. Five RustSec advisories against 48.0.6 now fail `cargo audit` in the Security job on every PR:
    - RUSTSEC-2026-0378 (`wasmtime`): panic lowering a host-created component model stream into a guest that expects a different payload type
    - RUSTSEC-2026-0379 (`wasmtime`): Cranelift on aarch64 can jump to the wrong target on a large `br_table`
    - RUSTSEC-2026-0375 (`wasmtime-wasi-http`): p3 guests can set an incorrect content-length for spliced response bodies
    - RUSTSEC-2026-0376 (`wasmtime-wasi-http`): guests can add conflicting content lengths
    - RUSTSEC-2026-0377 (`wasmtime-wasi-http`): p3 forwarded trailers aren't checked against `is_forbidden_header`
  - Each advisory names 48.0.7 as a fix within 48.x, so this stays a patch-level move, the same as the 48.0.4 to 48.0.6 bump in #11755.
- **Scope boundary:** only the wasmtime family moves in `Cargo.lock`: 30 packages, all 48.0.6 to 48.0.7, or 0.135.6 to 0.135.7 for Cranelift. No move to 49.x, and no other dependency changes.
- **Blast radius:** the WASM plugin host. As with any wasmtime patch release, precompiled `.cwasm` components are tied to the exact wasmtime version, so runtime-only builds need components precompiled for 48.0.7.
- **Linked issue(s):** Related #11755, Related #11475

### What this does, simply

ZeroClaw's plugin host uses Wasmtime to run WASM plugins. Five security fixes for the version we pin were published on 19/10, and the security check now fails every pull request until we take them. This moves to the patched release in the same 48.x line and changes nothing else.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** N/A. This is a lockfile-level patch bump. The Security job and the plugin tests cover it.

### How I tested

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** Security (`cargo audit`) proves the advisories are cleared. The build and test jobs build the plugin host.
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** None known.
- **Commands run and tail output:**

```text
cargo audit                                             exit 0 (master's Cargo.lock: exit 1 on RUSTSEC-2026-0375..0379)
cargo test -p zeroclaw-plugins --features plugins-wasm-cranelift --locked
  test result: ok. 417 passed; 0 failed   (lib)
  integration suites: 23, 11, 3, 3, 3 (+1 ignored), 2, 1 passed; 0 failed
cargo check --locked                                    ok
cargo check --locked --features plugins-wasm-cranelift  ok
```

- **Beyond CI, what did you manually verify?** `cargo audit` on master's `Cargo.lock` exits 1 on exactly these five advisories; on this branch it exits 0, with only the existing allowed warnings left.
- **Visual interface evidence:** N/A

## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? No
- New external network calls? No
- Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? No
- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? No
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? No

## Compatibility (required)

- Backward compatible? Yes, except that precompiled `.cwasm` plugins must match the wasmtime version, as with every wasmtime patch bump
- Config / env / CLI surface changed? No
- Rust/MSRV/toolchain floor changed? No

## Rollback (required for medium/high-risk PRs)

Low risk: `git revert <sha>`. Reverting brings the five advisories back.

prs.title: feat(channels): add optional Telegram rich messages
prs.body:
Send headings, lists, quotes, and tables through Bot API `sendRichMessage` when `channels.telegram.<alias>.rich_messages` is enabled. The flag defaults to false. With it off, replies stay on the existing HTML path, and markdown tables are sent as preformatted text so they are not split or interpreted as inline HTML.

## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master` (all contributions)
- **What changed and why:**
  - Telegram has no HTML table tag, so markdown tables were sent as ordinary text and could be split mid-table. Native rendering now exists behind `channels.telegram.<alias>.rich_messages` because some clients still cannot show rich messages.
  - With the flag on, final replies use `sendRichMessage` for headings, lists, quotes, and tables. Tables wider than 20 columns are fenced as code. Math delimiters outside code are removed so amounts like `$400` are not parsed as formulas, and markdown images become links.
  - With the flag off, the HTML path is unchanged except that every markdown table is wrapped in `<pre><code>`. A table that fits stays in one chunk. A longer table continues on the next message between rows, with the header repeated, and `(continues...)` / `(continued)` markers when a message is split.
  - Inbound updates that have a `rich_message` and no `text` are turned into plain markdown so the agent can still read them.
  - Streaming drafts stay plain text. On finalize, a prepared reply that fits the rich-message limit is edited in place. If that edit fails, the existing HTML edit, plain edit, and delete-then-send path runs. A failed delete on that path skips the replacement send.
- **Scope boundary:** This does not change other channels, the bot token, pairing, attachments, or draft streaming while a reply is still being generated. It does not turn rich messages on by default, and it does not add a client-capability probe.
- **Blast radius:** Every Telegram reply that contains a markdown table, including aliases that leave the flag off. With the flag on, final replies and over-long splits use `sendRichMessage`, falling back to HTML if Telegram rejects the rich payload. Inbound rich-only messages become normal user text.
- **Linked issue(s):** Fixes #8415

### What this does, simply

Telegram replies are HTML. HTML cannot draw a table, so a markdown table showed up as pipe characters, and a long answer could cut the table in half. Telegram's newer rich-message API can draw headings, lists, quotes, and tables, but not every client understands it yet.

This adds `rich_messages` on each Telegram alias. Leave it unset or `false` and ZeroClaw keeps sending HTML. Tables are then placed in a preformatted block so the grid stays intact. A table longer than one message continues with the header repeated. Set it to `true` and final replies go out through `sendRichMessage`. A running channel reads that alias setting from the live config on each send. If that call fails, the same text is sent as HTML, and a later retry continues at the first HTML piece that did not arrive. Draft updates while the model is still writing stay plain text either way. A message that arrives with only a rich body, and no normal text, is converted to markdown before the agent sees it.

```toml
[channels.telegram.home]
rich_messages = true
```

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** Yes
- **Interface(s) exercised:** `channel` (`telegram`)
- **Setup / preconditions:** A Telegram bot token, a configured alias, an authorized peer, and `zeroclaw channel start`. Use a client that can render rich messages, and if possible a second client that cannot. Compare `master` and this branch with the same chat.
- **Steps to run:**
  1. On `master`, start the Telegram channel and ask the bot for a short markdown reply with a heading, a quote, and a 2-column table.
  2. Check the same reply on this branch with `rich_messages` omitted or `false`.
  3. Set `rich_messages = true` on the alias, restart the channel, and ask again.
  4. Ask for a table with 21 columns.
  5. Send the bot a rich message that has no plain `text` field, if the client can do that.
- **Expected on this branch (after):** With the flag off, the table is a monospaced block and the rest is HTML. With the flag on, the heading, quote, and 2-column table render as rich content. A 21-column table stays fenced as code. A rich-only inbound message is answered instead of ignored. If `sendRichMessage` fails, the reply still arrives as HTML.
- **Prior behavior on `master` (before):** The same table is inline pipe text, and a long reply can split it. There is no `rich_messages` key. A rich-only inbound update is not read as the user message.

### How I tested

Rebased onto current `master` (`5162ca01b`) and rechecked the channel and config crates. No live Telegram client was available. Workspace clippy, `cargo nextest`, and the release builds were not re-run after the rebase.

```sh
cargo +1.98.0 test -p zeroclaw-config -p zeroclaw-channels --lib -- rich_
cargo +1.98.0 test -p zeroclaw-channels --lib -- table_i
cargo +1.98.0 clippy -p zeroclaw-channels -p zeroclaw-config --all-targets -- -D warnings
```

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** The unit tests cover table wrapping, currency and image rewriting, wide-table fencing, protected splits, inbound rich-message projection, and the `rich_messages` default. Clippy on `zeroclaw-channels` and `zeroclaw-config` covers the new Rust. GitHub CI still needs to run the workspace lint, full test, and release jobs.
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** GitHub CI on the rebased branch was not watched from here. The live Bot API, a real Telegram client, the macOS and Windows release builds, and the 32-bit check were not run.
- **Commands run and tail output:**

```text
cargo +1.98.0 test -p zeroclaw-config -p zeroclaw-channels --lib -- rich_
test result: ok. 8 passed (zeroclaw-channels); 1 passed (zeroclaw-config)

cargo +1.98.0 test -p zeroclaw-channels --lib -- table_i
test telegram::tests::telegram_markdown_to_html_wraps_table_in_pre ... ok
test telegram::tests::split_keeps_markdown_table_intact ... ok

cargo +1.98.0 clippy -p zeroclaw-channels -p zeroclaw-config --all-targets -- -D warnings
Finished `dev` profile [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s) in 1m 12s
```

- **Beyond CI, what did you manually verify?** Nothing against api.telegram.org or a Telegram client. Not verified: native rendering, the HTML fallback after a rejected `sendRichMessage`, draft finalize against a real chat, or client-specific unsupported-message placeholders.
- **Visual interface evidence:** `N/A`
- **Tested revision, interface, and evidence path:** `24946811c` on `feat/telegram-rich-messages`, rebased onto `e8d2e5fc8`. Evidence is unit-test assertions on the HTML and markdown strings, the live-config read, the rich HTML resume, and rich-only unauthorized updates. Not a Telegram client.
- **Screenshot or exact-output evidence:** None. No Telegram client was exercised.
- **Action or changed state and observed result:** The automated tests assert the prepared markdown and HTML. They do not show how a client paints the message.
- **If any command was intentionally skipped, why:** Full `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets` and `cargo nextest run --locked` were not repeated after the rebase. `cargo build --profile ci` was skipped because that job needs `clang` and `mold`. `cargo audit` and `cargo deny` were skipped because dependencies did not change.

## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? (`No`)
- New external network calls? (`Yes`)
- Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? (`No`)
- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? (`No`)
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? (`Yes`)
- If any `Yes`, describe the risk and mitigation: With the flag on, final replies call `sendRichMessage` on the same Bot API base URL and bot token the channel already uses. A failed rich send falls back to `sendMessage`. Inbound updates that contain only `rich_message` are projected to plain text and then follow the existing allowed-peer path, so a rich body is not a new trust boundary. The projection is lossy markdown, not executed HTML.

## Compatibility (required)

- Backward compatible? (`Yes`)
- Config / env / CLI surface changed? (`Yes`)
- Rust/MSRV/toolchain floor changed? (`No`)
- If backward compatibility is `No` or either surface/floor question is `Yes`: exact upgrade steps for existing users: No upgrade is required. Existing aliases load with `rich_messages = false`. To opt in, set `rich_messages = true` under `[channels.telegram.<alias>]` and restart the channel. Even without that, markdown tables in Telegram replies now go out as preformatted text instead of inline pipe characters.

## Rollback (required for medium/high-risk PRs)

Low-risk aside from the always-on table formatting change. Reverting this commit restores the previous HTML path.

- **Fast rollback command/path:** revert this commit, or set `rich_messages = false` to leave the rich API unused. Revert is required to restore the old inline table formatting.
- **Feature flags or config toggles:** `channels.telegram.<alias>.rich_messages` (default `false`)
- **Observable failure symptoms:** Log lines `Telegram sendRichMessage failed; falling back to HTML` and `Telegram finalize_draft rich edit failed; falling back to HTML`. Users then see the HTML fallback. If a later draft delete fails, the existing path logs `Telegram finalize_draft delete failed; skipping sendMessage to avoid duplicate` and does not post a second copy.

prs.title: feat(runtime): bind cron main jobs to the conversation they were created from (RFC #6954, 2b/3)
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master`. **Stacked on #11438**, which adds the port and the channel conversation owner this PR consumes. Until that merges, its commits show here first; the last commit is this PR. Draft until #11438 and the holding-crate exception #11440 have merged.
- **What changed and why:**
  - **The bug (#6105).** A reminder scheduled from a chat ran with no knowledge of that chat, and the chat never learned what the reminder said: the next message ("did you remind me?") reached an agent with no trace of it. `session_target = "main"` was documented as reusing "the primary session", but no such session exists. The path it named (`PathBuf::from("main")`) was only ever used as a memory session id.
  - **What `main` means now.** The conversation the job was created from. This is the clarification @Audacity88 asked for on #6105 ([comment](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/issues/6105#issuecomment-5893174404)): the RFC's "main interactive session" wording was too narrow, the binding must be runtime-owned, scoped to the owning agent and conversation, persisted with the job, never taken from tool arguments, and separate from delivery and permissions.
  - **What #11438 provides.** A surface declares the conversation it is serving around each turn, and publishes an owner that reads and writes that agent's conversations through the surface's own locks, cache and store. For channels, the owner serves a conversation only on a channel route its agent serves.
  - **Cron side (`zeroclaw-runtime`).** `cron_add` records the conversation for a `main` agent job in a new nullable `cron_jobs.conversation_binding` column, written in the same `INSERT`. It is not a field of `CronJob`, so it is not serialized to tools, the API, or RPC. Each run decides once, before it executes, what it does about that conversation, so what it loads and what it records cannot disagree. A completed run appends one exchange: the job's message, prefixed `[cron:<id> <name>]`, and the reply.
  - **Single-shot `agent::run`.** `AgentRunOverrides.bound_history` places the loaded history between the system prompt and the run's own message. Post-run skill creation and review look only at what the run itself did.
- **Rules that keep the binding from becoming access.** These go beyond the RFC text and are the part I would most like reviewed:
  - *Manual runs.* A manual run returns the job's output to whoever triggered it. It uses the conversation only when the trigger is a `cron_run` call made from that same conversation. From anywhere else (the gateway, RPC, the CLI, another conversation) the job runs unbound.
  - *Edits.* A patch that changes what the run is told, what it may use, or where its output goes (`command`, `prompt`, `name`, `delivery`, `model`, `allowed_tools`, `uses_memory`, `session_target`), compared by value, removes the binding unless it is made from the bound conversation. The test is part of the `UPDATE` statement itself. The editing conversation travels on `CronJobPatch.edited_from`, which is `#[serde(skip)]` and set only by `cron_update` from its turn. Every other caller leaves it unset, so the default is to unbind. Declaring an existing job in configuration also removes its binding.
  - *Ownership.* The binding is honoured only when the run executes under the agent the job is stored under, and only through an owner that serves the recorded route.
- **Degrade, never substitute.** A `main` job with no recorded conversation runs as it does today, without conversation context, and records `not_bound`. That covers jobs declared in configuration, jobs created outside a channel conversation, jobs that predate this change, and jobs switched to `main` by `cron_update`.
- **`persistence` values.** `not_bound`, `persisted`, `failed`, and one addition to the RFC's vocabulary, `skipped`: the run had its conversation but left nothing to record, because it failed or deliberately said nothing (`NO_REPLY`, or an empty reply). It mirrors the delivery axis's `skipped`. Without it, a quiet five-minute job would either flood the conversation with `NO_REPLY` exchanges or report an append that did not happen. If you would rather keep three values, tell me which one a quiet run should report.
- **Scope boundary:** Channels only. Conversations on the gateway, RPC, ACP and the CLI are not bound; `main` jobs created there degrade. The port is built so those surfaces can publish an owner later. No change to delivery, to `cron_runs` beyond the values above, or to how unbound jobs run.
- **Blast radius:** agent cron jobs with `session_target = "main"` created by `cron_add` during a channel turn after this lands. Those runs carry the conversation's history, so their prompts are larger. Existing jobs have no binding and are unaffected.
- **Linked issue(s):** Related #6954. Related #6105 (left open for maintainers to verify, as requested there). Related #10425 (slice 1). Related #10557 (the cron files here move with that extraction). Holding-crate exception: #11440.
- **Labels:** to be snapshotted after the labelers run.

### What this does, simply

Ask the assistant in a chat to remind you of something, and the reminder now belongs to that chat. When it fires, the assistant knows what you were talking about, and afterwards the chat contains what the reminder said, so "did you remind me?" gets a sensible answer. Reminders set up any other way behave as before.

### Where each path stands

| Where a `main` agent job comes from | Bound? |
| --- | --- |
| `cron_add` during a channel turn | Yes, to that conversation |
| `cron_add` in a gateway, ACP or CLI turn | No |
| Gateway API, RPC, CLI `cron add` | No |
| `[cron.<id>]` in configuration | No (and declaring an existing job removes its binding) |
| A job switched to `main` by `cron_update` | No |

| How a bound job runs | Uses the conversation? | `persistence` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Scheduler (poll loop, start-up catch-up) | Yes | `persisted`, or `skipped` for a failed or quiet run |
| `cron_run` from the same conversation | Yes | same |
| `cron_run` from another conversation; gateway and RPC manual triggers | No | `not_bound` |
| A scheduled or in-conversation run when the agent's channels are not serving, the channel now belongs to another agent, or the history cannot be read or written | No | `failed` |

Every execution path records through one of two functions, `execute_and_persist_job` (scheduler poll and start-up catch-up) and `run_manual_job_inner` (gateway `handle_api_cron_run`, RPC `handle_cron_trigger`, `cron_run`), and both are covered.

### Known limits

- **A run that finishes while a channel turn is in progress** in the same conversation lands between that turn's message and its reply. Nothing is lost, and the conversation then reads as two interleaved exchanges, as it does when two channel turns overlap. A `cron_run` made from the conversation always lands inside the turn that called it.
- **Run outputs stay agent-scoped.** `cron_runs` (run outputs) and `cron_list` (`last_output`) show a job's output to any conversation of the same agent, as they do today. A bound job's output can now draw on its conversation, so that existing visibility carries more than it did.
- **Durable writes.** On SQLite an exchange lands in one transaction, and a read error is reported, never read as an empty conversation. The JSONL session store has no transactions: there an exchange is appended one message at a time and taken back on failure, best effort. On either store a failed write is followed by a read-back under the same lock, and the cache mirrors exactly what the transcript kept, so a `failed` run never leaves the cache and the transcript in disagreement. This settles the non-blocking warning from the #11438 review.
- **At-least-once.** A daemon killed after the append and before the run record is written leaves the exchange in the conversation without a `cron_runs` row, and the job may run again. Delivery has the same window today.
- **Start-up.** The scheduler and the channels start independently. For the first 60 seconds after the scheduler starts, a scheduled run of a bound job waits for the agent's channels to come up. If they take longer, a job that was overdue at start-up runs without its conversation and records `failed`.
- **Not covered by a test:** owner publication inside `start_channels` itself (#11438). The end-to-end test publishes the same owner type over a test context.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test

- **Reviewer testing requested?** Yes, if you have a channel to hand.
- **Interface(s) exercised:** a channel conversation, `cron_add`, the scheduler, `cron_runs`.
- **Setup / preconditions:** a daemon with one agent on any channel, with `cron_add` available to it.
- **Steps to run:** in the chat, ask for a reminder a minute or two ahead and check the agent calls `cron_add` with `session_target = "main"`. Wait for it to fire. Then ask in the same chat what the reminder said.
- **Expected on this branch (after):** the follow-up answer refers to the reminder; `cron_runs` shows `persistence: "persisted"` for the run.
- **Prior behavior on `master` (before):** the agent has no record of the reminder in that conversation; `persistence` is always `not_bound`.

### How I tested

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** Rust lint and test jobs cover the runtime and channels crates; the parallel runtime gate covers the process-wide registry under 16 threads; Docs Style covers the Markdown.
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** no test runs `start_channels` end to end (see Known limits). `agent::turn::provider_call::streaming_fallback_tests::non_stream_cancellation_keeps_prior_rejected_reliable_attempt` fails intermittently in the parallel gate on my machine (not in the run reported below); it fails the same way on a tree without this change (1 of 3 runs) and is not touched here.
- **Commands run and tail output:** (head `82eebba6a6`, stacked on #11438 at `1c637b9bc1`, with `master` merged at `afc47d333c`)

```sh
cargo fmt --all -- --check                                   # exit 0
cargo clippy -p zeroclaw-api -p zeroclaw-infra -p zeroclaw-runtime -p zeroclaw-channels --tests --no-deps -- -D warnings   # exit 0
RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo doc --no-deps -p zeroclaw-api -p zeroclaw-infra -p zeroclaw-channels   # exit 0
cargo test -p zeroclaw-api -p zeroclaw-infra --lib
#   zeroclaw-api:      test result: ok. 282 passed; 0 failed
#   zeroclaw-infra:    test result: ok. 318 passed; 0 failed
bash scripts/ci/parallel_runtime_test_gate.sh                # 3 runs each, 16 threads
#   zeroclaw-runtime:  test result: ok. 5473 passed; 0 failed; 8 ignored   (x3)
#   zeroclaw-channels: test result: ok. 1979 passed; 0 failed; 2 ignored   (x3)
#   (a first attempt failed once in observability::tests::broadcast_hook_receives_events_from_factory_observer, not touched here; the full gate then passed three times)
bash scripts/ci/comment_hygiene_gate.sh                      # Comment hygiene gate passed.
bash scripts/ci/docs_quality_gate.sh                         # no prose em-dashes; markdownlint not installed locally
```

The same clippy, api/infra and channel gates pass on the merge result with current `master` (`e654b4b73f`), after `cargo test --no-run` of the four crates.

The three tests Audacity88 asked for on #6105:

- **The original sequence**, `reminder_scheduled_from_a_channel_conversation_is_visible_to_its_next_turn` (`zeroclaw-channels`). Real pieces end to end: a channel turn in which the model calls `cron_add`, the real scheduler loop running the job when it comes due, a second turn in the same conversation that sees the job's message and reply as one contiguous exchange, and a third turn that calls `cron_run` from inside the conversation. The job's model is a local HTTP stub that records what it was sent.
- **An unbound `main` job**, `main_job_without_a_recorded_conversation_is_not_bound`: with a surface serving the agent and another conversation in it, the run resolves to no conversation, records `not_bound`, and writes nothing.
- **A concurrent interactive turn**, in #11438: `bound_exchange_survives_a_concurrent_channel_turns_trim_resync` and `bound_exchange_is_contiguous_and_visible_to_the_next_channel_turn`. An exchange appended while a channel turn is in flight survives that turn's post-trim resync, cache and durable transcript agree afterwards, and both turns are kept. The third turn of the sequence test above exercises the same thing live: `cron_run` appends its exchange in the middle of the turn that called it.

Others, by what they pin:

- *Capture:* a `main` job records the conversation it is created from and exposes it in neither the tool's answer nor `cron_list`; an `isolated` job, a job created outside a conversation, and a turn serving another agent record nothing; tool arguments named like a binding are ignored.
- *What a run saw is what it records:* a run that started without its conversation never writes to it, even if the surface has come up by the time it ends; a surface restarted mid-run is written through its successor, and not at all when none is serving; unreadable and unwritable histories record `failed`; failed and quiet runs record `skipped` and leave the conversation untouched.
- *No access through a job:* a manual run uses the conversation only when triggered from it (outside any conversation, from another conversation, and from the same key under another agent all resolve unbound); a redirecting edit from outside the conversation unbinds, for every field in the list; the same edit from within keeps the binding; pausing, rescheduling and re-sending unchanged values keep it; the same key on another route is another conversation; `edited_from` in tool arguments is ignored; declaring the job in configuration unbinds it; a job claimed by another agent does not reach that agent's conversation under the same key. (The owner's own refusals, by route, are tested in #11438.)
- *What the run is sent:* a trailing unanswered message in the loaded history is kept and the run's message is joined to it, so no request carries two user messages in a row. (What the channel owner hands over is tested in #11438.)
- *Agent loop:* bound history sits between the system prompt and the run's message, whole; post-run skill steps see only the run's own messages.

The end-to-end tests were checked against a broken build: with the conversation scope removed from the channel turn and the history not handed to the run, the sequence test, the cron end-to-end test, and #11438's scope test all fail.

- **Beyond CI, what did you manually verify?** Read every path that runs a cron job (scheduler poll, start-up catch-up, gateway `handle_api_cron_run`, RPC `handle_cron_trigger`, `cron_run`) to confirm each goes through one of the two recording functions; every writer of `cron_jobs` (`add_*`, declarative sync, `update_job_inner`, ownership recovery, rename) for what it does to the new column; that tool execution runs inside the turn's task, so the task-local reaches `cron_add`, `cron_update` and `cron_run`. **Not verified:** a live channel on a deployed daemon.
- **Visual interface evidence:** N/A (no interface change).

## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? No
- New external network calls? No
- Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? No
- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? No. The new column stores a channel route and history key, which include channel sender identifiers, in `data/cron/jobs.db`. The same identifiers already key the session store on the same host.
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? Yes. A bound run's model now sees the bound conversation's history, and later channel turns see the run's reply. Both stay within one agent and one conversation, under the rules above.

## Compatibility (required)

- Backward compatible? Yes. The column is nullable and added with `add_column_if_missing`; an older binary on the same database ignores it.
- Config / env / CLI surface changed? No
- Rust/MSRV/toolchain floor changed? No
- Tool descriptions: `session_target` in `cron_add` and `cron_update` now says what `main` does.
- Run records: `persistence` can now be `persisted`, `skipped` or `failed`.

## Rollback (required for medium/high-risk PRs)

`git revert <sha>`. The column stays in existing databases and is ignored.

prs.title: fix(security): share one JWKS fetch among concurrent token checks
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master`. Targets **v0.8.7**.
- **What changed and why:**
  - The JWKS validation in the `oidc.<alias>` provider (#10255) refused a valid token as `Misconfigured` (`-32012 Authentication is misconfigured on this daemon (fail closed)`) when the token was checked while another check was fetching the JWKS.
  - **Cause:** when the key cache isn't fresh, `verify_jwks` calls `refresh_jwks_bounded`. It claims the refresh cooldown *before* the network fetch, so that bad tokens can't cause fetch storms. A second check arriving during that fetch found the cooldown claimed and got `Ok(false)`, "no refresh ran". `verify_jwks` maps that to `Misconfigured`, even when the cache still holds the token's key and has only passed its TTL.
  - **When it happens:**
    - on every fresh provider: the daemon builds one at start and at every config reload, with an empty cache;
    - at every cache expiry (`JWKS_CACHE_TTL`, 5 minutes), whenever requests arrive together.
  - **Effect seen:**
    - The web dashboard, signed in over OIDC, sends its reconnect and session checks together right after a config reload. One fetched the keys and the rest were refused, so the gateway ended the signed-in session and the user had to sign in again.
    - This happened in 2 of 8 reloads in a browser run against Keycloak, and one run logged four refusals in the same millisecond.
  - **The fix:**
    - The fetch runs on its own task and reports how it ended through a `watch` channel kept on the provider.
    - A check that finds a fetch in flight waits for it and gets its result, then reads the refreshed cache as before. Only one fetch runs at a time.
    - A check can find the cache stale but reach the refresh only after another fetch has already ended. It now uses the refreshed cache rather than being refused by that fetch's cooldown. It is still refused when the cache stays stale, after a failed fetch.
- **Scope boundary:**
  - **Unchanged:**
    - the cooldown, including its claim before the network call: an unknown `kid` still triggers at most one fetch per window;
    - the cache TTL;
    - failure handling: a failed fetch still denies every check that waited for it as `Misconfigured`;
    - introspection.
  - **Not added:** no grace for a key whose cache has expired. A waiter never falls back to the old key set; it waits for the fetch and uses its result.
  - **Refactor:** `discovery()`'s body became the free function `discover` so the detached fetch can run it. The fetch uses the provider's own HTTP client (a clone of `self.http`).
- **Blast radius:**
  - Every OIDC bearer verification with `validation = "jwks"`: RPC/WSS auth, gateway bearer auth, dashboard sign-in re-verification.
  - A check that used to be refused during a fetch now waits for that fetch. The wait is bounded by the fetch's own HTTP timeouts: 15 s per request, so up to about 30 s on a provider whose discovery isn't cached yet (discovery, then the JWKS).
  - A fetch now always runs to its end, even when the check that started it is dropped. It is one spawned task per fetch, at most one at a time per provider.
- **Linked issue(s):** Fixes #11902.

### What this does, simply

To check a sign-in token offline, the daemon downloads the identity provider's public keys and keeps them for five minutes. When several requests arrived while that download was running, only the request that started it got an answer. The others were told the daemon's authentication was misconfigured, though nothing was wrong. This happened most often right after the daemon started or reloaded its configuration, when every request needs the keys at once: a signed-in dashboard could be signed out by a simple config reload.

Now requests that arrive during the download wait for it and then use the keys it brought, including a request that arrives just as the download finishes. A download that fails still refuses everyone, as before. A download keeps going if the request that started it goes away.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** N/A: the new tests reproduce it deterministically. A JWKS endpoint under test control holds each fetch until the test releases it, and a test-only hold point fixes the one interleaving that needs it.
- **To see the symptom by hand:**
  1. Point a daemon at an IdP whose JWKS endpoint answers slowly (a few hundred milliseconds).
  2. Send two requests carrying the same valid bearer token at once, right after start.
  3. On `master` one of them gets `-32012 … misconfigured`.

### How I tested

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** the Rust test jobs run the seven new tests and the existing OIDC provider tests. clippy and fmt cover the touched file.
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** none.
- **New tests** (`security::auth_provider::oidc::tests`):
  - **The setup:**
    - A small TCP endpoint serves the JWKS. It reports each request as it arrives and answers only when the test releases it: with the keys, with a status, or not at all.
    - Each test holds one fetch there, then polls its other checks once. A check that waits for the fetch is still pending; a check refused on the spot is not, which is how `master` fails.
  - `verifications_during_a_jwks_fetch_are_not_refused`: a second check during the fetch, on a cold provider and on an expired cache. It waits, then both are allowed, with one fetch.
  - `a_burst_of_checks_shares_one_jwks_fetch`: 31 checks during a cold provider's fetch. All wait, then all are allowed, with exactly one fetch.
  - `a_failed_jwks_fetch_denies_every_check_waiting_for_it`: an expired cache that still holds the token's key, and a fetch answered 503. The 15 other checks wait; then all 16 are denied `Misconfigured`, with one refresh.
  - `unknown_kids_share_the_fetch_in_flight_then_the_cooldown_holds`:
    - while an unknown `kid`'s fetch is held, 15 more checks with that `kid` wait for it, then all are denied `BadCredential`, with one fetch;
    - 16 more inside the cooldown are denied without a fetch.
  - `a_jwks_fetch_outlives_the_check_that_started_it`: the starting check is dropped while its fetch is held. A check that was already waiting, and one made after the drop, both wait. Once the fetch is answered both are allowed, with one fetch.
  - `a_check_that_saw_the_cache_stale_as_a_fetch_ended_is_not_refused` (multi-threaded runtime), cold and expired:
    - a test-only hold point stops one check right after it finds the cache stale;
    - another check's fetch then completes;
    - the held check, released, is allowed, with one fetch.
  - `a_stalled_key_fetch_denies_every_check_within_the_client_timeout`: the JWKS stalls before its headers, stalls mid-body, or discovery stalls. With the client timeout shortened to 300 ms, the waiting checks are all denied `Misconfigured` within 5 s, with one request.
- **Commands run and tail output** (Linux, at this head):

```sh
cargo fmt --all -- --check                                          # clean
cargo test --locked -p zeroclaw-runtime --lib -- <the seven new tests> --exact
                                                                    # 5 runs: test result: ok. 7 passed; 0 failed
cargo test --locked -p zeroclaw-runtime --lib -- security::auth_provider::oidc::tests
                                                                    # test result: ok. 49 passed; 0 failed
cargo test --locked -p zeroclaw-runtime --lib -- security::        # test result: ok. 378 passed; 0 failed; 1 ignored
cargo test --locked -p zeroclaw-gateway --lib                       # test result: ok. 657 passed; 0 failed
cargo clippy --locked -p zeroclaw-runtime --all-targets -- -D warnings   # clean
```

- **Revert checks:**
  - **The fix reverted** (the test commit alone: `master`'s code plus the test-only hold point): **all 7 fail.**
    - Waiting checks are refused on the spot: "31 of 31 did not wait: Denied { reason: Misconfigured }", and "15 of 15 did not wait" in the failure and unknown-`kid` tests.
    - The held check is refused `Misconfigured`.
  - **Targeted mutations of the fixed code:**
    - a waiting check falls back to its cached key when the refresh fails → only the failed-fetch test fails;
    - the cooldown check removed → the unknown-`kid` test fails ("no fetch during the cooldown": 3, expected 2), and so does the held-check test (a second fetch);
    - one fetch at a time, but run inside the starting check's own future rather than its own task → only the dropped-starter test fails;
    - the freshness re-check removed → only the held-check test fails (`Denied { reason: Misconfigured }`).
- **Visual interface evidence:** N/A. No interface or log change.
- **Unrelated flaky test seen while testing:** `security::auth_provider::enrollment::tests::loopback_listener_skips_a_connection_that_never_sends_a_request` (and its sibling `…gives_up_after_too_many_silent_connections`).
  - It's a paused-clock test over real TCP and fails intermittently on `master`: about 3% of runs alone, and 2 of 10 `cargo nextest` runs of `security::`.
  - This branch doesn't touch `enrollment.rs`. Under `cargo nextest` its `security::` runs had no failures in 10, and alone the test fails at master's rate.
  - Under plain `cargo test`, where the new tests share its process, it fails more often.
- **If any command was intentionally skipped, why:** the full workspace `cargo test` is left to CI.

## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? No
- New external network calls? No. Same discovery and JWKS requests, now made from a spawned task and never in parallel.
- Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? Token verification timing only. Acceptance rules are unchanged: no stale-key grace, a failed fetch fails closed, and the unknown-`kid` cooldown is unchanged.
- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? No
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? No

## Compatibility (required)

- Backward compatible? Yes.
- Config / env / CLI surface changed? No
- Rust/MSRV/toolchain floor changed? No

## Rollback (required for medium/high-risk PRs)

`git revert` of the two commits. Without the fix, concurrent checks during a JWKS fetch are refused as `Misconfigured` again. The symptom is `-32012 Authentication is misconfigured on this daemon (fail closed)` on some of several simultaneous requests right after start, a config reload or a cache expiry.

0.2.190

There is now a single config for enabling 64-bit time_t: libc_unstable_time64. This can be set unconditionally; it opts in to 64-bit time_t on the following platforms that use 32-bit by default:

  • 32-bit Linux-GNU
  • 32-bit Linux-uClibc
  • 32-bit Linux-musl. Note that setting this flag also enables some other changes that happend in musl v1.2.
  • 32-bit Windows-GNU
  • ESP-IDF (all targets with this environment are 32-bit)

Most other 32-bit platforms are either already using 64-bit time_t, or are considered legacy and will not be gaining support from their upstream maintainers.

You can enable this using RUSTFLAGS:

RUSTFLAGS='--cfg=libc_unstable_time64' cargo ...

Note that there may still be some changes to features gated by this config option, hence "unstable"

prs.title: fix(infra): make the session store open safe for concurrent first openers
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master`. Targets **v0.8.7**.
- **What changed and why:**
  - When a daemon starts on a fresh data dir, its gateway, channels and RPC plane each open `sessions.db`, within about 10 ms of each other. `SqliteSessionBackend::new` wasn't safe for two first-time openers:
    - SQLite can refuse the switch to WAL with `SQLITE_BUSY` straight away, without waiting out the busy timeout;
    - adding the `session_metadata` columns was check-then-`ALTER` outside a transaction, so the slower opener failed with `duplicate column name`.
  - The open now sets the busy timeout explicitly, retries the WAL switch while it's busy (bounded by the same 5 s), and runs the schema, the column migration and the indexes in one IMMEDIATE transaction. A later opener waits for the first one and then finds every column already there.
  - The daemon built the RPC context with `make_session_backend(..).ok()`. When that open failed, the error was dropped without a log line, and every `session/*` RPC method answered `-32603 Session persistence is disabled` until the next restart. The daemon now logs each failure at ERROR, retries once after 250 ms, and logs the outcome.
- **Scope boundary:**
  - No change to the session schema, to the stored data, or to any other caller.
  - The gateway's own open still logs at WARN and continues without a store if it fails. With the open fixed, that path is no longer reached by this race.
  - Opening the store once per daemon and sharing it is a larger design question and isn't attempted here (see #9600).
- **Blast radius:**
  - Every `SqliteSessionBackend` opener: the gateway, channels and the daemon's RPC context, all through `make_session_backend`.
  - A second opener now waits for the first one's schema transaction (milliseconds) instead of failing.
  - A failed RPC store open now delays daemon start by 250 ms before the retry.
- **Linked issue(s):** Fixes #11898. Related #9600.

### What this does, simply

ZeroClaw keeps conversation sessions in a SQLite file. When the daemon starts for the first time on a new data directory, several parts of it try to create that file at the same moment. The setup code assumed it was alone, so sometimes one part lost the race and gave up. The daemon's RPC plane then kept running without any session storage, without saying so: signing in still worked, but listing, reading or writing sessions failed until the daemon was restarted.

This PR makes the setup code safe when several openers arrive together: the second one waits for the first and then uses the finished database. It also makes the RPC plane report a failed open loudly and try once more, instead of silently running without storage. Daemons whose data dir already exists are unaffected, because the race only exists while the database is being created.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** N/A: the new unit test reproduces the race deterministically enough (fails on `master` at the first trial), and the end-to-end form needs disk pressure to show up.

### How I tested

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:**
  - the Rust test jobs run the new `zeroclaw-infra` test and the new daemon tests;
  - clippy and fmt cover the touched files.
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** none for the unit tests. The end-to-end symptom depends on timing and is covered by the manual run below.
- **Commands run and tail output:** (on Linux, at this head)

```sh
cargo fmt --all -- --check                                    # clean
cargo test --locked -p zeroclaw-infra --lib                   # test result: ok. 313 passed; 0 failed
cargo test --locked -p zeroclaw-infra --lib -- session_sqlite::tests::concurrent_first_openers_of_a_fresh_store_all_succeed
                                                              # 5 runs: ok each time
cargo test --locked -p zeroclaw-runtime --lib -- daemon::tests  # test result: ok. 100 passed; 0 failed; 1 ignored
cargo clippy --locked -p zeroclaw-infra -p zeroclaw-runtime --all-targets -- -D warnings  # clean
```

- **Revert checks:**
  - **The open fix reverted** (the test commit alone, on `master`): the new test fails at once, in two runs:
    - `trial 0, opener 1: Failed to add session metadata column trim_breadcrumb: duplicate column name: trim_breadcrumb`;
    - `trial 1, opener 3: database is locked`.

    Restored, it passes.
  - **The retry removed** from `open_rpc_session_backend`: both new daemon tests fail. Restored, they pass.
- **Beyond CI, what did you manually verify?**
  - **Before, on `master`:** under disk-sync pressure (two writers calling `fsync` on the same filesystem), 1 of 30 fresh daemon starts answered `session/list` with `-32603 Session persistence is disabled` right after a successful native `initialize`. It still failed 2 s later and was fine after a restart. Without pressure: 0 of 40.
  - **After, on this branch, same harness and pressure:** 0 of 30. Given master's rate of about 1 in 30, this is a smoke check rather than proof; the unit test is the real check.
  - Two threads opening a fresh store through `make_session_backend` on `master` failed one opener in 35 of 100 trials. The errors were `duplicate column name` for seven columns, and `database is locked`.
  - Not verified: macOS and Windows filesystems. The fix uses only SQLite locking, which behaves the same there.
- **Visual interface evidence:** N/A. No user-visible interface state changed. The new log lines are daemon logs.
- **If any command was intentionally skipped, why:** the full workspace `cargo test` was left to CI.

## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? No
- New external network calls? No
- Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? No
- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? No
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? No

## Compatibility (required)

- Backward compatible? Yes. Same schema; existing databases open as before.
- Config / env / CLI surface changed? No
- Rust/MSRV/toolchain floor changed? No

## Rollback (required for medium/high-risk PRs)

Low risk: `git revert` of the three commits. Without the fix, a fresh daemon can again come up without its RPC session store. The symptom is `Session persistence is disabled` from `session/*` until restart; with the runtime commit kept, the log also carries `RPC session store failed to open`.

prs.title: fix(memory): keep keyword recall when the query embedding fails
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master`
- **What changed and why:**
  - In hybrid mode, SQLite recall no longer gives up when the query embedding fails. It logs a warning and returns the keyword results through the same BM25-only path a deployment without an embedder uses. Before, the `?` on the embedding returned before the keyword search ran, `memory_inject` swallowed the error, and the turn ran with no memories.
  - The OpenAI-compatible embedding client now has a 60 s request timeout and a 10 s connect timeout. Before, it had none, so an embedder that accepted the connection and never answered held recall, and the turn waiting on it, indefinitely.
- **Scope boundary:**
  - `search_mode = "embedding"` still returns the error, because it has no keyword results to fall back to.
  - `search_mode = "bm25"` and `embedding_provider = "none"` are unchanged.
  - Qdrant recall still fails on an embedder error, since it has no keyword index; it does get the new timeout through the shared embedding client.
  - This PR does not make recall wait less for a slow but working embedder. Racing the embedding against a short deadline is a separate follow-up.
- **Blast radius:** SQLite memory recall in hybrid mode (the default), and every caller of `OpenAiEmbedding` (`openai`, `openrouter` and `custom:` embedding providers), including store and reindex. All of these embed one text per request, so 60 s leaves ample room.
- **Linked issue(s):** Closes #11896. Related #11893 (touches the same recall lines; whichever lands second rebases).

### What this does, simply

Before every reply, ZeroClaw looks up related memories using two searches: a keyword search and a meaning-based search that needs an embedding model. If the embedding model was down, the code gave up before the keyword search ran, so the agent answered with no memories at all. If the embedding model hung, the agent waited forever. Now a broken embedding model costs only the meaning-based half: the keyword matches still come back, a warning is logged, and a hung request gives up after a minute.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** N/A. The unit tests drive both failure modes directly: a failing embedder, and a local server that accepts and never replies.

### How I tested

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** `cargo test` on `zeroclaw-memory` runs the new tests; clippy and fmt cover the rest.
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** None.
- **Commands run and tail output:**

```text
cargo fmt -p zeroclaw-memory -- --check                              ok
cargo test -p zeroclaw-memory --lib -- <the four embedder-failure tests>
  test result: ok. 4 passed; 0 failed
cargo test -p zeroclaw-memory --lib
  test result: ok. 558 passed; 0 failed; 1 ignored
cargo clippy -p zeroclaw-memory --tests --no-deps -- -D warnings     ok
RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo doc --no-deps -p zeroclaw-memory    ok
```

- **Beyond CI, what did you manually verify?**
  - `hybrid_recall_keeps_keyword_results_when_embedding_fails`: a memory stored and recalled with an embedder that always errors is still found by keyword.
  - `embedding_only_recall_still_reports_an_embedder_failure`: embedding-only mode still returns the error.
  - `an_embedder_that_never_answers_fails_instead_of_hanging`: a local server accepts the connection and never replies, and the request fails on its own timeout (set to 1 s for the test) within a 5 s guard.
  - Negative check: with the old recall code and the old client restored, the two behaviour tests fail.: `hybrid_recall_keeps_keyword_results_when_embedding_fails` fails on the `expect` because recall returns the embedder error, and `an_embedder_that_never_answers_fails_instead_of_hanging` hits its 5 s guard. `embedding_only_recall_still_reports_an_embedder_failure` and `store_degrades_gracefully_when_embedding_fails` pass both before and after, as they should.
  - Not verified: a live self-hosted embedder outage on this branch.
- **Visual interface evidence:** N/A
- **If any command was intentionally skipped, why:** The full workspace test run was skipped because the change is confined to `zeroclaw-memory`.

## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? No
- New external network calls? No
- Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? No
- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? No
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? No

## Compatibility (required)

- Backward compatible? Yes
- Config / env / CLI surface changed? No
- Rust/MSRV/toolchain floor changed? No

## Rollback (required for medium/high-risk PRs)

Low risk: `git revert <sha>`.

- **Observable failure symptoms:** the warning "memory recall: query embedding failed; using keyword results only" shows the fallback in use. An embedding request that runs past 60 s now fails with a reqwest timeout error, where before it waited.

prs.title: fix(providers): keep a quota provider out until its stated reset
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master`
- **What changed and why:**
  - `ReliableModelProvider` now reads a stated reset time from a 429 body (`resets_in_seconds`, or `resets_at` as unix seconds). OpenAI Codex sends this when a subscription seat's rolling window is used up, and the window can last hours.
  - When a reset is stated, the provider's cooldown runs until that time, capped at 6 hours, instead of the 10 s default or the 60 s Retry-After cap. A wrong or stale value therefore cannot sideline a provider for days.
  - A non-retryable (business quota) 429 that states a reset now also sets that cooldown. Today it moves to the next provider but sets no cooldown, so the exhausted provider is asked again on every call until the window resets.
- **Scope boundary:** 429s without a stated reset behave exactly as today, including Retry-After parsing and its 60 s cap, and business quotas without a reset are still tried each turn. Single-provider chains set no cooldown on the non-retryable path, as before. This PR does not change error classification (#11767) or carry response headers into the error (#11768).
- **Blast radius:** provider fallback ordering in `reliable.rs` only, on the four call paths (chat, chat with tools, streaming, streaming with tools). Only a 429 whose body contains one of the two reset keys behaves differently.
- **Linked issue(s):** Closes #11894. Related #11767, Related #11768, Related #10779

### What this does, simply

When a Codex subscription runs out, Codex says when it will be available again, often around two hours later. ZeroClaw ignored that and kept asking Codex first on every message, got the same refusal, then fell back. Each turn paid an extra failed round trip, and the logs filled with the same error. With this change ZeroClaw remembers the stated reset time and goes straight to the fallback until then, never for more than six hours. Nothing changes for providers that don't state a reset time.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** N/A. Reproducing it live needs an exhausted Codex seat; the unit tests below drive the same chain with the real Codex 429 body.

### How I tested

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** `cargo test` on `zeroclaw-providers` runs the new chain-level tests; clippy and fmt cover the rest.
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** None. The change is provider-local and covered by unit tests through the public `chat` path.
- **Commands run and tail output:**

```text
cargo fmt -p zeroclaw-providers -- --check                         ok
cargo test -p zeroclaw-providers --lib -- stated_reset exhausted_seat business_quota_refusal rate_limit cooldown
  test result: ok. 18 passed; 0 failed
cargo test -p zeroclaw-providers --lib
  test result: ok. 1984 passed; 0 failed; 4 ignored   (at 3cc3bdc994; see the openai.rs note below)
cargo clippy -p zeroclaw-providers --tests --no-deps -- -D warnings  ok
RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo doc --no-deps -p zeroclaw-providers ok
```

- **Beyond CI, what did you manually verify?** New tests:
  - `stated_reset_is_read_from_the_quota_body`: parses the Codex body and a `resets_at` body. It returns nothing for a body without either key, or for a reset that is already due.
  - The cooldown test also checks that a stale `resets_at` next to `Retry-After: 30` gives 30 s.
  - `a_stated_reset_sets_a_long_bounded_cooldown`: 7144 s is kept as is, a larger value is capped at 6 hours, and a plain Retry-After of 600 s still caps at 60 s.
  - `an_exhausted_seat_is_skipped_until_its_stated_reset`: across two turns, the primary returning the Codex 429 is called once, and the fallback answers both turns.
  - `a_business_quota_refusal_with_a_stated_reset_is_skipped_until_then`: the same, for a non-retryable quota body with a reset.
  - `a_business_quota_refusal_without_a_reset_is_still_tried_each_turn`: without a reset, the primary is called on both turns and no cooldown is set, matching today.

  Not verified: a live exhausted Codex seat on this branch. The body in the tests is the one we saw from Codex on a v0.8.5 build.
- **Unrelated local failure:** `native_tool_round_flags_reach_stream_and_chat_wires_without_changing_defaults` in `openai.rs` failed in two of three full-suite runs on my machine, once with a refused connection to its local mock server and once on its 5 s timeout. It passed 3 out of 3 when run alone. This PR doesn't touch `openai.rs` or the code that test drives, so I read it as a timing flake under load.
- **Visual interface evidence:** N/A
- **If any command was intentionally skipped, why:** The full workspace test run was skipped because the change is confined to `zeroclaw-providers`.

## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? No
- New external network calls? No
- Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? No
- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? No
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? No

## Compatibility (required)

- Backward compatible? Yes
- Config / env / CLI surface changed? No
- Rust/MSRV/toolchain floor changed? No

## Rollback (required for medium/high-risk PRs)

Low risk: `git revert <sha>`.

- **Observable failure symptoms:** a provider is skipped longer than expected after a 429. The existing "ModelProvider rate-limited; trying next provider" record carries `cooldown_ms`, so the duration taken is visible.

prs.title: feat(memory): embed recall queries with a configurable prefix
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master`.
- **What changed and why:**
  - Instruction-tuned embedding models (Qwen3-Embedding, E5, BGE) are trained to embed a stored passage as-is and a query with an instruction in front, and rank worse than keyword search without it. Memory embedded both sides the same way, so these models could not be used as trained. The issue has measurements from one deployment's own recall path.
  - New `[memory] embedding_query_prefix`, unset by default. When set it is prepended to the recall query, and only the query, at the SQLite recall site and both Qdrant recall paths (`recall`, `recall_for_agents`), through one helper, `embeddings::query_embedding_text`.
  - Store and re-index paths are untouched, so stored vectors do not change and setting or changing the prefix needs no re-embedding.
  - The SQLite embedding cache keys on the text actually embedded, so a prefixed query gets its own cache entry instead of reusing the vector of identical stored text. With no prefix (or an empty one) the embedded text and the cache sharing are exactly as before.
- **Scope boundary:** no trait change, no provider-native query modes (Gemini `task_type`, Cohere `input_type`), no per-route prefix on `[[embedding_routes]]`, no default change. The keyword (BM25) side of hybrid search is unaffected: the prefix only reaches the embedder.
- **Blast radius:** memory recall on the SQLite and Qdrant backends when the option is set; nothing when it is unset. Lucid recalls through its local SQLite store and inherits the behaviour. The prefix is read when the backend is built; a live `refresh_embedder` swap keeps it, and changing the prefix itself takes effect at the next start.
- **Linked issue(s):** Closes #11892.
- **Labels:** to be snapshotted after the labelers run.

### What this does, simply

Some of the best free embedding models want to be told "this is a search question" when they embed a question, and not when they embed the notes being searched. ZeroClaw could not tell them that, so those models found the wrong memories. This adds one setting for that sentence. Nothing changes for anyone who does not set it.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** Optional.
- **Interface(s) exercised:** memory recall (`cli`, `web`, channels alike); no surface-specific behaviour.

prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master`
- **What changed and why:**
  - Issue 10999 asks for the official Discord plugin to be documented under its real package name and proven end to end from a published binary. This adds the operator page and the maintainer runbook for that. It is a draft until the pieces it documents have merged (listed below).
  - `channels/discord.md` gains "Running Discord as a plugin (experimental)": what the host needs, install and bind (`zeroclaw plugin install discord --channel-alias main --egress declared`, or `plugin bind` for an installed package), why the grant is `discord.com` plus `*.discord.gg`, the instance key for the alias `main`, the token through the masked `config set` prompt, turning plugins on, routing `plugin.main` to an agent, a peer group that admits numeric user IDs, what to check once it runs, and a comparison with the built-in channel. A callout warns against giving one bot token to both.
  - `plugins/distributing-plugins.md` gains "Package names and Cargo features": the registry package is `discord`; `channel-discord` is the Cargo feature that compiles the built-in channel; FND-001 and FND-004 say `channel-discord` and `channel-discord.wasm` for what is now the `discord` package. It also tells publishers to keep a package's name, because every instance key derives from it.
  - New `maintainers/plugin-release-acceptance.md`: the acceptance runbook. It covers recording the environment, installing by name, binding, and exercising the plugin. A 14-row evidence template (inbound, outbound, built-in channel idle, negative control, reconnect, shutdown, denied destination and recovery, denied sender, missing platform permission, invalid token, trust policy) is followed by redaction, posting, and cleanup. The page is registered in `SUMMARY.md` and the maintainers index.
- **Scope boundary:** Docs only, English source only; translations follow the normal sync. No edits to FND-001 or FND-004, which are ratified; the distribution guide records the mapping instead. No edits to pages that say release binaries ship without the plugin host, which the #10994 work owns, or to the binding docs #11302 adds.
- **Blast radius:** four existing pages gain a section or a line; one new page.
- **Current prerequisites and merge hold** (the PR remains draft):
  - #11302 is merged; its binding commands, readiness report and linked `binding-a-channel-instance` heading are now in this receiving source.
  - #11303 and #11348 are merged; the documented polling, shutdown and guest-health lifecycle is in public master.
  - #11304's WebSocket-denial record remains a prerequisite. Its current `95dcb66` CI is green, but current review and landing remain separate. #11228's selected host baseline likewise still needs its protected Runtime-owner review and landing.
  - The original [Discord port #161](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw-plugins/pull/161) is merged as `a5fb8292511a11446fe591689dead3285a65fad5`. Its landed tree exactly matches [successful current validation](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw-plugins/actions/runs/38808378778): ten jobs pass, including 65 individually named Discord tests, both Clippy lanes and the Wasm build. Iftekhar’s authorship and the original PR/topic are preserved. It remains `registry = false` against `wit/next`; source landing does not establish package publication or final released-pair acceptance.
  - A compatible published host archive and a separately reviewed released-WIT/Discord registry promotion are required before install by name. Published v0.8.5 lacks the port's required WebSocket contract; current registry/release assets contain no Discord package.
  - The existing functional test of the original Discord port #161 worked and has screenshots, as confirmed during release review. Reuse that working test and visual evidence. The 14-row published-pair template remains blank in this documentation PR; that is not evidence that no Discord test occurred. Map the existing receipts to their tested host/package revisions and fill only genuine remaining published-pair gaps before making a release acceptance claim.
- **Linked issue(s):** Related #10999. Related #7432 (R6).

### Current source reconciliation

Signed `26b216a43451d1860191a6aff4300a685c210c51` normally merges public master `996355b83c403e8e9b8080dff5f9b75cea188459` into the original docs topic. The merge was clean, with no manual source changes: four whole author pages, the original SUMMARY insertion, all master entries and all 14 blank acceptance rows are preserved. The binding anchor comes from already-merged #11302. No #11228 or #11304 feature parent was added.

Root and independent static review checked all 15 added links and their headings against this receiving source. These are source checks, not a built-book or live-command result. #11310 subsequently landed as `266ce2e`; its public signer changes are reconciled as current-master context for the actual tested CI merge. [Automatic Quality Gate 38499975529](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/actions/runs/38499975529) completed with its required gate successful on this head. The current native readback confirms that result; it does not turn static link checks into built-book or live-command evidence; older `25d38658` CI and author-local checks supply no successor execution credit. No local Rust, docs helper or live Discord command was run for this publication.

### What this does, simply

ZeroClaw can talk to Discord in two ways: the Discord support built into the program, or a Discord plugin installed separately that runs in a sandbox and can reach only the servers you allow. This PR explains how to set up the plugin, how it differs from the built-in support, and how maintainers prove the published plugin installs and runs on a released copy of ZeroClaw before telling people it works.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** Optional: read the new section in `channels/discord.md` and the new runbook. The commands can only be run once the dependencies above merge.
- **Interface(s) exercised:** Documentation source review for this PR. The user-confirmed working #161 test and screenshots are credited above; this documentation change adds no new operator CLI or live Discord execution. Exact final released-pair acceptance remains separate.
- **Setup / preconditions:** Read the five changed pages. Live testing needs the exact compatible published host/package pair, dedicated test bot and explicit grants described in the runbook.
- **Steps to review:** Check the binding link and the package/config/egress guidance, then confirm that the evidence template keeps all 14 outcomes and redaction requirements.
- **Expected on this branch (after):** The Discord operator guide and maintainer acceptance runbook are linked from the book; the binding anchor resolves in receiving source.
- **Prior behavior (before):** These operator and acceptance instructions were absent; the earlier topic also lacked the merged binding anchor.


### Follow-up: invalid-token acceptance control

The invalid-token row now requires a syntactically valid invalid or revoked
token entered through the masked prompt. It distinguishes Discord's
authentication refusal from malformed-token rejection during local
configuration. The evidence cells remain blank; this change records no new
live acceptance result.

Validation for `25d38658`:

- Full-file `docs_quality_gate.sh` on the changed runbook: zero lint errors.
- `docs_links_gate.sh` against parent `7b4e389d`: all six collector controls
  passed; no added links.

  the same declared merge and publication prerequisites.

- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** the link gates strip `#fragments`, so anchors are unchecked in CI. I checked them separately (below).

```text
$ BASE_SHA=$(git merge-base origin/master HEAD) bash scripts/ci/docs_quality_gate.sh
No prose em-dashes in changed docs files.

No added HTTP(S) links detected in changed docs lines.

```

- **Beyond CI, what did you manually verify?** Historical author checks follow. Current static source/link preservation is recorded above; the older missing-anchor exception is resolved by the public-master import.
  - Every anchor link in the changed pages resolves against the source headings, except `plugins/index.md#binding-a-channel-instance`, which #11302 adds.
  - `git merge-tree` against the heads of #11302, #11262, #11310, #11311, #11284, #11303, #11304, and #11348: clean.
  - Each runtime claim was checked against `master` source:
    - plugin senders are matched exactly (`plugin_sender_allowed` in `plugin_runtime.rs`);
    - the `channel inbound message` and `reply delivered` records run inside a scope carrying `channel = plugin.<alias>`;
    - `/health` names the component `channel:plugin.<alias>`; on `master` it tracks only the listener, and with #11348 (head `de4f86dca6`) it reads `error` on a failed poll and otherwise follows the plugin's health check, which is what the page states;

    - only a Cranelift build compiles `.wasm`;

The example IDs are placeholders.
